_what: The owner's decision brief: one entry per open register item waiting on the owner's decision, with its question, options, what the build does today, a recommendation and quotes from the design document; then the order to decide in, the groups that share one choice, the conflicts between answers and the ones safe to accept as recommended. Drafted, checked from two sides and merged by a multi-agent pass; tools/build_brief.py renders it and --check holds it to the register and the document.
summary: Of these 93 decisions, you answered 47 on 25–26 September; the build follows them, and the next version of the document takes their edits. 46 are open. 36 come from reading v3.6 and Screens v3 against each other and the build in October; the other 10 were found since: F56 and G43 building the home economy, F55 re-running §13.2's table, G44 in the security briefing, four reading your design handoff, C55 (landscape), D98 (the 390-point frame), D75's camera and one-finger controls and G70 (which raids open a Trace), and two folding it in, C56 (the second epoch's slot, after launch) and C57 (one guard's cone or every one). Answer C45 first: it confirms that your recorded answers stand over the v3.6 text that still contradicts them, and the screens are being built on that. Then the look, as one choice: D89 (surfaces) and D90 (typefaces), with D91 (icons and motion) and D92 (shading), which TD.2's tokens and every screen follow, and with them the handoff's frame: D98, C55 and D75. Then the heist group, G47 and G51 with G48 and C47, before the simulation contract locks (T5.1). F55 decides what the next harness work is. The rest can be answered in any order within their groups.

groups.title: What a raider stakes and a defender gains
groups.note: One choice: how much Starlight passes between the two accounts in a heist. With F39 B the fee is 2% of B(V), C41 B returns it on clean and loud heists and half on a partial, and G37 B pays it to a defender only for a pair's first foil of the day. The passed-on fee then becomes small, so G31's carried-loot share becomes the main defence reward and §13.1's rise in that share is the lever for 'Defenders are paid best'.

groups.title: The base haul B(V) and its inputs
groups.note: F36's value is an output of raidworth.py. It moves with G17's difficulty steps and currency split, F38's roster fill and which raids G20's caps leave paid, and with the fee from F39 and C41. Answer the inputs first, then re-run the model and accept whichever of A, B or C the owner picks with the recomputed number. Fixed figures such as 4,600 or 5,500 should not go into the document before that re-run.

groups.title: Strays and roster fill
groups.note: C42 keeps §11.5's one-in-eight find rate. F38 decides what a found stray costs. Answer them together so §11.5, §14.6 and §9.5 each state one stray rule.

groups.title: Daily and weekly limits on repeatable rewards
groups.note: All four apply §20.3's 'every repeatable reward has caps' to raids. If the recommendations are taken, a player faces up to four limits: the day ceiling (10 × B), 20 paid raids a week, the pair rule once a day, and Renown on the first two heists a day. Friendly heists pay nothing and sit outside all of them. Pick them as one set so §24.12's 'A cap was reached' message can name each limit plainly.

groups.title: Leagues and Renown
groups.note: F40 decides whether Renown is capped or minted. G27 refits the boundaries with tools/league_model.py under that rule. G30's option C (echo Renown) belongs to F40's decision, and its option D (echoes rate the raider but move no Renown) is compatible with any F40 answer.

groups.title: Money, the shop and the season track
groups.note: F41 decides whether a Starglass balance exists. That determines whether G28 sells packs and a 6-Starglass premium track, and whether G32's negative balance is possible. F42 fixes which activities earn stars, and G28's tier price is derived from them.

groups.title: Defence strength and hold bands
groups.note: All three are judged against §13.2's hold bands, and the harness measurements move as each is decided. Settle F33 first, then F35. After both, re-measure before trusting any hold figure quoted for G19.

groups.title: Adopting sim readings as the written rules
groups.note: The shared choice is whether sim/'s tested readings become §7, §8 and §18.3's text. The recommendations change two of them: Delay's reactions (G23 B) and the regrow-time combining rule (G24 B). Ship both in one rule-sheet version bump before launch pins replays. G36's era strengthening reuses G25's reading of 'stronger'.

groups.title: Published pacing tables
groups.note: G22 states what the tables assume and F37 adds the non-raider's floor. Both need the tables regenerated after the economy-core decisions, because the 337–385 and 76–78 day figures were computed on the build's economy.

groups.title: Server cost budget
groups.note: The paid plan is needed from the first heist whatever is chosen. §24.1 then re-derives writes and adds a reads budget from an edge-platform run. G21's rebuild interval and its running Renown total are what that run checks.

groups.title: Matchmaking filters
groups.note: All three state §12.22's candidate filters. The window runs from two below to three above, there is no strength filter, and the build's band and 'recent' definitions stay, with echoes rating the raider. Edit them into §12.22 and §12.3 in one pass.

groups.title: Deletion and retention
groups.note: One privacy model. F43 says what deletion removes and F50 how it survives backups and exports. G39 gives the web route to it. G38 sets how long closed items are kept and G29 how long telemetry is kept. Keep the time limits consistent: 90 days for raw events, 7 days for closed items, 30 days for exports and a 31-day journal replay.

groups.title: Workshop naming
groups.note: Word lists for every age (C43) are acceptable only if the lists are large enough to avoid frequent duplicates, which is G26 B's 64 × 64.

groups.title: Friends and notifications
groups.note: Both change the social surface for 13-to-15 players and the night rule. Invite codes with minors hidden from feeds, and one raid message a day, are independent edits to server/src/notifications.mjs and the feed query.

groups.title: Your recorded answers against v3.6
groups.note: v3.6 took part of one of the 47 answers recorded in September (G28's wording for §18.8) and none of the rest, so a screen can have three sources. C45 asks that the answers stand; F57 is the Shop's case of it.

groups.title: Screens v3's look against §21
groups.note: One choice about the visual language: §21.8 and §21.3 describe paper panels, Baloo 2, flat icons, motion at 150 to 250 ms, one three-step toon and a home layout the designs do not use. Decide the surfaces and typefaces first, then the icons, motion and shading by the same rule (a look goes to the designs, a measured rule stays); contrast (G59) is measured on whichever surfaces win, and the budgets (D93, C52) decide how much of the designs' 3D survives on a phone.

groups.title: The heist, its crew and its result
groups.note: The orders a crew can be given, what the server knows of the crew, and how the result reads and explains itself. They change the replay format, so they are answered before the simulation contract locks (T5.1).

groups.title: What a target shows before the heist
groups.note: All four set what the Observatory, the scout and the planner may show. F46's answer already made scouting free; these say what that free view holds, and G58 the name it shows for a Keeper, one word-list rule at every age.

groups.title: Codex, weaving, the Lab and Sages
groups.note: The rules the Codex, Weaving, the Lab and the Sage hall need before their screens can be built; most are one or two sentences each.

groups.title: Defence: curation, reports and terrain
groups.note: What the defender sees of a raid and how a defence is curated and measured; G57 and G69 share the per-raid facts the server must record, and G70 says which of those raids open a Trace.

groups.title: People, minors and the first session
groups.note: What players see of each other, what protects 13 to 17, and what may come before the first heist.

groups.title: Characters and visitors
groups.note: Births, the visiting Stray and the sheets' details, with the Twinned and the paradox-born under the heist group.

groups.title: Your handoff's frame: scale, orientation and camera
groups.note: Your handoff fixes the phone frame three ways the build does not: the 390-point layout scaled to the device, portrait only, and the design's camera with pinch and twist. Each meets a measured rule: §21.1's 48 points and §23.5's 13, the orientation §23.3 and §24 disagree on, and §20.8's one finger. C44's home is drawn inside whichever frame wins. Answer them with the look, since TD.2's tokens and TD.10's camera follow them.

conflicts.problem: F39 B quotes fees of 48, 72, 820 and 1,845 at Vault levels 1, 2, 8 and 10. Those are 2% of B(V) at the build's 2,400 base. F36 recommends a 4,600 base, which makes the same fees 92, 138, 1,572 and 3,537 (4,600 × 1.5^(V−1) × 0.02). F36's 4,600 was also computed with the build's fee left out, and F36 itself says counting the fee lifts the base to 5,500, so each figure depends on the other.
conflicts.resolution: Decide F39 as a formula (2% of B(V)) and write the fee in the document as that formula, not as fixed numbers. Then fix C41, re-run raidworth.py with the fee counted as F39 B and C41 B define it, and take F36's base from that run.

conflicts.problem: F36 C requires a raid to beat staying home on every day. G20 C deliberately makes every raid after the 20th in a week pay no haul, so an engaged player's raids on days 6 and 7 fail that check by design.
conflicts.resolution: Define F36's check over paid raids only, meaning days when the player still has paid raids left under G20's cap. raidworth.py's binding day should leave out capped raids.

conflicts.problem: G27 A adopts the boundaries Ember 128, Tide 184, Star 300, Nova 644 and Paradox 1,160. F40 shows these are stale even for the build (113, 161, 276, 601 and 1,125 under its own foiled rule), and F40 D's two-a-day rule will move them again.
conflicts.resolution: Adopt G27 A as a method: boundaries fitted by tools/league_model.py to §14.7's shares and regenerated when the rules change. Do not adopt those numbers. Answer F40 first and write in the refitted boundaries.

conflicts.problem: Every G28 option assumes packs of €1 to €50, a premium track costing 6 Starglass, and a free track that gives Starglass. F41 C removes the currency, the packs and the free Starglass.
conflicts.resolution: Answer F41 first. If F41 C is chosen, G28 B keeps its 10-star tier and catch-up, drops the pack list and the free track's Starglass, and prices the premium track as a store product at about €6.

conflicts.problem: G32 B handles refunds with a negative Starglass balance. F41 C abolishes the balance, and its rationale says it removes G32's negative balances, so G32's options have nothing to act on.
conflicts.resolution: If F41 A or B is chosen, G32 B stands. If F41 C is chosen, re-ask G32 as a single question: is a refunded product's item revoked? The recommendation is to revoke that product's entitlement (the analogue of option D), because no balance is left to carry a debt, and refunds otherwise become free items.

conflicts.problem: G28 B keeps a stray on the free season track as a reward. F38 B makes every stray after the first heist's two, the season track's included, wait to be adopted at the birth price, so the track reward would cost Essence.
conflicts.resolution: Choose one wording. Either reword the track reward as 'a stray to adopt' under F38 B, or exempt the one track stray a season from pricing and re-run the birth rate (1.3455) with that exemption.

conflicts.problem: C42 A's rationale settles the full-roster case by having strays wait for a free home, as the model does. That is F38 A's behaviour, and F38 B replaces it with adoption at the birth price.
conflicts.resolution: C42 A's one-in-eight rate stands under any F38 answer. Drop C42's aside, and let F38 alone decide what happens to a found stray.

conflicts.problem: G22 A's spread sentence (Keeper 40 on day 337–385) and F37 B's 76–78 days were computed on the build's economy. F38's rationale puts Keeper 40 on day 306–323 once F36 C, F38 B and F39 B are all adopted.
conflicts.resolution: Answer the economy-core items first, regenerate the pacing tables, and then write G22's spread sentence and F37's day figure from the regenerated run.

conflicts.problem: F44 D edits §12.22 step 5 to say the 0.25 tier is reached by challenge links and friendly heists. F48 B makes those pay no haul, so no payout tier applies to them.
conflicts.resolution: Answer F48 first. Under F48 B, step 5 names only Trace targets and a list whose Keeper filter has widened.

conflicts.problem: F40 D lets only a player's first two validated matchmade heists of the UTC day move Renown. G30 D makes echo raids update the raider's rating while moving no Renown. Neither entry says whether an echo raid uses up one of the two.
conflicts.resolution: Count only heists that actually move Renown, meaning live matchmade raids. Echoes, friendly heists and challenge plays do not use up the two.

conflicts.problem: G21 B is justified by '§24.1's goal that the free tier carries the early game', but F47 finds validation needs the $5 plan from the first heist. G21's side fix, a running Renown total on the standing row, also adds a write to each Renown-moving heist, and F47 A's measured 14 rows a clean heist does not include it.
conflicts.resolution: Keep G21 B, but ground it in G33's reads budget, not in the free tier. Include the running-total write in G33's edge-platform run that re-derives F47's figures.

conflicts.problem: F46 rejects options C and D partly because they exceed '§24.1's five-writes budget', a budget F47 A retires in favour of the measured figure of about 14 rows a heist.
conflicts.resolution: F46 B still stands on fairness and on ward positions, which no option can hide. Measure its lease cost against F47's re-derived budget, not the five-write figure.

conflicts.problem: G19 B cites realm 3's measured hold of 34.4% as inside its 30–45% band. That figure is §13.2's v3.3 table, measured at one guard post (audit_register.py F34). F33's recommendation says realm 3 stays above its band under every option.
conflicts.resolution: Choose G19 B on its law-slot grounds only (level 3's two slots match §5.1's Heart), drop the in-band claim, and re-measure the Heart after F33 and F35.

conflicts.problem: F35's option C text says 1 m, but its recommendation picks C at 0 m: no guard hears the Vault, and the Vault's Sound::Breaking is removed as well. It argues the defender lever is not needed because holds run at 72–100%, measured before F33 D brings 1–3 Glares down to 68–77%.
conflicts.resolution: Record F35 as 'C, reach 0 m' explicitly, since that is a variant of option C. F33 D leaves holds above band, so the 0 m argument survives, but re-check it after F33 is built, with the 1 m timed call as the one-constant fallback.

conflicts.problem: F37 B makes daily goals (about 2 pages a day) a non-raider's main progress source. F42 A's rationale keeps goals off the season track so they never become a daily obligation, and notes goals do not yet run on the server (D64).
conflicts.resolution: Adopt both, and let unclaimed goal pages carry over for a few days so a missed day costs nothing (§19.12). Server-side goals (D64) become a prerequisite for F37 B.

conflicts.problem: F40's old recommendation (D) let only the first two heists of each UTC day move Renown. That is a daily allowance lost if unused, so league placement rewarded playing every day. In the model a player who skips weekends ends in Star or above 11% of the time against 62% for a daily player, and a Saturday-only player never does. §20.3's "No obligations" rules that out, and so does §9.6's week-cap promise that G20 C makes true.
conflicts.resolution: F40 now recommends B: ten Renown heists a week, counted from G20's week start (Monday 00:00 UTC, weekStart in server/src/service.mjs). If G20 moves the week start, F40's count moves with it. The ten are counted apart from G20 C's twenty paid raids. A raid past the twentieth pays no haul, but it still moves Renown if the raider has Renown heists left.

conflicts.problem: The existing F40/G27 entry names D's two-a-day rule as the next change to the boundaries. Under F40 B the scratch refit gives Ember 128, Tide 176, Star 254, Nova 458 and Paradox 806.
conflicts.resolution: G27 A is adopted as a method, as already resolved. Write in the boundaries for whichever F40 option is chosen: 128, 176, 254, 458 and 806 if B is chosen.

conflicts.problem: The existing F40/G30 resolution says echoes, friendly heists and challenge plays do not use up "the two". Under F40 B the allowance is ten a week, not two a day.
conflicts.resolution: The same rule applies to the ten. Count only live matchmade raids that moved Renown. Echoes, friendly heists, challenge plays and a pair's later heists of the day (G37) do not use up the ten.

conflicts.problem: F39 B's option text said the fee is 'returned after a clean heist', which is C41 A's rule, while the brief recommends C41 B (returned after a clean or loud heist, half after a partial). F39's kept-fee shares (32% and 23% of raid Starlight), pacing (Keeper 40 on day 318–323), kept total (2.1 million) and raid-worth bases (2,900; 3,200 and 5,500) were all computed with clean-only return. Under F39 B with C41 B they are about 20% and 14%, day 315–321, 1.3 million, and 2,700; 3,000 and 5,000.

F36.why_it_matters: B(V)'s base is the one dial on the raid faucet, and §32.9 hands it to the model's re-run. The re-run cannot set it: 2,400 fails on the roster the model staffs, and the value that passes depends on which day the check is read and on choices §14.1 and §9.3 leave open. Until one reading is chosen, the base, every haul, the pacing tables in §9.3, §14.2 and §14.3, and §9.6's claim that 2,400 is 'the smallest hundred that passes' are all provisional.

F38.question: How should strays join the roster, given that free strays fill every home as it is built and leave §9.5's birth-rate rule no rate to set?
F38.why_it_matters: §9.5 tunes the birth price so an engaged player's 38th character arrives on the day everything is built. Free strays (one in eight successful heists, plus one per season) fill each home as soon as it opens, so the 38th arrives with the last Hearth level whatever a birth costs. The shipped 1.3265 is not tuned to anything, and the birth row's 'day 378 today' is false. The Nursery's law-weighted births also shape almost none of the roster, and the birth curve §32.9 derives as an Essence sink barely runs.

F39.question: What should the entry fee be keyed to, now that 2% of a saving player's Starlight costs more than raids bring in?
F39.why_it_matters: §14.1's player saves for the next Spire level, and the last three Spire levels cost 249,400, 548,800 and 1,207,300. A fee of 2% of what the player holds therefore grows to 14,000–24,000 a raid while hauls pay a few thousand. By §9.6's own test (a raid that pays less than staying home is skipped), a saving player should stop raiding, which neither the model nor the pacing tables assume. The raid-worth check also leaves the fee out.
F39.today: server/src/economy.mjs entryFee() (line 158) charges min(clamp(2% × held Starlight, 100, 25,000), held). server/src/service.mjs grant() (line 564) computes it at line 580 (none for a Trace, a friendly heist or a challenge), debits it at line 581, and returns it only after a clean heist (lines 618–619). The economy model's entry_fees() (tools/economy_model/model.py line 683) charges the same and keeps (1 − success rate × 0.35) of it. rerun.CHOICES shows that removing the fee moves Keeper 40 from day 357 to day 318.

Under the build's reading no player §14.1 models ever reaches either cap, so the promise is false.

F41.question: Is Starglass a currency sold in packs, or are cosmetics and the season pass priced in real money, with Starglass kept only as the gift wrapper §19.12 describes?
F41.why_it_matters: §19.12 and §27.2 say every cosmetic is priced in real money and Starglass is only a gift and season-pass wrapper. §9.1, §9.5 and §22.1 make it a general currency: sold in packs, given free on the season track, and the only way to pay for cosmetics. Until one reading wins, the shop, the purchase flow, the free track's rewards and the §20.2 caps are built against a rule the document contradicts. The 1:1 rate has no defined target either: every written price is in euros, but Brazilian players (§20.6) pay in reais at the stores' own local prices.
F41.today: The server treats Starglass as a currency. server/src/shop.mjs keeps it in the ledger in hundredths of a euro (1 Starglass = €1 = 100 units) and sells five packs (starglass-1, -5, -10, -20, -50). The €1 and €50 ends come from §22.1 through tools/design_facts.py STARGLASS_PACKS_EUR; the €5, €10 and €20 packs are shop.mjs's own. A purchase intent enforces §20.2's €25 and €50 monthly caps, counted in each pack's euro list price, before the store is asked; a store receipt that arrives with no intent (a restore, a family approval) is still honoured. The monthly summary is reported in 'EUR'. Starglass buys cosmetics from src/cosmetics.json (empty, D64) and the premium track at PREMIUM_PRICE = 600 (server/src/track.mjs). The free track gives 25 units at tiers 10, 20, 30 and 40, one Starglass a season. Receipts are checked by stores.mjs receipts(), which server/src/main.mjs wires in as verifyReceipt. App Store transactions are checked against pinned Apple roots (RULEBORN_STOREKIT_ROOTS, RULEBORN_BUNDLE_ID). Play purchases are checked against the licence key and consumed through googleapi.mjs (RULEBORN_PLAY_PACKAGE, RULEBORN_PLAY_LICENCE_KEY, RULEBORN_PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT). A store left unconfigured refuses every receipt. The client has no shop screen.

options.label: Keep the build: a euro-pegged currency
options.means: Starglass is a currency and 1 Starglass = €1, stored in hundredths. Packs of €1, €5, €10, €20 and €50 are the only things bought with money. Cosmetics, gifts and each season's premium track (6 Starglass) are bought with Starglass. The free track gives 1 Starglass a season. A non-euro store charges its own local price for each pack, and Starglass prices still read as euros.
options.consequences: Players buy a balance and then spend it. §19.12's own evidence ([156]) finds this raises spending even at 1:1. 'Every cosmetic shows its real-money price' is true only for players in euro stores. Pack sizes leave remainders (the €5 pack does not buy a 6-Starglass pass). A 13-to-15-year-old can never buy the €50 pack under the €25 cap. A refund after the Starglass is spent can leave a negative balance (G32). The free track hands out €1 of spending power a season to every player who reaches tier 40, which comes to one premium track every six seasons. A gift is cheap to build: Starglass spent on an item granted to a friend, all on the server. §22.2's revenue assumptions do not change.
options.numbers: 1 Starglass = 100 ledger units (shop.mjs). Packs €1/5/10/20/50 (shop.mjs PACKS). Premium track 600 units = €6 (§22.1, PREMIUM_TRACK_EUR). Free track 4 × 25 = 100 units = 1 Starglass a season (track.mjs tierRewards), so six seasons buy one €6 pass. Monthly caps €25 and €50 (§20.2).

Change §27.2's Currency row to match. §22.1: list the five packs. §9.1 and §9.5 stay as they are.

So both rows are reworded, and §19.12's cross-reference '(9.1, 22.1)' becomes '(9.1, 22.4)', because §22.1 no longer lists Starglass. There are no leftover balances or remainders, a refund takes back one item (G32), and §20.2's caps are checked item by item. The developer maintains one store product per cosmetic and per season's pass in both store consoles. §22.4's gifts become store purchases granted to another account, which is more work than A's server-side gift from a balance. Free-track Essence rises from 20,000 to 22,000 a season, as in B.
options.numbers: Premium track about €6 (§22.1). Free-track Essence 22,000 a season (tiers 10 to 40 at 500 each, track.mjs). Caps €25 and €50 (§20.2).

options.build_change: shop.mjs: replace PACKS with one product per catalogue item and per season's premium track. redeem() grants the item, or a premium_tracks row, instead of booking Starglass. Remove spendStarglass and the 'starglass' ledger currency, with a migration for existing rows. track.mjs: buyPremium is paid by a receipt, and tiers 10 to 40 give Essence. tools/design_facts.py drops STARGLASS_PACKS_EUR. Add a gift flow in which a store purchase grants its item to another account (not built).

recommendation.rationale: §19.12 refuses soft-currency pricing on the evidence of [156], §27.2 records the decision as 'Every cosmetic priced in real money', and §22.1 promises every price in real money before purchase. C follows that evidence furthest, but it does not leave §19.12 untouched: the row's own remedy keeps Starglass as a season-pass wrapper at 1:1, and C rewrites that sentence, and §27.2's, to a gift wrapper only. B can show local prices too, but only by keeping a currency and deriving a rate for each store; C is the only option under which the money-illusion rule holds with no currency and no rate, and it removes G32's negative balances. It costs one store product per item and a store-backed gift flow, against A's already-built balance, so the choice rests on the document's ethics, not on saving work.

F42.question: Is the season track's currency called season stars, and which of heists, defences, discoveries and goals earn it?
F42.why_it_matters: §18.2 climbs the track with 'season points' from heists, defences and discoveries. §9.1 calls them 'Season stars', earned from heists, defences, discoveries and goals. A reader cannot tell whether these are one currency, and the source list decides what the track rewards: raiding only, or also the Lab and daily goals. Today the server can verify only heists and defences.
F42.today: server/src/track.mjs calls them season stars and books them only in Track.settle, inside a validated heist's grant. The raider gets 10 × §12.9's Renown multiplier, the defender gets the rest of 10, and an echo's owner gets nothing. Stars count only on a raider's first validated heist on a given defender in a UTC day (server/src/service.mjs, G37). Stars from discoveries and goals are not built: the Lab and daily goals run on the device, and the server cannot check them (D64).

G28.question: Which figures should the season track and the shop ship with: stars earned, a tier's price and catch-up, each tier's rewards, and the packs?
G28.why_it_matters: §18.2, §18.8 and §22.1 give fifty tiers, a pass at about €6 and packs from €1 to €50, but no star amounts, tier price, tier rewards, pack list or cosmetic prices. Without them, the track's pace and what it adds to the economy are undefined. §18.8 also calls the season 'Cosmetic only, on both tracks', while §18.2's free track gives pages, Essence and a stray, all of which count in heists. The economy model includes the season's stray but not the free track's Essence and pages.
G28.today: Each figure is a named constant. server/src/track.mjs: HEIST_STARS = 10, so the raider gets 10 × §12.9's Renown multiplier and the defender the rest of 10; an echo's owner gets none, and a pair moves stars once a UTC day (G37). TIER_STARS = 20 ('a §14.1 regular player's day of clean raids'), and tier 1 costs nothing (§14.8). Track.scaled() sets the price to max(1, round(20 × time left ÷ season)), fixed when a player first appears in a season (server/src/seasons.mjs standing()). Stars are spent on tiers and gone when the season ends. A past season's unclaimed tiers are bought with this season's stars at that season's price. tierRewards(): tier 50 gives a stray; tiers 10, 20, 30 and 40 give 25 units (a quarter Starglass); tiers 5, 15, 25, 35 and 45 give 5 pages; the other 40 tiers give 500 Essence. The premium track gives a cosmetic every fifth tier, cycling through §18.2's six kinds. It costs 600 (€6) and can be bought for a past season at the same price. server/src/shop.mjs: packs of €1, 5, 10, 20 and 50. A league's season-end cosmetic is a realm skin, an outfit is worn by a crew role, and a law visual by a law. premium_tracks records one row per season in place of §24.8's 'season pass expiry'. src/cosmetics.json is empty, and pages and strays exist only as claim rows (D64). tools/economy_model turns on season_strays but has no free-track Essence or pages.

F44.question: Which should change so that normal matchmaking stops offering 0.25-payout targets: the Keeper-level window, the 0.25 tier, or §12.22's claim that the tier is unreachable?
F44.why_it_matters: C13 was closed by §12.22's fifth step, which says the 0.25 payout 'is unreachable through normal matchmaking by design'. But §12.3 and §12.22 admit targets within 3 Keeper levels, and §9.6 pays 0.25 at three or more below, so a target exactly three levels below is offered and pays a quarter. Step 4's widening also drops the Keeper filter. Either the stated intent or the numbers are wrong, and the server follows the numbers.
F44.today: server/src/matchmaking.mjs keeps a target when |target level − raider level| ≤ KEEPER_WINDOW = 3 (facts MATCH_WINDOW (150, 3), which tools/design_facts.py reads from §12.22). server/src/economy.mjs difficulty() pays 0.8 at one below, 0.5 at two below and 0.25 at three or more below; above the raider's level it pays 1.0 plus 0.1 a level, capped at 1.2 (G17). When the band is thin and the list widens (matchmaking.mjs, the widening loop over rating, keeper, renown), the Keeper filter is dropped entirely, so any level can be offered. The generated fallbacks that should fill thin bands first are not built (D66), so widening is common while the player base is small.

options.label: Keep the build: window 3, tier from three below
options.means: Targets within 3 Keeper levels either way. A target exactly three below is offered and pays 0.25. §12.22's fifth step is rewritten to say so.
options.consequences: Raiders can be offered a target that pays a quarter of an at-level haul. It will often be the easiest entry in the list, because a lower-level island predicts higher success. The candidate pool is unchanged, and the 0.25 tier is part of normal play.
options.numbers: Difficulty at three below: 0.25, against 0.5 at two below (§9.6). The pool spans 7 Keeper levels (−3 to +3).
options.doc_edit: §12.22, step 5: replace 'is unreachable through normal matchmaking by design' with 'is reached in normal matchmaking only by a target exactly three levels below, and otherwise by challenge links, friendly heists, Trace targets and a widened list'.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does (server/src/matchmaking.mjs, server/src/economy.mjs).

options.label: Window within 2, both ways
options.means: Targets within 2 Keeper levels either way. The 0.25 tier is reached only by challenge links, friendly heists, Trace targets and a list whose Keeper filter has widened, and step 5 is edited to name that last case.
options.consequences: An unwidened list never offers a quarter-pay target. The candidate pool shrinks to 5 Keeper levels, so thin bands fall back to echoes and widening more often while the player base is small, and each widening can again offer 0.25 targets. Raiders lose targets three above, which paid the same 1.2 cap as two above.
options.numbers: 5 of 7 levels, about 71% of the pool if candidates are spread evenly across nearby levels. Difficulty at +2 and +3 is the same 1.2 cap (economy.mjs, G17).
options.doc_edit: §12.3: 'within 3 Keeper levels' becomes 'within 2 Keeper levels'. §12.22, step 1: 'Keeper level within 3' becomes 'Keeper level within 2'. §12.22, step 5: 'It exists for challenge links, friendly heists and Trace targets' becomes 'It exists for challenge links, friendly heists, Trace targets and a list whose Keeper filter has widened (step 4)'.
options.build_change: tools/design_facts.py MATCH_WINDOW = (150, 2); regenerate server/src/facts.json; re-pin the matchmaking tests.

options.label: Tier from four below
options.means: §9.6's difficulty becomes: level or above 1.0 to 1.2, one below 0.8, two or three below 0.5, four or more below 0.25. The window stays at 3.
options.consequences: A raid exactly three levels below pays twice what it pays today (0.5 instead of 0.25), so farming weaker players pays half an at-level haul rather than almost nothing. The pool is unchanged. The raid faucet rises for those raids, which the economy model does not see, because it assumes same-level targets. Widened lists still reach the 0.25 tier.
options.numbers: Three below: 0.25 becomes 0.5. Pool: 7 levels.
options.doc_edit: §9.6, Difficulty row: 'two below 0.5, three or more below 0.25' becomes 'two or three below 0.5, four or more below 0.25'. §12.22, step 5: 'three or more levels below' becomes 'four or more levels below', and 'It exists for challenge links, friendly heists and Trace targets' gains 'and a list whose Keeper filter has widened (step 4)'.
options.build_change: server/src/economy.mjs difficulty(): three below pays 0.5. tools/design_facts.py DIFFICULTY and its regular expression change, and facts.json is regenerated. tools/economy_model/data.py reads DIFFICULTY.

options.label: Window from two below to three above
options.means: A raider is offered targets from 2 Keeper levels below to 3 above. The 0.25 tier stays at three or more below and is reached only by challenge links, friendly heists, Trace targets and a list whose Keeper filter has widened, and step 5 is edited to name that last case.
options.consequences: An unwidened list never offers a quarter-pay target, and no payout changes. Raiders keep punching up three levels. In an unwidened list a defender can be raided only by players from three below to two above; since a defender loses nothing by default (§9.4), that matters only in the Open Vault league. The pool shrinks less than under B.

It keeps more of the candidate pool than B while the player base is thin, and raiders can still punch up three levels. Defenders lose nothing by default (§9.4), so the new limit on who can raid them matters only in the Open Vault league. Step 5 must also name the widened list, because widening still drops the Keeper filter (D66).

Only then do the filters widen, in order — rating, then Keeper level, then Renown — and ruins fill what remains (12.10).

G31.question: What is a foiled crew's carried loot worth for the defence reward, and which of §13.1's two shares decides when that reward rises?
G31.why_it_matters: §9.4 pays the defender 'the entry fee plus 5% of what the crew was carrying', but a crew carries bag units and nothing gives them a price, so the reward's size is undefined. §13.1's measure names two shares, weekly changers and first-week publishers, and then applies 'Below 15%' as if there were one, so it is unclear which triggers the rise to 20%, or when in a season it is read. The defence reward is also missing from the economy model, so its effect on the faucet is unmeasured.
G31.today: The simulation reports 'left', the bag units a crew took and did not bank (dropped, or held by caught members). server/src/economy.mjs defenceShare() returns nothing when left is 0, and otherwise values them as the clean haul they would have made, before the raider's fatigue and caps, and pays the season's percent of that, half in Essence and half in Starlight. server/src/service.mjs grant() also passes the entry fee to the defender, holds the share to the defender's own §9.6 day and week caps, and pays it once a day per pair (G37). server/src/seasons.mjs defenceMeasure() reads only the first share, over a season's last seven days: a session event counts as active, a publish or island change counts as a change, and seeded accounts are excluded. setDefenceShare() sets the next season's percent at each close (facts DEFENCE_SHARE_RISE (15, 5, 3, 5, 20)). The page for a law cast in a foiled heist waits on casting, which the simulation lacks.

options.label: Keep the build: what was carried, and the weekly share
options.means: Carried loot is priced as the clean haul the unbanked bag units would have made on this island (B(V) × difficulty × richness × fill of what was left), before the raider's fatigue and caps, and paid half in Essence and half in Starlight. §13.1's rule reads the share of players active in a season's last seven days who published a changed defence in them, and sets the next season's share at the close.
options.consequences: A defender earns most for catching a crew after it has loaded, and only the entry fee for stopping one at the door. At 20%, a full-bag foil pays more than an average raid attempt. The minted share is never more than B's figures below. Half is paid in Essence, which §9.1 does not list as coming from defence rewards. One unusual final week can trigger or block a rise.
options.numbers: A full-bag foil at the same Keeper level with richness 1.0: 5% pays 180 at Vault level 2, 911 at level 6 and 4,613 at level 10; 20% pays 720, 3,645 and 18,452 (B(V) from §9.6's table × the share, floored as economy.mjs does). An average raid attempt pays 440 to 611, 2,227 to 3,095 and 11,275 to 15,666 (§9.6). A crew caught before loading pays the fee only (2% of the raider's Starlight, 100 to 25,000, §9.4).
options.doc_edit: §9.4: 'plus 5% of what the crew was carrying' becomes 'plus 5% of the clean haul the crew's unbanked load would have made on this island, before the raider's fatigue and caps, paid half in Essence'. §13, Defending pays: 'A foiled heist gives the defender the raider's entry fee and the mirror of the Renown the raider loses.' becomes '... the raider's entry fee, the share of the crew's unbanked load in 9.4, and the mirror of the Renown the raider loses.' §9.1 Essence 'Earned from': add 'defence rewards'. §13.1: the measure is 'the share of players with a session in a season's last seven days who published a changed defence in them, read at each season's close'; the first-week share is reported, not a trigger.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does (server/src/economy.mjs, server/src/service.mjs, server/src/seasons.mjs).

options.label: Price the island's full haul; weekly share
options.means: Every foiled heist pays the defender the fee plus the share of the clean haul a full crew would have made on this island (fill 1), whatever the crew held when caught. The measure is as in A.
options.consequences: Stopping a crew at the door pays as much as catching it at the Vault, so the reward follows the foil, not the crew's greed, and defenders can predict it. §13's 'Knocked-out raiders leave behind whatever they were carrying' no longer changes the reward. The faucet grows by a fixed amount per foil, and the economy model does not count it.
options.numbers: Every foil pays 180, 911 or 4,613 at 5% (Vault 2, 6, 10), and 720, 3,645 or 18,452 at 20%. At §9.6's 37.5% foil rate, that mints 1.9% of a clean haul per heist at 5%, or 7.5% at 20%. The raider's average attempt is 12.2% to 17.0% of a clean haul (§9.6), so B adds 11% to 15% to the raid faucet at 5% and 44% to 61% at 20%.
options.doc_edit: §9.4: 'plus 5% of what a clean heist by a full crew would have paid on this island'. §13's Defending pays line, §9.1's Essence row and §13.1 as in A.
options.build_change: server/src/economy.mjs defenceShare(): remove the early return when left is 0, and value the haul at banked = capacity instead of left. The simulation's 'left' stays for the replay. Re-pin the defence tests.

options.label: Build's price; the rule reads first-week authorship
options.means: The price is as in A. §13.1's rule reads the share of a season's new players who publish a defence of their own, after the 60-second guided build, within seven days of joining. The weekly changers become a report.
options.consequences: The trigger follows how newcomers take to designing. The guided build must be excluded: it is not optional, so if it counted the share would sit near 100% and the rule would never fire. Established players who stop redesigning no longer move the reward.
options.numbers: Rise: 5 points a season, at most three times, 5% to 20%, when the share is below 15% (§13.1). Values as in A.
options.doc_edit: §13.1: name the first-week share as the one the 15% reads, and exclude the guided build. §9.4, §13's Defending pays line and §9.1 as in A.
options.build_change: server/src/seasons.mjs defenceMeasure(): count accounts created in the season that published a snapshot other than their guided build within seven days. The server must be able to tell the guided build's publish from later ones, which it cannot today.

options.label: Build's price; weekly share averaged over the season
options.means: The price is as in A. The weekly changer share is taken at the end of each of the season's eight weeks, and the rise reads their mean at the close.
options.consequences: Follows §13.1's 'It is measured weekly' literally, and one unusual final week cannot trigger or block a rise. The first-week share is reported, not a trigger. The server gains a weekly job and a small table.
options.numbers: Eight readings a season (§18.1's 56 days ÷ 7). Rise and values as in A.
options.doc_edit: §13.1: the measure is 'the share of players with a session in a week who published a changed defence in it, taken weekly; the rise reads the season's mean at the close'. §9.4, §13's Defending pays line and §9.1 as in A.
options.build_change: server/src/seasons.mjs: store a defenceMeasure() reading at the end of each week, and have setDefenceShare() average the season's readings. Re-pin the season tests.

recommendation.rationale: A follows §9.4's own words and §13's 'Knocked-out raiders leave behind whatever they were carrying'. Tying the reward to the load keeps the minted amount at or below B's added 11% to 61% of the raid faucet, and it pays most for catching a crew at its most committed, which is §12.19's loading decision. The weekly share is the one that can actually move: the first-week share counts a guided build that every player must do. The rule acts once a season, and at that moment 'the last 7 days' is the season's last week; D is a cheap refinement if end-of-season behaviour proves unusual. A still needs §9.1's Essence row fixed and the reward added to the economy model.

quotes.text: Defence rewards: a foiled heist gives the defender the entry fee plus 5% of what the crew was carrying, a share that rises by 13.1's rule.
Share of active players who changed their defence in the last 7 days, and who published a defence of their own in their first week
Below 15%, the defence reward's share of what a foiled crew was carrying (9.4) rises by 5 points a season, at most three times, from 5% to 20%

A foiled heist gives the defender the raider's entry fee and the mirror of the Renown the raider loses.
Star Wells, heists, defence rewards
The largest non-cosmetic rewards in the game go to islands other people choose to play: defence rewards, creator marks, and the fund (18.9).

Optionally, whether the rise fires when either share is below 15%. The defence reward added to tools/economy_model (rerun.py lists 'raids against the player: defence rewards' as not modelled), so its share of the faucet is measured.

F47.question: Should §24.1's write budget and cost table be re-derived from what the built server measurably writes, or should the server be rebuilt to write less?
F47.why_it_matters: §24.1 calls five writes a player a day 'the design constraint' and prices infrastructure at €0 up to 10,000 monthly players and $5 to $15 at a million. The load test shows one clean heist writes about 14 rows and an engaged day at least 46. A re-simulation takes about 15 ms against the free plan's 10 ms, so the free plan cannot validate a heist at all. The budget, the €0 columns, the $5-to-$15 figure and the claims that the Apple fee is the only recurring cost are all wrong as written, and the owner must either restate them or accept a rewrite of how a heist is recorded.
F47.today: server/load.mjs plays §14.1's players through the real service and records server/load.json; tools/check_all.sh fails if the writes move. Re-run for this brief: engaged 46.01, regular 23.58 and casual 10.53 rows a player a day, against facts WRITE_BUDGET 5. A validation takes about 15 to 16 ms at the median and 21 to 23 ms at the 95th percentile on this machine's Node, varying from run to run (load.json: 15 ms, p95 20.6 to 22.1), against FREE_CPU_MS 10. These are floors: the load test's heists are foiled and its raiders hold no Starlight (G33). A clean heist in steady state, measured for this brief, writes 13 to 14 rows: the lease issued and settled, the heist, four ledger lines, one or two Renown lines, a stars line, two rating updates, a telemetry event and the defender's notification (server/src/service.mjs grant() and settle(), seasons.mjs, track.mjs, matchmaking.mjs, notifications.mjs).

options.label: Keep the build; re-derive §24.1 from measurement
options.means: The server keeps its append-only ledger, Renown and stars tables, a lease row, two rating rows, a notification and an event per heist. §24.1's budget becomes the measured figures: about 14 rows a clean heist, and at least 46, 24 and 11 rows a day for engaged, regular and casual players. It states the daily share of monthly players it assumes (a third, from §25.1). Validation runs on the $5 plan from the first heist.
options.consequences: Nothing changes for players. The cost table becomes $5 at 1,000 and 10,000 monthly players (not €0), $5 to about $21 at 100,000, and about $60 to $615 at a million: $60 to $415 on the load test's floor, and $115 to $615 if every heist were clean. At 1,000 and 10,000 players the recurring bill grows from $99 a year to about $160; at a million it is about $820 to $7,500 a year, so above about 100,000 players the servers cost more than the Apple fee. If §22.2's base rates held at a million players (about €255,000 a month), infrastructure would be about 0.2% of revenue, so §22.5's 'rounding error' conclusion holds. No option restores the €0 columns: even §24.10's fallback to 20 ticks, if CPU scales with ticks (not measured), leaves the median at about 10 ms and the 95th percentile at about 15 ms.
options.numbers: Monthly writes = monthly players × 1/3 (§25.1) × rows a day × 30. Cost = $5 + (writes − 50 million) × $1 per million (§28.3). A clean engaged day: 4 × 14 + 5 session events + 5 telemetry batches = 66 rows, so a million players write 660 million rows ($615). A casual day: 14 + 2 = 16 rows, 160 million ($115). load.json floors: 460 million ($415) and 105 million ($60). The free plan's 100,000 writes a day (§28.3) carry about 2,200 to 9,500 daily players on the load test's floors (load.json freePlanPlayersADay), or 1,500 to 6,250 if every heist were clean.
options.doc_edit: §24.1, Dynamic tier row: remove 'several times what a million players generate'. Cost table: Infrastructure $5, $5, $5 to about $21, about $60 to $615. Unavoidable cash row: drop 'That is the whole recurring bill' and add the $5 plan. Replace 'The dominant cost of this game is the Apple fee, not its servers. At a million monthly players the infrastructure is about $5 to $15 a month...' with 'The Apple fee is the larger cost below about 100,000 monthly players; above that, database writes are, at about $60 to $615 a month at a million'. Replace 'Where the free tier breaks' with 'The free plan cannot validate a heist (about 15 ms against 10 ms), so the $5 plan is needed from the first heist'. Budget line: the measured rows a heist and a day, with a third of monthly players active on a day. §24.5: the Apple row loses 'the only unavoidable recurring cost'; the infrastructure row becomes '$5 a month from launch; about $60 to $615 at a million monthly players' and loses 'the smaller half of the bill'; 'the servers are not the cost. The Apple fee is.' becomes 'the servers cost $5 a month until the game is large, and then a fraction of a percent of revenue'. §22.5: 'The entire unavoidable bill is $99 a year to Apple and $25 once to Google' gains 'and $5 a month for the database plan'. §27.2's backend row: 'about $5 to $15 a month at a million' becomes 'about $60 to $615 a month at a million', and 'the only unavoidable recurring cost' becomes 'with the $5 database plan, the unavoidable recurring costs'.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does. tools/design_facts.py WRITE_BUDGET and the §24.1 regular expression follow the new budget line, so server/load.mjs compares against it.

options.label: Settle a heist in one row, then re-derive
options.means: The heist row carries its ledger lines, both Renown lines and its stars as JSON. Balances, Renown and stars become sums over heist rows plus the ledger's non-heist lines (purchases, track, prices). The lease, the event, the two ratings and the notification stay. A clean heist writes about 7 rows, and §24.1 is restated at that figure.
options.consequences: Nothing changes for players. An engaged clean day writes about 38 rows instead of 66, which at a million monthly players is about $335 a month instead of $615, and saves nothing below 100,000. The ledger is split across two places, so every balance query reads JSON, and the append-only triggers on ledger, renown and season_stars must be rebuilt for the heist row. It is a rewrite of the server's core settlement. Validation still needs the $5 plan, and A's §24.5, §22.5 and §27.2 cost edits are still needed.
options.numbers: 14 − 7 folded rows (4 ledger + 2 Renown + 1 stars) = 7 a clean heist. Engaged 4 × 7 + 10 = 38 rows a day, 380 million a month at a million players ($335). Casual 7 + 2 = 9 rows, 90 million ($45).
options.doc_edit: §24.8: the heists table holds the heist's ledger lines, Renown and stars. §24.12's append-only ledger is described as the heist rows plus other ledger lines. §24.1 is restated at about 7 rows a heist and the costs above, with A's §24.5, §22.5 and §27.2 cost edits.
options.build_change: server/src/service.mjs grant() and balance(), track.mjs settle() and stars(), seasons.mjs Renown sums, db.mjs schema, triggers and a migration. Re-baseline server/load.json and rewrite the settlement tests.

options.label: Hold five writes; one row a heist, all else derived
options.means: Each heist writes one row and nothing else. The lease is a signed token with no row. Ratings, Renown, stars, the ledger and the defender's notification are all derived from heist rows. Sessions write nothing, and telemetry is one batch a day.
options.consequences: An engaged player writes 5 rows a day, so §24.1's five and $5 at a million players both hold, with the million-player figure landing exactly on the 50 million included. The cost moves to reads: an offer recomputes Glicko-2 ratings by replaying an island's heists in order, and every balance sums all of a player's heists. These reads are billed and not measured (G33). §13.1's activity measure must come from the daily batch. It is the largest rewrite of the server's data model, and validation still needs the $5 plan.
options.numbers: Engaged 4 heists + 1 batch = 5 rows a day. A million monthly players × 1/3 × 5 × 30 = 50 million, the included amount ($5). Casual: 2 rows a day, 20 million.
options.doc_edit: §24.8: the tables become accounts, islands, snapshots and heists, with everything else derived. §24.13's lease becomes a signed token. §24.1's budget and table stay as written, except the €0 columns become $5.
options.build_change: Rewrite db.mjs, service.mjs, seasons.mjs, track.mjs, matchmaking.mjs, notifications.mjs and telemetry.mjs around the heist row. Re-baseline load.json and rewrite most server tests.

options.label: Trim the cheap writes; keep the ledger, then re-derive
options.means: The lease is a signed token, and the heist row's unique lease id stops a second submission. The defender's notification is derived from heist rows. Session events ride the telemetry batch. The ledger, Renown and stars tables stay as built. A clean heist writes about 11 rows, and §24.1 is restated at that figure.
options.consequences: Nothing changes for players. At a million monthly players it saves about $170 a month against A's clean figure, and nothing below 100,000. §24.12's ledger is untouched. §24.13's one-lease-per-target rule is enforced when a heist is submitted rather than when it starts, so a second device can play a heist that is then refused. §13.1's activity measure reads sessions from the telemetry batch. Validation still needs the $5 plan, and A's §24.5, §22.5 and §27.2 cost edits are still needed.
options.numbers: 14 − 2 lease rows − 1 notification = 11 a clean heist. Engaged 4 × 11 + 5 batches = 49 rows a day, 490 million a month at a million players ($445). Casual 11 + 1 = 12 rows, 120 million ($75).
options.doc_edit: §24.13: a lease is a signed token, and 'One lease per target per player at a time' is checked at submission. §24.1 restated at about 11 rows a heist and the costs above, with A's §24.5, §22.5 and §27.2 cost edits.
options.build_change: server/src/service.mjs lease() and submit(), notifications.mjs, telemetry.mjs, seasons.mjs defenceMeasure(); re-baseline server/load.json and re-pin the lease and notification tests.

recommendation.rationale: Every option needs the $5 plan from the first heist, because validation takes about 15 ms against the free plan's 10. Measured costs at a million players stay a fraction of a percent of §22.2's revenue, so §22.5's conclusion that 'this game cannot be killed by its own bills' survives. B and C spend one developer's time rewriting the append-only ledger that §24.12's trust rules rest on (never paying twice, never overwriting currency). D leaves the ledger alone but saves only about $170 a month at a million players and nothing below 100,000, so it can wait until the game reaches that scale.

then $0.001 per million reads and $1.00 per million writes

F35.question: How far away is cracking the Vault heard: at 5 m with the 5-second call as built, at 5 m per hit with the call deleted as brief 37's rule now ends, only by a guard beside the Vault (1 m), or by no guard at all (0 m)?
F35.why_it_matters: Brief 37's rule, run exactly as §32.9 writes it, finds no reach from 1 m to the Heart's 12 m that passes either of its tests, and the ten-second whole-Heart call fails too. That is because even with no call at all, holds are already 72 to 100%, far above §13.2's bands, and depth across two or more realms is already under 35 points. So the rule ends by deleting the call on evidence that says nothing about the call. Meanwhile the 5 m that v3.4 ships cuts the optimal crew's lead from +42 to +4 points. §12.17 still says 5 m is what 'the harness measured as passing the depth gate', and §32.9's row calls it 'the noise-off case (… 58 to 82 points)'. On today's harness neither is true.
