recommendation.rationale: Pick D: no guard hears a hit on the Vault. A and B leave the optimal crew about +4 to +8 ahead at the Vault, which §19.27 calls making 'the systems are decoration'. D is the only setting that passes the one-realm gate: +42.0 ± 4.0, n=200. C is the close second: +33.0 ± 3.9 (gated +33.5), 2 points under 35 and inside one standard error of it, but 9 points below D, with the optimal crew losing 23 paired runs and gaining 3 (p < 0.001). The panel split. The player-experience and scope judges chose C, to keep a guard posted beside the Vault as a lever for defenders. The balance judge chose D. The recommendation goes with D for three reasons. The player judge's own fallback is met: 1 m came out clearly under the no-call result, and that judge said the Vault should then be heard by no guard. The scope judge's reason for C was build risk, and D is less code: delete the call block and its constants, and drop Task::Crack from the breaking match; the harness already models it exactly. And the defender lever C keeps is not needed now, because holds already run 72-100% with no call at all, above §13.2's bands. If F33 and F34 bring holds into band and the Vault then proves too easy, C can be put back at 1 m, and the harness already measures it. Confidence is medium. The panel went two to one the other way, C is a near miss rather than a clear failure, and depth across two or more realms still fails at any reach (+24.5 at two realms with no call).

quotes.text: Brief 37: the smallest whole number of metres at which the optimal crew beats the careless one by at least 35 points and hold rates sit inside every realm level’s band (13.2).
If none up to the Heart’s width does both, the whole Heart is called every 10 seconds with a countdown on the Vault; if that fails, the timed call is deleted.
The reach ships at 5 m, the per-hit distance, which the harness measured as passing the depth gate; the sweep in 32.9 sets its final size.
Cracking the Vault is heard further than anything in the table.
Cracking is loud: every hit is heard within 5 m, and every 5 seconds of cracking every guard within the crack’s reach of the Vault, 5 m by the walking path, hears it and starts Investigating it.
The realm alarm, which is the pressure device here.
The optimal crew succeeds at least 35 points more often than the careless one on the same islands.
If skill does not separate outcomes, the systems are decoration
every five seconds of cracking every guard within the crack’s reach — 5 m by the walking path, drawn as a ring around the Vault while anyone cracks — hears it and starts Investigating it (12.6)

F35.also_needed: The owner confirms D (0 m) or chooses C (1 m) if a guard posted beside the Vault must be able to hear it. Either way the harness default changes to match the build, so the Vault figure is measured as built. Re-check the choice once F33 is built, as the F35/F33 conflict already asks. Presentation keeps the cracking sound, the shake and the health bar for the player. Depth across several realms stays open under F33, F34 and F32. Deferring until F33 and F34 settle holds, which an earlier draft offered as D, is dropped: all three judges rejected it, and with depth failing from two realms up (+12, +5, +2 at n=40) a later re-run of brief 37 would still end by deleting the call, which is B.

panel.variant: C, with two additions. First, keep cracking loud for the player: the sound, the shake and the Vault's health bar stay, but guards cannot hear it. The realm alarm stays the pressure device. Second, write the fallback into §32.9 now: once the harness has per-hit hearing, if the 1 m result comes out clearly under the no-call result, no guard hears the Vault at all (0 m, option D). The noise test is not re-run to reopen 5 m.
panel.reasoning:
From the player's side, the build's 5 m breaks the "Clever beats strong" pillar at the moment that matters most. The harness gives the optimal crew only +4.0 ± 3.3 over the careless one at the Vault, against +42 with no call. After a well-played run, the player reaches the Vault and finds the planning made no difference there. §19.27's own words for that are "the systems are decoration". I checked the sim, and in play the 5 m call adds almost nothing on top of per-hit hearing. lib.rs:1946-1952 puts any guard that hears a Sound::Breaking straight into Investigating, and a hit lands every 0.8 s, heard at 5 m (noise.rs Breaking = 10 half-metres). So A and B play almost the same. The real choice, as the register says, is whether a hit on the Vault is heard at 5 m. Deferring (the old option D, now dropped) keeps the +4 Vault and waits on a hold test that has nothing to do with the question. Multi-realm depth fails before the crack is even considered, so the re-run would probably delete the call anyway.

A also has a clarity problem. The build keeps calling guards every 5 s after the first hit until the Vault opens, "even if cracking stops" (lib.rs:2222-2248). §12.6 says "every 5 seconds of cracking". So a crew that stops to hide still pulls guards in, which is punishment the player cannot read.

C is the most readable rule: only a guard standing right beside the Vault hears it. Defence then comes from posts, wards and geometry, which the player can see and plan around. That gives agency to both raider and defender. C costs the fantasy line "Cracking the Vault is heard further than anything in the table." (§12.17). But §12.6 names the realm alarm as the heist's tension: "The realm alarm, which is the pressure device here." So the climax can stay loud in presentation without being loud to guards. C also removes a rule, the ring and the timed call, which fits one-developer scope.

Confidence: medium. The +33 at 1 m comes from a harness with no per-hit hearing, which is why the fallback is written in advance. [Editor's note: C as now written keeps the 1 m timed call, gated on cracking, instead of a per-hit sound, and the harness measures it exactly at +33.0 ± 3.9, so this fallback's condition can be judged now.]

panel.variant: D, 0 m, rather than C's 1 m: a hit on the Vault is heard by no guard (a guard beside it still sees the crew), and the timed call and ring are deleted. Hits on anything else stay at 5 m. The owner sets the number now, not a sweep. If the owner wants the Vault to make some sound, 1 m is the fallback, but it has to be measured with per-hit hearing first, and on my proxy it misses the gate.
panel.reasoning: I re-ran the harness myself (report.run_batch, n=200, realm level 3, one realm, the same seeds in every row; script at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ruleborn/4036626a-ccc0-53cd-b585-d7b6007ab17e/scratchpad/brief/f35_judge.py, about 1 minute on 4 workers). My no-call, 1 m/5 s and 5 m/5 s rows match the draft exactly: none +42.0 ± 4.0 (optimal 50.0%, careless 8.0%); 1 m call every 5 s +33.0 ± 3.9; 5 m call every 5 s +4.0 ± 3.3. I also added two rows as a stand-in for per-hit hearing, which the harness lacks: the same call fired every 1 s, close to one hit every 0.8 s (sim.py WIND_UP_TICKS). 1 m every 1 s gives +25.5 ± 4.0 (optimal 35.0%, careless 9.5%). 5 m every 1 s gives +8.0 ± 4.1. Two conclusions follow. (1) The draft's C figure of +33 is optimistic. With per-hit hearing, 1 m probably lands near +25, 10 points under §19.27's 35, so C as drafted likely fails the gate it was chosen for. (2) B is really A: per-hit hearing at 5 m is +4 to +8, so deleting only the call buys nothing. The only setting that passes the one-realm depth gate is a Vault no guard hears (+42). The careless crew barely moves across all these rows (7 to 17%). All the noise does is take away the optimal crew's reward for a quiet, well-timed crack, which is exactly what §19.27 calls making the systems decoration. The Vault does not lose all its pressure without a sound. It is still defended by posts, wards and sightlines (§13's power budget), and §13.2's detection-and-response layer already has 'the Spire's reach, which re-seals the Vault while it is being robbed, 8 units a second from the moment it opens, taking back what no bag holds yet', plus the sim's grace clock from the first hit. Deferring (the old option D, now dropped) fails on the numbers. No-call depth is +24.5 at two realms (the n=40 sweep gives +12, +5, +2 across two to four realms), and holds are 72 to 100%, so re-running brief 37 after F33/F34 would still end at 'delete the call', leaving the per-hit 5 m and about +4 depth in place. For one developer, 0 m is also the least work: delete lib.rs:2222-2248 and the constants in heist.rs:21-31, skip Sound::Breaking for Task::Crack at lib.rs:1840-1883, and add no ring and no new sound. The document edit is D's: 'is heard by no guard; a guard beside it still sees the crew'. The §32.9 row becomes '0 m, set by the owner against the no-call baseline (F35)', and the '58 to 82 points' clause and brief 37's rule are struck. Multi-realm depth (+24.5 at two realms) fails whatever the reach and belongs to F33/F34/F32, not F35. Confidence: medium. [Editor's note: option C is now written as the scope judge built it, the 1 m timed call with no per-hit sound, which the harness measures exactly at +33.0 ± 3.9 (+33.5 gated). The +25.5 proxy above applies only to a per-hit 1 m sound, which C no longer builds.]

panel.variant: C as now written: build "guard beside the Vault" with the code that already exists, not as a new 1 m sound. Keep the timed call in sim/src/lib.rs:2222-2248 and set CRACK_REACH_METRES from 5 to 1 (sim/src/heist.rs:31). By path::steps_to that covers the walkable tiles orthogonally next to the Vault, which is exactly the set the harness's crack_reach=1 measures (tools/heist_harness/sim.py:736-757). Take Task::Crack out of the `breaking` match (lib.rs, around 1846-1851) so a Vault hit makes no Sound::Breaking. Change the harness default from 5 to 1. Drop the ring from §12.6, §12.17 and summary line 85, because "beside the Vault" needs no drawn extent. The client has no crack ring yet, so nothing has to be removed there. Doc edits are as in C, except that §12.6/§12.17 say "every 5 seconds of cracking, a guard beside the Vault hears it and starts Investigating it; a hit on the Vault is not heard further". If the owner prefers per-hit hearing, the fallback is D, a Vault no guard hears (crack_noise=False plus no Breaking for Task::Crack). The harness already models that exactly, at +42.
panel.reasoning:
I re-ran it myself at n=200, realm level 3, one realm, same seeds as the brief (tools/heist_harness report.run_batch). With no call: optimal 50.0%, careless 8.0%, lead +42. With a 1 m call: 40.0% and 7.0%, lead +33. With 5 m: 14.5% and 10.5%, lead +4. So the brief's figures hold, and the 5 m that v3.4 ships leaves the §19.27 gate ("The optimal crew succeeds at least 35 points more often than the careless one") at about +4. That is where A, B and deferring (the old option D, now dropped) all leave it. From the scope and build-risk side, there are three problems with the choices on offer.

(1) Deferring keeps a rule that cannot be tested today. Brief 37 needs holds inside §13.2's bands, but with no call at all they are 72-100%. A one-developer project should not ship a ledger row whose test can only fail.

(2) B and C as first drafted both need per-hit hearing added to the harness before any Vault number is true. That is new modelling work. Until it lands, the harness and the sim disagree about the one mechanic being decided.

(3) C's literal build has two flaws. First, a new 1 m Sound is emitted from the cracker's tile, not the Vault's, so it reaches guards next to the cracker, which is not the same as guards "beside the Vault". Second, it goes through steps_scaled (noise.rs), so on moss (x0.75) a 1 m radius becomes 1.5 half-metres, which rounds to 0 steps and makes the Vault silent, and the noise-radius law can make it louder. The "fixed number the owner sets" would in fact be flipped by the surface and by laws, and no test would catch that without new fixtures.

My variant gives the same design result: only a guard beside the Vault hears it, and posts, wards and geometry defend the Vault, which §13 already budgets. It costs one constant change and one match arm in the sim, with no new Sound, no ring to build (the client has none), and no harness modelling. The harness's crack_reach=1 row then measures the build as built, so +33 is the shipped figure, not an upper bound on an unmodelled mechanic. A is cheapest in code, but it locks in a depth gate that fails at the Vault for good. It also still owes the client a ring that is not built, so "no build change" is not quite true. [Editor's note: option C is now written as this variant, and option D is now a Vault no guard hears.]

F45.question: Should a universe's strength (stability capacity plus its five best characters' levels) filter which targets are offered?
F45.why_it_matters: §12.3 and §12.22 list different filters, and §12.22 is the section that spells out the steps. The server follows §12.22 and has no strength filter, so §12.3 promises a filter no build applies. Strength is also missing from §12.22's widening order, so a thin band has no rule for relaxing it.
F45.today: server/src/matchmaking.mjs:226-255 (offer) filters Renown within 150, Keeper level within 3, and predicted success within BAND_WIDTH (0.15) of the raider's recent success. It adds echoes, then widens rating, then Keeper level, then Renown. There is no strength filter, and no depth filter either (§12.22's depth is not built, D66). Stability capacity and character levels are held on the device: the bundle (sim/src/island.rs:26-37) carries realm and Vault level but no Spire, Anchor or character levels, and server/src holds no stability data.

options.label: Keep the build: no strength
options.means: As built, targets are filtered by Renown within 150, Keeper level within 3, and predicted success within 15 points of the raider's recent success (matchmaking.mjs:235-239). §12.22's depth filter is not built (D66). §12.3's sentence points to §12.22 and loses the 20% strength clause.
options.consequences: For players, nothing changes from the build. Winnability rests on the Glicko ratings, which learn from real outcomes, and Keeper level within 3 bounds progression gaps. Bands stay as full as they are while the player base is small.
options.numbers: none
options.doc_edit: §12.3 first paragraph: replace 'within 150 Renown of yours, within 3 Keeper levels, and within 20% of your universe's strength (…)' with 'from the band 12.22 sets'.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Add strength to §12.22
options.means: §12.22 step 1 adds a filter: the target universe's strength within 20% of the raider's. Strength is §5.5's capacity (Spire 30 + 8×level, plus each Anchor Stone 8 + 5×level, +8% for each epoch after the first) plus the levels of the five best characters. The widening order must name where strength goes, for example first, before rating.
options.consequences: Offers are held to similar builds even while ratings are still wide. Bands get thinner, so more echoes and generated fallbacks. Strength is reported by the device and the server cannot check it against the snapshot, so a modified client could under-report to be offered weaker targets.
options.numbers: From §5.5 and tools/economy_model/data.py:156-161: Spire 1 alone plus five level-1 characters is 38 + 5 = 43, so 20% is ±9, about one Spire level (8 points). Spire 5 plus five Anchor Stones at levels 5, 5, 4, 4 and 3 (§8.5's day-41 figure) is 70 + 145 = 215. At §5.5's stated maximum, 516 + 50 (five characters at §10.2's cap of 10) = 566, so 20% is ±113, before §5.5's +8% an epoch. Characters are at most 50 of 566 (9%), so the filter is mostly a stability filter.
options.doc_edit: §12.22 step 1: add the strength filter and its definition. Step 4: add strength to 'rating, then Keeper level, then Renown'. §12.3: point at §12.22.
options.build_change: The device reports Spire, Anchor and top-five character levels at publish, stored on the snapshot or account row (server/src/db.mjs, service publish) and carried in the target lists (service.mjs:212-238). offer() gets a strength filter and a widening step (matchmaking.mjs:236-252).

recommendation.rationale: The rating already does what the strength filter was for: §12.15 wants the median target winnable, and ordering by predicted success delivers that from outcomes a player cannot fake. Keeper level within 3 already bounds progression gaps, and with one-way theft (§9.4) the defender loses nothing, so the filter protects no one. A strength figure reported by the device would let modified clients steer toward weaker targets, which cuts against fairness, and it would thin bands while the player base is small and add server and format work for one developer.

quotes.text: within 150 Renown of yours, within 3 Keeper levels, and within 20% of your universe's strength (stability capacity plus the levels of your five best characters)
Renown within 150, Keeper level within 3, an island difficulty rating within one band of the raider's recent success rate
Only then do the filters widen, in order — rating, then Keeper level, then Renown — and ruins fill what remains (12.10).

G30.question: Should §12.22 adopt the server's matchmaking readings as they stand (a 15-point band, the last 20 heists as 'recent', a heist scoring 1 unless foiled, echoes moving no Renown and rating no one), or change one of them?
G30.why_it_matters: §12.22 names Glicko-2 and 'one band of the raider's recent success rate' but gives no band width, no window for 'recent', no score for a Loud or Partial heist, and no rule for Renown or ratings on echoes. Each is a constant or branch in the server that the document does not back. The figures decide how wide offers range, how fast lists react to a streak, whether the rating learns while echoes fill the lists, and how season standings move.
G30.today: server/src/matchmaking.mjs sets the following. BAND_WIDTH = 0.15 (:53), the width of §13.2's bands. RECENT = 20 validated heists of any kind, raids, echoes, friendly heists and challenge plays (:57, :127-136). A new raider's rate is the middle of the authored band, 62.5% (:130-133). A heist scores 1 unless foiled, one rating period per heist (:113-125). Islands are rated by owner and realm, and a republish keeps the mean and widens back to 350 (:105-109). §12.22's figures are the generated band, and authored islands use 100 minus §13.2's 30-45 hold band (:42-50). The offer is the in-band candidate nearest the band's middle with one easier and one harder (:258-271). server/src/service.mjs:643-655: an echo moves no Renown, pays its owner nothing and rates neither side, not even the raider (:655), though the raider still earns the haul and season stars (track.mjs:94-96 zeroes only the owner's side). matchmaking.mjs:193-195: a shielded new player's echoes are withheld like their live islands. :144: seeded accounts are never shielded. :28-34 and :145-147: raiding a seeded island, an echo, a friend or a challenge does not end the raider's own 72 hours.

options.label: Keep the build's readings
options.means: The document states the build's readings as its own. A band is 15 points of success rate. 'Recent' is the last 20 validated heists of any kind (matchmaking.mjs:127-136), and 62.5% for a new raider. A raid scores 1 for the raider unless foiled and is its own rating period. Islands are rated per owner and realm, and a republish keeps the mean and widens back to 350. Echoes and friendly heists move no Renown and rate neither side (service.mjs:651, :655), but an echo raider still earns the haul and season stars. A new player's echoes are shielded like their live islands; seeded accounts are never shielded, and raiding a seeded island does not end the raider's own shield.
options.consequences: Ratings measure the same thing as §13.2's bands (a raid succeeds unless foiled, as the harness counts it: tools/heist_harness/sim.py:216), so the guarantee compares like with like. But while echoes fill most lists, echo raids move a raider's 'recent' rate and never their rating. A raider winning 80% of echoes against predicted success near 62% falls outside the 15-point filter, the rating filter is the first thing widened away, and step 3 orders targets on a rating that has not learned.
options.numbers: Noise in 'recent' at p = 0.625: the standard error is 10.8 points over 20 heists, about 0.7 of a 15-point band (my calculation). At four heists a day (§9.6, §14.3), 20 heists is 5 days.
options.doc_edit: §12.22 step 1: 'one band — 15 points of success rate, §13.2's width — of the raider's success over their last 20 validated heists (a new raider: the middle of the authored band)'. Step 2: 'a raid scores 1 for the raider unless foiled and is its own rating period; a republished island keeps its mean and returns to 350'. §12.3 echo paragraph: 'moves no Renown and rates nothing'.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Graded score by outcome
options.means: Same as A, except the rating score follows §12.9's Renown multipliers: Clean 1, Loud 0.8, Partial 0.5, Foiled 0. The recent success rate still counts anything not foiled.
options.consequences: A Partial becomes a small loss for a settled raider, so ratings reward clean play. But predicted success then estimates graded score while §13.2's bands count non-foiled raids, so step 3's 'median winnable' compares two different measures.
options.numbers: server/src/glicko.mjs update, my run. A settled raider (1,500, deviation 80) against a settled island at the authored prior's mean (1,411, deviation 80; expected 0.618) moves +13.1 on a score of 1, +6.2 at 0.8, −4.2 at 0.5 and −21.5 on a foil. A new raider (1,500, deviation 350) against a new island at its prior (1,411, deviation 350; expected 0.568) moves +136.1, +70.5, −27.7 and −191.5.
options.doc_edit: As A, but step 2 reads 'scores the outcome's Renown multiplier from 12.9 (1, 0.8, 0.5, 0)'.
options.build_change: matchmaking.mjs:118: score = {clean:1, loud:0.8, partial:0.5, foiled:0}[verdict.grade].

options.label: Echoes pay the raider Renown
options.means: Same as A, except an echo moves Renown for the raider at §12.9's formula against the snapshot owner's current Renown. The owner loses nothing, and there is still no rating.
options.consequences: Early raiders' league standing grows while echoes fill the lists. Renown is created with no mirror loss, so league totals inflate in step with how much of the pool is echoes. Whether Renown should be created at all is F40's question.
options.numbers: §12.9: 20 × (1 ± 150/1000) gives 17 to 23 Renown per clean echo heist inside the ±150 window, ×0.8 Loud, ×0.5 Partial, and −8 when foiled. None of it is taken from a defender.
options.doc_edit: As A, but the §12.3 echo paragraph adds 'the raider's Renown moves as against the owner; the owner's does not'.
options.build_change: service.mjs:651: call seasons.settle for echoes with the defender's side zeroed (seasons.mjs:132), as track.settle already does for season stars (track.mjs:94-96: 'if (echo) s.defender = 0').

options.label: Echoes rate the raider
options.means: Same as A, except an echo raid updates the raider's rating against the echo's island rating (its owner's rating for that realm, which the build already uses to predict success on the echo, matchmaking.mjs:185), while the island's own rating does not move. Friendly heists and challenge plays leave both alone and drop out of 'recent'. The rating and 'recent' then learn from the same heists.
options.consequences: Raider ratings converge while the player base is small, which is when echoes fill the lists, so the rating filter and step 3's guarantee work from the start. Nothing changes for defenders. The window stays 20: 40 would cut the noise from 10.8 to 7.7 points but take 10 days at four heists a day to catch up after a player improves.
options.numbers: glicko.mjs update, my run: a new raider (deviation 350) moves +136 on one win against a new island and −192 on a foil, so a few echo raids move it most of the way. Standard error of 'recent' at p = 0.625: 10.8 points over 20 heists, 7.7 over 40.
options.doc_edit: As A, but the §12.3 echo paragraph reads 'moves no Renown and rates the raider only'. §12.22 step 1: 'recent' is the last 20 validated raids, echoes included.
options.build_change: service.mjs:655: for an echo, call a raider-only update in matchmaking.settle (skip the island store, matchmaking.mjs:113-125). matchmaking.mjs:127-136: join leases and keep mode = 'raid'.

recommendation.rationale: Keep A's readings (15 points, 20 heists, a raid scores 1 unless foiled), because they measure what §13.2's bands count. But §12.22 has the deviation narrow 'with every observed attack', and §12.3 makes echoes count as live candidates, so an echo raid is evidence the raider's rating should use. As built, the rating filter drops out just while echoes fill the lists and §12.15's winnable median is ordered on a rating that has not learned. D fixes that with a two-line server change for one developer; echo Renown (C) belongs to F40's decision on whether Renown is created, not here.

quotes.text: a wide deviation, 350 on Glicko-2's scale, which narrows with every observed attack under Glicko-2's update (volatility 0.06, system constant 0.5)
Otherwise the band keeps its 15-point width and its lower edge moves down 5 points at a time until the measured hold sits inside with at least one standard error to spare.
Echo universes: when fewer than three real universes fit, echoes count as live candidates: snapshots of real universes from the last 14 days.
Robbing an echo takes nothing from its owner; its loot is created by the game.
Renown for a clean heist = 20 × (1 + (defender's Renown − raider's Renown) ÷ 1,000), kept between 8 and 40, then multiplied by the outcome above.

G30.also_needed: Also decide a new raider's starting rate: the build's 62.5% (middle of the authored band), 67.5% (middle of §12.22's realm-level-1 band), or §15.1's 'about four heists in five'. The options are single changes from A; if the owner wants two of B to D, name both and both edits apply.

F46.question: Should scouting be enforced by serving a target's island only with a paid lease, be made free, or stay a paid client-side courtesy as built?
F46.why_it_matters: §12.4 sells laws, guards and ward counts for 20 Aether a realm and keeps ward positions secret. But every listed island's bundle, with every law, guard post and ward position in it, can be downloaded by hash with no sign-in. Honest players pay for information that a modified client reads for free, and the ward positions §12.4 protects most cannot be hidden from any device that plays the heist.
F46.today: server/src/http.mjs:86 and :319-328: GET /v1/bundles/:hash needs no Authorization and is served 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable'. Target lists are stored the same way and fetched by hash; only the index naming them (GET /v1/targets, http.mjs:360-362) needs a signed-in account, any account. service.mjs:214-238: each band's list carries every island's bundle hash, owner, realm, realm and Vault level, exposed loot, Keeper level, Renown and rating. sim/src/island.rs:26-37: a bundle holds the Vault position, guards (role, x, y), wards (kind, x, y) and laws (id, x, y). service.mjs:332-371: a lease is free; the entry fee is taken at validation (service.mjs:580-581, §24.13). No paid scout exists in server/src or client/.

options.label: Keep the build: paid courtesy
options.means: Bundles stay public by hash with the year-long cache. The paid scout (20 Aether a realm) and hidden ward positions are only what the honest client chooses to show.
options.consequences: Honest players pay to see laws, guards and ward counts that a modified client reads free, along with every ward position. The Lantern Wisp, the Archivist's Reveal and the Cartographer's maps are worthless to that cheater.
options.numbers: A scout of a three-realm universe costs 60 Aether (20 × 3). Against v3.4's §9.3 Aether a day, that is 7.5% on day 2 (800), 0.55% on day 31 (11,000) and 0.065% on day 301 (91,900). At four heists a day (§9.6, §14.3) it is 30%, 2.2% and 0.26% (my calculation; tools/economy_model/data.py PUBLISHED_DAILY_PRODUCTION_V34).
options.doc_edit: §12.4: add that scouting decides what the game shows, not what a device can read. §24.1 unchanged.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does (the scout screen itself is still unbuilt)

options.label: Make scouting free
options.means: Drop the 20 Aether price. Laws, guard number and roles, and ward counts become free information on every target card. Ward positions are still not shown by the client and still come from the Lantern Wisp, the Archivist's Reveal and the Cartographer's maps, and §12.4 says plainly that a modified client can read them.
options.consequences: Honest players no longer pay for what a cheater gets free, and §13's 'laws are always visible before you commit' holds without a price. An Aether sink worth about two minutes of day-301 income goes; early on it is a real cost, 7.5% of day-2 Aether a heist. The Observatory's scouting discount and Trace's 'free scout' no longer mean anything, and the Cartographer's map needs rewording.
options.numbers: The sink lost: 140 Aether for all seven realms is 2.2 minutes of day-301 income on §9.3's v3.4 figure of 91,900 a day (the economy model's sink table prints '1 minutes' because it still reads the v2.3 192,100). Early on it is 60 Aether a heist, 7.5% of day-2 Aether.
options.doc_edit: §12.4: merge the paid-scout sentence into free information and drop the price. §7.9: the scout report's laws are free. §9.1: remove 'scouting refunds on success' from Aether's sources and 'scouting' from its uses. §9.2: remove scouting from Aether's sinks. §9.5: delete the Scouting row. §10.2 Observatory levels: drop 'scouting N% cheaper'. §11.8 Cartographer: reprice or reword 'for Starlight instead of Aether'. §12.3 Trace: 'with no entry fee'. §24.1 unchanged.
options.build_change: Server none. Client: the target card shows laws, guards and ward counts. tools/economy_model: drop SCOUT_AETHER_PER_REALM (data.py:377) and its uses at sinks.py:158-159 and report.py:230.

options.label: Enforce: bundle only with a paid lease
options.means: The lease is the scout: it charges 20 Aether a realm and returns the target's bundle. Target lists, the index and GET /v1/offer carry only §12.4's free information and no bundle hash, and a current target's bundle is not served by public hash.
options.consequences: The paid information is really paid for. Ward positions still reach any modified client the moment it leases, because the device simulates the whole island (§24.1, §24.12). Every target a player wants to look at becomes a lease with a write and a debit, and target bundles leave the year-long edge cache (§24.1, §24.4), though bandwidth stays free. A lease is no longer free to take.
options.numbers: §24.4: a session pulls about ten opponent islands. Under C each one a player looks at is a lease: an authenticated request, a lease row and an Aether debit. At a million monthly players, a quarter active daily, one to ten scouts each is 0.25 to 2.5 million leases a day, 7.5 to 75 million a month, against the 10 million requests a month §28.3 says the $5 plan includes. At two writes each that is 2 to 20 writes a player a day against §24.1's budget of five (F47). Row reads stay far inside the 25 billion included; bandwidth stays free.
options.doc_edit: §24.1 and §24.4: target bundles excepted from the year-long cache. §24.8: lists carry no hashes. §24.12 Lease: 'charges the scout and returns the bundle'. §12.4: 'a scout is a lease'.
options.build_change: service.mjs lease() (:332-371): debit Aether per realm and return the bundle. service.mjs:212-238 and matchmaking.mjs candidates/offer: lists identify targets by owner and realm, not hash. http.mjs:319-328: refuse a current target's hash without the caller's live lease, with private cache headers.

options.label: Hash only with a paid lease
options.means: Target lists carry owner and realm, not the bundle hash. A lease charges the scout price (20 Aether a realm) and hands out the hash. Bundles stay public by hash with the year-long edge cache.
options.consequences: The price is paid before any device learns where a new island is, and §24.4's cache stays. But a handed-out hash is public for good: a player can share it, and a community index of hashes defeats the price for everyone who uses it. Friendly and challenge links still expose islands. Ward positions reach a modified client at lease, as in C. Every look at a target now costs the scout price and a lease write.
options.numbers: Same price as C: 60 Aether for a three-realm universe, 7.5% of day-2 Aether. The same 7.5 to 75 million leases a month and 2 to 20 writes a player a day as C; only the bundle fetches stay edge-cache hits.
options.doc_edit: §24.8: lists name islands, not hashes. §24.12 Lease: 'charges the scout and hands out the bundle's hash'. §12.4: 'a scout is a lease'. §24.1 unchanged.
options.build_change: service.mjs:212-238: lists carry owner and realm, not the bundle. lease() takes owner and realm, debits Aether per realm and returns the hash. offer() identifies candidates by owner and realm. http.mjs:319-328 unchanged.

recommendation.rationale: C and D both turn every look at a target into a paid lease with its writes, up to four times §24.1's five-writes budget, to enforce information worth 0.55% of day-31 Aether, and neither can hide ward positions, the one thing §12.4 protects most; D is also defeated by anyone who shares a hash. A leaves honest players paying for what a cheater reads free, which cuts against fairness. B removes that, keeps §13's promise that laws are visible before you commit, and costs the one developer only a client card; the sink it drops matters mainly in the first days, where §15.1 already asks the game to be generous.

quotes.text: A paid scout (20 Aether per realm, less with Observatory levels) shows each realm's laws, the number and roles of its guards, and how many wards of each type it has, but not where they are.
Immutable, content-addressed island bundles on zero-egress object storage, cached at the edge for a year
Budget: about 100 to 200 kilobytes and five writes per active player per day
Target selection is a file, not a query. Candidate lists per difficulty band are generated periodically as static objects, so choosing a target costs a cached download rather than a database search.
The server hands out a target snapshot, a seed, a single-use token and an expiry a day away. Nothing is created yet
The route rule (there's always a way in), the scouting rules (laws are always visible before you commit) and the loss caps keep both sides worth playing.

F46.also_needed: For C or D: the price per million requests above the $5 plan's included 10 million, which §28.3 does not give, and F47's write budget has to absorb the debit on every lease.

F40.question: How should the league boundaries meet §14.7: keep the season-end shares and accept a fast climb, keep the shares and let only ten heists a week move Renown, make Renown with a grant per clean heist, or keep the shares and let only two heists a day move Renown?
F40.why_it_matters: §12.9 moves Renown between players, so the only new Renown comes from §18.1's floors. Under that rule, boundaries that give §14.7's shares let an engaged player reach Star in about week 2, not around month 2, and the leagues end up sorted by how many heists a player makes a day. Boundaries that give the arrival times leave about half the population in Dust at season end. Until the owner picks, §14.7 promises something the formula cannot deliver, and server/src/leagues.json rests on a choice the document never made. Any limit on which heists move Renown also decides whether the leagues reward playing every day, which §20.3's "No obligations" rules out.
F40.today: The build keeps the shares. tools/league_model.py plays §12.9 and §18.1 forward over 4 seasons with 1,500 players. It uses §14.1's mix, assumed at 20/40/40, and §14.5's success arc from 80% to 60%, and fits the boundaries to §14.7's shares. server/src/leagues.json is its output: Dust 0, Ember 128, Tide 184, Star 300, Nova 644, Paradox 1,160. bash tools/check_all.sh fails if the two drift apart. server/src/seasons.mjs settle() (lines 124–159) books the mirror amount and mints Renown only where floorOf() stops a loss; pulledBack() is at line 103. Re-running the model today gives the same numbers. Season-end shares: Dust 3.5%, Ember 29.7%, Tide 30.8%, Star 25.7%, Nova 9.0%, Paradox 1.3%. An engaged player's median arrival: Ember day 2, Tide day 4, Star day 8, Nova day 57. One difference between model and build: when a raider already at their floor is foiled, tools/league_model.py (line 136) still gives the defender 8 Renown, but settle() gives only what the raider actually lost, as §13 says ("the mirror of the Renown the raider loses"). Played with the build's rule, leagues.json's boundaries leave 11.3% in Dust at season end instead of 3.5% (Ember 29.7%, Tide 24.4%, Star 24.3%, Nova 9.5%, Paradox 0.9%). A refit gives Ember 113, Tide 161, Star 276, Nova 601, Paradox 1,125, with an engaged player arriving on days 2, 3, 8 and 42. Whichever option is chosen, the model's foiled rule has to match the build before leagues.json is regenerated. The register suggests a smaller pull-back to spread the leagues, but it barely moves the arrivals: pulling back a quarter gives Ember day 2, Tide 4, Star 9, Nova 56, and no pull-back gives Star 9, Nova 53 (scratch variants of the same model).

options.label: Keep the build's reading: shares win
options.means: The boundaries stay fitted to §14.7's season-end shares, each split into thirds for divisions. Renown stays zero-sum apart from the floors, and every heist that settles moves Renown. §14.7's arrival column is rewritten to what this produces. The reading is the build's, but leagues.json has to be refitted to the build's own foiled rule: Ember 113, Tide 161, Star 276, Nova 601, Paradox 1,125.
options.consequences: Most players see §14.7's league mix at season end: about 30% Ember, 30% Tide, 25% Star, 10% Nova, 1% Paradox. The leagues sort players by how many heists they play a day, not by how cleverly. §12.22 keeps everyone's success in the same band, so each raid gains Renown on average and the extra raids decide the order. In the model every Nova and Paradox player at season end plays 4 heists a day, and with the shipped boundaries 99% of engaged players, 42% of regular players and 1.5% of casual players end in Star or above. An engaged player passes Ember and Tide in the first week and reaches Star on day 8, before §14.5's league placement in days 31 to 60. Nova takes about six to eight weeks. Renown pays nothing directly, so the economy is unaffected.
options.numbers: Boundaries, shares and arrivals come from python3 tools/league_model.py, which matches server/src/leagues.json. Under the model's three alternative assumptions (40/40/20 mix, success held at 80%, every success clean) the boundaries move to Ember 121–140, Tide 174–198, Star 336–375, Nova 693–700 and Paradox 1,234–1,301. That is within 15% of the built values except Star, which rises 12 to 25%. With the build's foiled rule (scratch variant, same seed): refit Ember 113, Tide 161, Star 276, Nova 601, Paradox 1,125; shares Dust 3.9%, Ember 29.9%, Tide 29.8%, Star 24.9%, Nova 10.5%, Paradox 1.0%; engaged arrivals on days 2, 3, 8 and 42. League by kind of player from a scratch run of the model at the shipped boundaries.
options.doc_edit: §14.7: change the arrival column to Ember "Within days", Tide "In the first week", Star "In the second week", Nova "Around week 6, for strong players". Keep the share column. §14.5: move "League placement" out of the days 31 to 60 row, since leagues are reached in the first weeks. §18.1: add that Renown only moves between players except where a floor stops a loss, and that the boundaries are fitted to §14.7's shares by tools/league_model.py.
options.build_change: tools/league_model.py season(): on a foiled heist, give the defender only what the raider lost above their floor, as seasons.mjs settle() does. Regenerate server/src/leagues.json (Ember 113, Tide 161, Star 276, Nova 601, Paradox 1,125 in the scratch refit); check_all.sh then passes on the new file. No change to seasons.mjs or service.mjs.

options.label: Shares win, and ten heists a week move Renown
options.means: A player's first ten validated matchmade heists of the week, from Monday 00:00 UTC (G20's week), move Renown as §12.9 says. Ten is five days of two, as §9.6's week cap is five days' worth. Later heists that week pay their haul and move no Renown, as G37's rule already does for a second heist on the same player. The ten can be played on any days. The boundaries are refitted to §14.7's shares.
options.consequences: The shares hold. Every player gets the same ten Renown heists a week, on whichever days they play, so the leagues reward neither more heists a day nor more days a week. In the model a player who plays four heists on each weekday ends in Star or above as often as one who plays four every day (49% and 48%), and a player who plays eight heists on Saturdays only, and so uses eight of the ten, does so 31% of the time. Engaged and regular players end the season in the same places (52% and 53% in Star or above), and casual players, with seven of the ten, reach Star about one time in ten. An engaged player reaches Ember in the first days, Tide in the second week and Star around week 4. That is before §14.7's "Around month 2" and just before §14.5's league placement in days 31 to 60; a regular player reaches Star around day 42. In the model, which has no skill term, the median player never reaches Nova, and Nova goes to whoever does best with their ten. A heist past the tenth still pays Starlight and Essence, so playing more is still worth it. Missing a whole week still costs that week's ten, as missing play costs Renown under every option, because the leagues rank Renown.
options.numbers: Scratch variant of tools/league_model.py with the build's foiled rule and a limit of ten Renown heists a week, each season's first day read as a Monday, refitted with calibrate() on the model's seed: Ember 128, Tide 176, Star 254, Nova 458, Paradox 806. Shares: Dust 3.6%, Ember 30.0%, Tide 30.2%, Star 24.7%, Nova 10.5%, Paradox 1.0%. An engaged player arrives at Ember on day 3, Tide on day 8 and Star on day 23; a regular one on days 8, 16 and 40; a casual one reaches Ember on day 47 and Tide on day 61. Nova and above on that seed: 59 engaged, 110 regular and 3 casual players. Across five more seeds at these boundaries (n = 5 runs of 1,500 players, mean ± standard error): Dust 3.7 ± 0.1%, Star 24.2 ± 0.4%, Nova 10.3 ± 0.2%; an engaged player's median arrival at Ember day 3.4 ± 0.2, Tide day 8.8 ± 0.2, Star day 28.2 ± 0.9; a regular player's at Star day 42 ± 2. Star or above at season end: engaged 51.8 ± 1.4%, regular 53.4 ± 1.2%, casual 9.5 ± 0.4%. Irregular players: the mix changed to engaged 20%, regular 35%, casual 35%, five-day 5% (four heists on each weekday, none at weekends) and Saturday-only 5% (eight heists each Saturday), at each option's own boundaries, n = 5 seeds. Star or above: under B, engaged 48.1 ± 1.1%, five-day 48.6 ± 2.1%, Saturday-only 31.0 ± 2.6%; under D, engaged 62.5 ± 1.3%, five-day 11.4 ± 1.9%, Saturday-only 0.0%; under A's refitted boundaries, engaged 99.6 ± 0.2%, five-day 83.2 ± 0.9%, Saturday-only 5.9 ± 0.9%. Fitting the boundaries to §14.7's arrival days instead of its shares was also run, over 12 rounds with the model's flat-8 foiled rule (Ember 241–258 and Tide 476–509 give Ember around day 7 and Tide around day 21) and leaves 46–50% of players in Dust at season end, so it is not offered.
options.doc_edit: §12.9: add "Only a player's first ten heists of the week, from Monday 00:00 UTC, move Renown; later ones pay their haul." §14.7: keep the shares; keep Ember "In the first week" and Tide "By week 3", set Star to "Around week 4" and Nova to "For strong players". §18.1: say Renown is made only where a floor stops a loss. §14.5 needs no change.
options.build_change: server/src/service.mjs grant(): count the raider's heists since weekStart(now) (line 74, G20's week) that moved Renown, and call seasons.settle() (line 651) only while that count is below 10; stars and defence shares keep G37's rule. Record on the heist row whether it counted, because a foiled raider at their floor books no Renown line. lease() tells the raider when the week's ten are used. tools/league_model.py: the same limit with weeks from Monday, plus the foiled fix from A. Regenerate server/src/leagues.json (Ember 128, Tide 176, Star 254, Nova 458, Paradox 806 in the scratch refit). Add a test.

Ember and Tide still come in days, inside §14.7's "in the first week" and "by week 3". Renown becomes even more a measure of how much someone plays: a four-heist-a-day player earns four grants to a casual player's one, whatever their skill. In the model every Nova and Paradox player at season end plays 4 a day and no casual player reaches Star, which leans against §20.3's no-grind rule.

A grant of 10 gives boundaries Ember 206, Tide 468, Star 971, Nova 2,056, Paradox 3,326. Shares: Dust 3.4%, Ember 29.5%, Tide 29.8%, Star 26.4%, Nova 10.1%, Paradox 0.8%. Under the model's flat-8 rule the figures are Ember 218, Tide 498, Star 1,012, Nova 2,054, Paradox 3,303, with arrivals on days 3, 9, 24 and 132, and Renown per player at season end rises from 319 to 973. options.label: Shares win, and only two heists a day move Renown
options.means: A player's first two validated matchmade heists of the UTC day move Renown as §12.9 says. Later heists that day pay their haul and move no Renown, as G37's rule already does for a second heist on the same player. The boundaries are refitted to §14.7's shares.

An engaged player reaches Ember in about the first week, Tide in the second and Star around week 5 to 6, close to §14.7's "around month 2" and inside §14.5's league placement in days 31 to 60. In the model, which has no skill term, the median player never reaches Nova. Nova and Paradox go to whoever does best with their two heists: in the model 31% engaged and 69% regular players. Casual players (one a day) mostly end in Ember or Tide. A third or fourth heist still pays Starlight and Essence, so playing more is still worth it, but the leagues stop rewarding heists a day. They reward days instead: two unused heists are lost each day, so a player who skips days falls behind. In the model a player who plays four heists on each weekday ends in Star or above 11% of the time against 62% for one who plays every day, and a player who plays eight heists on Saturdays only never does. D stops that with a daily allowance that is lost if unused, so it ranks players by days played instead: in the model a player who skips weekends reaches Star or above 11% of the time against 62% for a daily player. §20.3's "No obligations", §19.7's "Let players set their own rhythm" and §19.12 rule that out, and §9.6 sets its week cap at five days' worth for the same reason. F48.question: Should a friendly heist or a challenge-link play pay the raider a haul, and if so at what rate?
F48.why_it_matters: §12.11 calls a friendly heist "for fun", but §12.22 gives it the 0.25 payout tier. The build pays a normal haul with no entry fee. Two friends can then farm each other: one leaves a rich island unguarded and the other raids it clean every time, and nobody loses anything. A new player befriended by a veteran fills the day cap in one heist, with only §9.6's caps as a brake. Nothing in the document says whether this is intended.
F48.today: server/src/service.mjs grant() (lines 564–661). A lease in mode friendly or challenge costs no entry fee (line 580). It pays §9.6's full haul, with B(V) from the friend's Vault level and difficulty set by the two Keeper levels, capped by capHaul() at the raider's own caps. It counts toward the raider's fatigue and the daily and weekly caps (raidsEarlierToday, paidSince). It moves no Renown and no season stars, rates no island (lines 605, 651–655), gives the defender no share, and records the friend's pages as friendPages = verdict.caught. G37's once-a-day rule for each pair applies only to mode 'raid' (lines 601–603), so friendly heists between the same two players are unlimited apart from the caps. A challenge link pays the same, once per player per link (challengeLease(), lines 388–398). Any number of links can be made (friends.mjs challenge()). Each friendly or challenge heist also queues a raid notification to the friend (grant() line 653, notifications.raided), so it counts toward G34's message volume. A link made by a player 16 or over needs no friendship: challenge() refuses strangers only for a 13-to-15's links (lines 376–386), so two accounts that are not friends can trade links for full hauls.

options.label: Keep the build's reading: pays a full haul
options.means: A friendly heist or challenge play pays §9.6's haul like any raid, keyed to the friend's Vault level. The difficulty tier comes from the two Keeper levels, and the haul counts toward fatigue and the day and week caps. There is no entry fee. It moves no Renown, stars or rating, and the friend earns a page for each raider caught.
options.consequences: Friendly heists become the best-paying raids in the game. At the same Vault level, four clean full-bag heists pay 5.9 to 8.2 times a matchmade day. With a higher-level friend it is worse: B(V) is the friend's Vault level and the caps are the raider's own, so a Vault-2 player whose friend is at Vault 10 fills the 36,000 day cap with one friendly heist and the 120,000 week cap in four days. That is 8.8 to 12.2 times a matchmade week of 9,814 to 13,636. Challenge links made by players 16 and over need no friendship, so one account can make any number of links and another can play each once for a full haul. Only §9.6's caps limit any of this, which loosens §9.6's inflation control and makes finding a willing friend worth more than scouting.
options.numbers: At Vault level 2 (base 3,600, §9.6), four clean full-bag friendly heists at median richness pay 3,600 + 3,060 + 2,601 + 2,210 = 11,471 (economy.mjs haul(), fatigue 0.85). At the richest island (× 1.65) they pay 18,927, and with a friend two or more Keeper levels up as well (× 1.2) 22,712. §9.6's matchmade day is 1,402 to 1,948, so the same-level case is 5.9 to 8.2 times more. A Vault-10 friend (B(10) = 92,264, §9.6): one clean heist is worth 92,264 × 1.0 to 1.2, cut to the 36,000 day cap. The caps are 10 × the raider's base a day (36,000) and 33.3 × base a week (120,000), from economy.mjs dayCeiling() and weekCeiling(). A matchmade week is §9.6's day × 7.
options.doc_edit: §12.11: add "A friendly heist pays the raider a haul as any heist does (9.6), counted to the caps, with no entry fee; it moves no Renown, stars or rating." §17.6: say the same of challenge links, once per player. §12.22 step 5 stands.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: For fun only: no haul
options.means: A friendly heist or challenge play pays the raider no haul. It has no fee, moves no Renown, stars or rating, and does not count toward the haul caps or fatigue. The crew rests afterwards as after any heist (§12.9), which keeps page rewards bounded. The friend still earns a page for each raider their guards catch, and both see the replay.
options.consequences: There is no Starlight or Essence to farm, whatever the two players' levels, so the economy is untouched and no collusion needs watching. A friendly heist is a practice raid, as §29.2 describes it. It costs no Starlight but uses a crew's time, so it competes a little with paid raids. Page rewards stay at the pace rest allows. Players who want Starlight use matchmaking. The 0.25 tier then exists only for Trace targets.

A willing friend's island is still a safe clean heist with full bags, so friendly heists still pay 1.5 to 2 times a matchmade attempt at the same level. Playing with friends is rewarded a little and cannot be farmed hard. §12.22 step 5 is read as a flat rate for these modes.

G35.question: How do two players become friends (invite codes, platform friends lists, or both), and do a 13-to-15's heists appear in anyone's friends' feed?
G35.why_it_matters: Friendly heists, the friends' feed, challenge links and invite gifts all depend on friendships, and the document never says how one starts. The answer sets whether iPhone and Android players can be friends, where the names in the feed come from, and who can see a 13-to-15's activity. §20.2 keeps a 13-to-15's profile private and says nothing about the feed.
G35.today: server/src/friends.mjs. invite() creates a 12-hex-character code that stays open for 7 days (INVITE_DAYS) and can be used once. accept() makes the friendship. There is no age check, so anyone holding a 13-to-15's code, or holding a code a 13-to-15 accepts, becomes their friend. remove() lets either player end it. feed() lists every heist from the last 7 days (FEED_DAYS) in which a friend was the raider or the defender, with account ids only; each row carries both the raider's and the defender's id, so the other party appears even when they are not the viewer's friend. A 13-to-15's heists are included. feed()'s comment says the device knows its friends "by their platform names", which assumes platform friendships; a friend made by invite on the other platform has no such name. Accounts have no display name (db.mjs accounts table; workshop.mjs line 189 says "Accounts have no display name yet"). challenge() links stay open 7 days and each player can play one once. A 13-to-15's link works only for their friends (service.mjs lines 376–386). A friend can raid a new player through the newcomer protection (service.mjs lines 363–371). No client screen for friends is built.

options.label: Keep the build's reading: invites, minors shown
options.means: Friends are made only by one player sharing a 7-day, single-use invite code and the other accepting it. Either can end the friendship. The feed shows a player every heist from the last 7 days in which one of their friends was the raider or the defender, with both account ids and the grade, including heists where the other party is a 13-to-15 who is not their friend.
options.consequences: It works across iPhone and Android with one mechanism, matching §24's one account across devices, and it matches §17.6's personal invites and §23.2's Friends screen. A 13-to-15 can befriend anyone whose code they are sent, adults included; that person then sees their heists and can play their challenge links. A minor also shows up, by account id, in the feed of every friend of anyone who raided them or whom they raided. The feed has no names to show until the device or server has a name source, so "Marta's crew" cannot yet be written.
options.numbers: Invites and challenge links last 7 days, and the feed reaches back 7 days (friends.mjs INVITE_DAYS, CHALLENGE_DAYS, FEED_DAYS).
options.doc_edit: §17.6: add a row or sentence: "Friends are made by a personal invite one player shares and the other accepts; either can end it." §20.2 or §20.7: say that a 13-to-15's heists show in friends' feeds.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Invites, and minors hidden from every feed
options.means: As A, but a 13-to-15's heists never appear in any feed: not in their friends' feeds, and not in the feed of anyone whose friend raided them or was raided by them. They still play friendly heists with friends, and challenge links go to in-game friends only, as §20.7 says.
options.consequences: This reads §20.2's "Profile: Private" as covering activity too. A stranger who gets a minor's invite code learns nothing from the feed, and a minor raided through matchmaking never appears to the raider's friends. The feed is a little emptier for friends of younger players. Invites still work across platforms. The name source is still missing, as in A.

options.doc_edit: §17.6: add the invite sentence as in A. §20.2 Profile row, or §20.7: add "A 13-to-15's heists do not appear in any friends' feed."

options.label: Platform friends and invites
options.means: Friends are made two ways. Friends on Game Center or Google Play Games who both play become friends, with each player's consent. Invites cover everyone else, including friends on the other platform. Minors are shown as in A.
options.consequences: Players find friends they already have with no code, and the platform supplies names and its own parental controls. It adds two platform integrations and their consent screens to a one-developer build, and Play Games' friends list needs a separate permission from the player. Friendships from the two sources have to merge without duplicates, and invite-made friends still need a name source.

Friends' feed, friendly heists, invitations, gifts

To in-game friends only
