recommendation.rationale: All three judges agreed on the goal: under §13.2's rule that no single layer decides outcomes, the Glare must stop being a realm-wide switch, and A and B fail that test (one Glare plus others holds 94-95%). Two judges (player experience, scope) chose the investigate-at-tile rule with a one-per-realm cap. Their case rested on the earlier draft's figures, and each named, as its main risk, that sending guards to the tile might prove stronger than the proxy that was measured. The balance judge measured the rule as written, and I reproduced it at n=400: 1 Glare holds 91.8%, and with the cap 1 Glare + 3 others holds 100%. So that dissent carries: limiting the Glare's reach to §12.17's own 4 m alarm spread is the only tested rule that turns it into a dial (1 to 3 Glares 68-77%, the generator's six 89.5% to 61.2%). It also meets what the other two judges wanted: a readable, recoverable setback, no stacking switch, and a one-line change that reuses existing spread code with no editor rule. Confidence is medium: 6 Glares still sit about 5 points above the best Glare-free kit (3 Wells, 88.8%), the harness crews know where every ward is, the 8 m alarm-4 reach is unmeasured, and realm 3 stays above its band under every option.

panel.reasoning:
From the player's side, the Glare as built (option A) is a hidden tile that ends the raid. Line 5880 of the design document says the Glare is "Hidden until revealed or fired", and it triggers when a crew member comes within 2 tiles. It then Alerts every guard in the realm within about half a second. So a crew that did not scout that one tile finds out the raid is over, not that it made a mistake it could recover from. That goes against §12.17 ("nothing here is random: a player who scouts an island can predict exactly what will happen") and §1.2's pillar ("Heists are won by reading an island's rules and finding a way through, not by bigger stats."). In a 20-minute session, an instant loss the player could not see coming is the most frustrating kind of failure.

Option B stops a Keeper stacking Glares, but it keeps the switch. On the harness, one Glare plus five other wards holds realm 3 at 96.2%, so one hidden tile still decides the raid, and the player feels exactly what they feel under A.

Option C turns the Glare into the kind of setback a heist story is made of. The alarm goes off, every guard walks to that spot, and a crew that moves during the 2-second blind can slip away or use the empty rooms. §12.17's Investigating row ("Walks to the spot and searches nearby for ten seconds, twenty from alarm level 3") already spells out behaviour the player can read. But C alone still lets a Keeper stack Glares: 2 hold 88.8% and 3 hold 97.5%. A realm full of Glares plays as a minefield, a raid ended by an early misstep, and it breaks §13.2's "If one layer decides outcomes, the others are decoration."

Option D keeps C's readable, recoverable effect and caps the Glare at one per realm. The cap is also something the player can scout: a crew knows there is at most one Glare to find. The best kit with a Glare (71.2%) lands level with the best kit without one (67.5%), inside the ±5-point standard error at n=80, so a Keeper chooses among kinds rather than buying one decisive ward. That fits §1.2's rule that wins come from reading an island's rules, not from bigger stats.

The build cost is small: one effect line in sim/src/lib.rs, one check in island.rs check(), and the matching lines in the harness. That suits one-developer scope.

Confidence is medium. The harness crews know where every ward is. The investigate rule that was measured is weaker than the one written. And realm 3 still holds above its 30–45% band under every option, so §5.2's ward counts need re-measuring over the kits a Keeper can build.

No damage." panel.reasoning:
I re-ran the harness at n=400 a cell, with the brief's settings: realm 3, 2 posts, one geometry band, three realms crossed, crack noise off, competent crew, defensive laws, v3.4 rules. The standard error is about ±2.5 points near 50% and ±1.5 near 90%. The harness copy and driver are in scratchpad/brief/f33j (run.py; GLARE_MODE in tools/heist_harness/sim.py).

1. The draft's C and D rest on the wrong measurement. The rule they describe, with every guard going to Investigating and walking to the Glare's tile, makes the Glare stronger than today:
- 1 Glare holds 91.8% against the build reading's 78.0%.
- 2 Glares hold 99.8%.
- The generator's six hold 99.2% against 89.5%.
- D's best allowed kit (1 Glare + 3 others) holds 100%.
The draft's 57.5% came from raising suspicion to 600 with no destination, which is not what §12.17's Investigating does ("Walks to the spot"). What makes a Glare decisive is pointing every guard in the realm at a tile on the crew's route. Whether they arrive Alerted or Investigating barely matters. A weaker version, where every guard only turns toward the Glare as if Suspicious, still holds 74.2% with one Glare and 98.8% with two.

2. B barely helps. One Glare plus 3 others holds 94.5%, and one plus 5 others holds 94.2%, so the jump from a single Glare stays.

3. Limiting the reach is the only rule tested that turns the Glare into a dial:
- Alerting only guards within 4 m of the tile: 1 Glare 68.2%, 2 Glares 75.2%, 3 Glares 76.5%.
- The generator's six fall from 89.5% to 61.2%.
- Each extra Glare now adds a few points instead of shutting the realm.
It reuses a distance rule §12.17 already states for the alarm. This fits "If one layer decides outcomes, the others are decoration" (§13.2), and it is a one-line build change for a one-developer scope. Investigate-at-tile within 4 m is not a dial either: 87.0%, 93.8%, 97.8%.

4. The draft's "best Glare-free kit 67.5%" is wrong. Three Gravity Wells hold 88.8%, while Well kits of 1 to 6 hold 30.2, 30.5, 88.8, 75.8, 72.5 and 32.0%. Snare/Well alternating kits of 1 to 6 hold 36.2, 41.0, 64.2, 63.2, 50.0 and 34.2%, 8 of them hold 95.8%, and no wards at all hold 36.2%. So ward count is not a dial for any kind. §13.2's check (31.5) must run over the kits a Keeper can build whatever is chosen here, and realm 3's six-ward, two-post budget likely needs resetting. One Glare stays above the 30-45% band under every option.

5. The build is probably stronger than any harness figure above. The harness sets ALERTED for one tick, and the Alert lapses after the 0.5 s state floor. sim/src/lib.rs (lines 1249-1257 and 2600-2606) instead applies near-zone fill for 5 s with every guard's interest on the Glare's tile. That is closer to the 91.8% rule than to the 78.0% one.

6. Economy: none of the options changes a Starlight price, and a ward costs 350 Starlight at level 1 (tools/economy_model data). The cost-three version in B and D saves at most 700 Starlight a realm, which is negligible. The economy model assumes raids succeed 60% of the time from day 31 (data.heist_success_rate). The build reading's generator mix at realm 3 (89.5% hold, about 10% success) breaks that assumption much more than the reach dial does (61.2% hold).

Confidence: medium. It is high that C and D as written go the wrong way. It is lower that 4 m is the right radius, because 1-post realms and the 8 m at alarm 4 were not measured, and the harness crews know where every ward is.

panel.variant: D, built on what the sim already has so the change stays small. (1) The Glare's effect is the heard event cracking already uses (§12.17: "It is a heard event, not a suspicion increment, because suspicion added below 600 drains before it can move an unaware guard."). In sim/src/lib.rs fire_ward (about lines 2600-2606), call the existing lure(gi, w.tile) for every awake guard, which sets interest to the tile and enters Investigating, or set guard.heard = Some(w.tile) as the crack path at line 1915 does. Then delete the revealed_until/reveal_spot near-zone fill at lines 1249-1257. In the harness, set g.heard to the Glare's tile and raise suspicion to at least INVESTIGATING (sim.py line 608). The harness already holds Investigating until the heard spot has been searched (sim.py about lines 522-529). This also measures the rule as described, with guards sent to the tile, which the brief's C/D numbers do not yet do. (2) The budget rule is one line in sim/src/island.rs check(): a Glare takes three ward places, so wards.len() + 2*glares must stay within WARD_LIMITS[level], and a second Glare is refused with a new Problem. The client editor's ward counter shows places used, not wards. Regenerate golden replays with the existing `cargo run --bin golden -- --write`, because Island::example() places a LanternGlare at (3, 9). Rewrite the harness test test_one_lantern_glare_outweighs_a_realm_of_other_wards (tools/heist_harness/test_harness.py:827) into the kit check: best Glare kit minus best Glare-free kit, within the standard error.
panel.reasoning:
From the scope and build-risk side, D is the only option that makes the ward budget something one developer can test, and it is cheap because both halves reuse code that already exists and is tested. Options A and B leave a switch in place: one Glare plus other wards holds 96.2% at realm 3. The §13.2 build-blocking check can then only pass by special-casing kits, so the rule that "no single layer decides outcomes" can't be tested at all. C by itself still lets a Keeper stack Glares (2 at 88.8%, 3 at 97.5%, against 67.5% for the best Glare-free kit). That means the kit check stays red, and every change to ward counts later has to be re-measured against an all-Glare kit. D brings the best Glare kit within realm 3's six places (71.2%) level with the best Glare-free kit (67.5%), inside the ±5-point standard error at n=80. That turns the §5.2 count back into a dial the harness can check with one assertion.

The engine cost is small. The sim already has the Investigating-at-a-tile verb: lure() at lib.rs about line 1168, used by illusions and sounds, and the heard path at line 1915, used by cracking. The Glare becomes one more caller of it, and a special reveal/near-zone branch goes away, so the perception code gets a little smaller. The budget rule adds one weighted count and one new Problem next to the existing TooManyWards check in island.rs line 414. The editor and the server (which runs the same sim check) pick it up without new systems. The content cost is none: no new art, no new ward, and the §10.3 row keeps its shape.

It also fits the document's goals. The Glare becomes a readable event at a known tile, matching §1.2's "Heists are won by reading an island's rules and finding a way through, not by bigger stats." and §13.2's "If one layer decides outcomes, the others are decoration." Confidence is medium. The harness crews know where every ward is. The investigate rule has only been measured in its weaker form (suspicion raised, guards not sent to the tile). Realm 3 stays above its 30-45% band. Realms with eight places (1, 2, 5) allow one Glare plus five others and have not been measured under D.

G19.question: How many wards and guard posts may the Heart hold, given that it has no realm level?
G19.why_it_matters: §10.2 counts wards and posts by realm level, and the Heart has none, so nothing limits its defence. Every raid ends in the Heart, where the Vault stands, so its budget moves hold rates more than any single outer realm's. The build currently answers in two different ways: the economy model uses level 1, while the sim and server let the island's own level byte decide.

The builder cycles the level freely (client/scripts/builder_screen.gd line 122). tools/economy_model/model.py (around lines 443-447) gives the Heart level 1's counts: 8 wards, 1 post.

Quiet Week's 'Heists are 30 seconds longer' pushes it to 270 s, or 8,100 ticks, which neither §5.4 nor §24.10 allows, and §12 and §12.2 put a heist at 2.5 to 4 minutes. None of them says whether the 30 seconds apply before or after the cap. The simulation's validator is the rule the server checks replays by, so this decides which Quiet Week replays are accepted.

G26.question: Which figures should §18.6, §18.7 and §20.12 give the Workshop: the server's current ones, the same rules with a larger quota and larger word lists, or no figures in the document at all?
G26.why_it_matters: The server already enforces the Workshop with figures the document never gives: how many islands a player may publish, how much storage they get, what 'cleared' means, what a player can report an island for, what a completion 'spike' is, and whether a remix earns its original anything. If nobody decides, the build's guesses become the game's rules without review. Four of them are visible to players: the name pool, the slot count, the report reasons, and the quota when it refuses a publish. Two of the build's figures hurt the creators §18.7 rewards: the quota is a lifetime cap, and the name pool produces duplicate names almost at once.
G26.today: server/src/workshop.mjs holds each reading as a named constant with a test (server/test/workshop.test.mjs). Names: an adjective plus a noun from server/src/words.json, 16 × 16 = 256 names, in English and Brazilian Portuguese (workshop.mjs:22, 76-81). Constellation names come from the same lists (social.mjs found(), lines 58-61; D63). Slots: SLOTS = 5, and BUILDER_SLOTS = 3 more for §18.7's Builder, so 8 (workshop.mjs:30-31). Quota: QUOTA_BYTES = 64 KiB, summed over every island the creator ever published, withdrawn and removed ones included, because nothing is deleted. A withdrawn island frees its slot, but its bytes still count (workshop.mjs:36, 133-139). Cleared: the creator's re-simulated replay gets any grade but foiled and banks loot (workshop.mjs:64-66). Report reasons: unfair, unplayable, copied, offensive, other (workshop.mjs:58). Spike: at least 50 completions in a day and more than 5 times the island's daily mean over the week before; the island is flagged and queued for a person (workshop.mjs:50-51, spike()). Remix: the new island names its original (remix_of) and earns the original nothing.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: The document states the server's figures: word lists as in server/src/words.json (16 adjectives × 16 nouns, both launch languages); 5 published islands, 8 for a Builder; a 64 KiB lifetime quota per account that counts everything ever published; 'cleared' means the creator's own run banks loot at any grade but foiled; five report reasons (unfair, unplayable, copied, offensive, other); a spike is a day with 50 or more completions and more than 5 times the previous week's daily mean; a remix names its original and pays it nothing.
options.consequences: Nothing changes in the build. The name pool is small and shared with constellations. Two islands are more likely than not to share a name by about the 19th island, and at 10,000 published islands each name is used about 39 times. The quota is a lifetime cap: at the example island's size a creator can publish about 133 times in total. One who withdraws and republishes to fix an island three times a week reaches that within a year and can never publish again. At §24.1's 10 KB per island only 6 fit, fewer than a Builder's 8 slots.
options.numbers: 16 × 16 = 256 names (words.json). A 50% chance of a shared name at 1.18 × √256 ≈ 19 islands (birthday bound); 10,000 ÷ 256 ≈ 39. The example island bundle is 449–491 bytes (sim's exampleIsland through server/src/sim.mjs); 65,536 ÷ 491 ≈ 133 publishes (146 at 449 bytes); 133 ÷ 3 a week ≈ 44 weeks. 65,536 ÷ 10,240 = 6.4 at §24.1's 'ten kilobytes each'. 5 + 3 = 8 slots sits inside §20.12's 'five and ten'.
options.doc_edit: §18.6 Safety: name the word lists (or cite words.json) and list the report reasons. §18.6 Publishing: define 'cleared'. §18.7 Anti-gaming: define a spike (50 a day, above 5 times the prior week's daily mean), and say a remix earns its original nothing. §20.12 Limits on publishing: replace the range with 5 islands (8 for a Builder) and a 64 KiB lifetime quota that counts everything ever published.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Build's rules, figures that don't bite
options.means: The rules stay as built: 5 slots and 8 for a Builder, a quota that counts everything ever published, and clearing, report reasons, spikes and remix as in A. Two figures change. The lifetime quota rises to 1 MiB, and the word lists grow to 64 adjectives × 64 nouns = 4,096 names, for islands and constellations alike.
options.consequences: No creator is locked out in practice: about 2,135 publishes of the example island fit. Cost control holds: in the worst case, a million accounts each full, storage costs about $15.6 a month. A shared name becomes likely only by about the 75th island, and at 10,000 islands each name is used about 2.4 times. Translators write 48 new adjectives and 48 new nouns in both launch languages, each Brazilian Portuguese adjective in both genders and each noun with its gender. Workshop.name() generates the 4,096 combinations.
options.doc_edit: As in A, with a 1 MiB lifetime quota and 64-word lists.
options.build_change: workshop.mjs: QUOTA_BYTES = 1024 * 1024. words.json grows to 64 adjectives and 64 nouns, with new words appended so existing indices (stored on islands and constellations) never change.

options.label: Rules in the doc, figures in data
options.means: §18.6, §18.7 and §20.12 state the rules without numbers, and name server/src/workshop.mjs and server/src/words.json as where the figures live, to be tuned in soft launch like any other data.
options.consequences: Figures can be retuned without a document edit. The document stops being the single source that tools/design_facts.py collects facts from, so the Workshop's figures are checked against nothing. The lifetime lockout and the duplicate names in A remain until someone retunes them.
options.numbers: none
options.doc_edit: One sentence in §18.6 and one in §20.12 pointing to the two files. Remove 'Between five and ten' from §20.12.
options.build_change: none to behaviour. The G26 comments in workshop.mjs point at the document sentence instead of the register.

recommendation.rationale: The build's rules are sensible, enforced and tested, and writing them into the document keeps it the source of truth, which suits one-developer scope. But two of its figures work against the players §18.7's ladder is meant to reward. A 64 KiB lifetime quota locks a creator out after about 133 publishes, and 256 names shared with constellations produce a duplicate by about the 19th island. Raising the quota to 1 MiB and the lists to 64 × 64 are data changes, and the worst-case storage bill stays about $16 a month, so §20.12's cost control holds.

quotes.text: Safety: island names come from word lists, every island can be reported, featured islands are reviewed by a person, and players aged 13 to 15 browse curated lists only (20.7).
Publishing: an island must be cleared by its creator before it can be published, so every island can be solved.
Between five and ten published islands per account, with a storage quota per account.
Anti-gaming: completions by the same player count once; completions from a creator's own constellation count at a quarter; sudden spikes are reviewed by a person.
A creator badge on your profile; your name shown on the island; 3 extra island slots

C43.question: May players aged 16 and over type their own island names, or do all players name islands from the word lists?
C43.why_it_matters: §18.6 says every island name comes from word lists. §20.7's table says so only for ages 13 to 15, which implies free names for older players. §20.4's word filter does not cover island names. If free names are allowed, typed island names reach every browser of the Workshop with no filter and no review. The same question applies to constellation names: §20.4 filters them as if players type them, but the build takes them from the same word lists.
C43.today: The server follows §18.6 for everyone. publish() refuses any name that is not an adjective index and a noun index into server/src/words.json ('name_not_from_the_word_lists', server/src/workshop.mjs:106-108). There is no free-text name field and no filter for island names. In the Workshop the age band is used only for browsing: a 13-to-15 account sees only the featured list (workshop.mjs:210-211, 'curated_lists_only'). Constellation names use the same word lists (social.mjs found(), D63).

options.label: Keep the build's reading: word lists for all
options.means: Every island name, at every age, is an adjective and a noun from the word lists.
options.consequences: No player can type an island name, so there is nothing to filter or review and no moderation cost. Older players lose the freedom of a custom name. The size of the pool alone decides how often names repeat: at 256 names, two islands are more likely than not to share a name by about the 19th island (G26 sets the size). The build names constellations from the same lists, so §20.4's line on constellation names should follow the same rule (D63).
options.numbers: 1.18 × √256 ≈ 19 islands for a 50% chance of a shared name (words.json, 16 × 16).
options.doc_edit: §20.7, the 'Publishing Workshop islands' row: 'Yes, names from word lists' in all three age columns (or one row note saying names come from word lists at every age).
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Free names from 16
options.means: Players 16 and over type their island's name. Players 13 to 15 pick from the word lists.
options.consequences: Typed names are shown to everyone who browses, including 13-to-15 players on curated lists if such an island is featured. Every name must pass §20.4's word filter in both launch languages (§20.10's free automated moderation), and every reported name joins the 24-hour human review queue. The Workshop then carries player-written text, which §20.10's cheapest safe configuration otherwise keeps out of it, and the client needs a second way to name an island.
options.numbers: §20.4's 24-hour review applies to each reported name. Neither the document nor the build gives a volume figure.
options.doc_edit: §20.4: add island names to the word filter's list. §18.6 Safety: 'names come from word lists for players aged 13 to 15; older players type them, filtered (20.4)'.
options.build_change: workshop.mjs publish(): accept a text name for accounts whose age_band is 16-17 or 18+, run it through a word filter for en and pt-BR, and store it. Featured lists shown to 13-to-15 players show only word-list names or the filtered text. Report reasons gain a name category.

recommendation.rationale: The document's safety posture (§20.10's cheapest safe configuration, and §24.1's 'Deterministic word lists … no machine learning') and one developer's moderation capacity both favour a single rule that needs no filter. It keeps §18.6 as written and matches the build, so the only edit is one row of §20.7. Its cost, frequent duplicate names, is fixed by the size of the lists (G26), not by opening free text.

G27.question: How are the six leagues' Renown boundaries set: fitted to §14.7's season-end shares as built, fitted to §14.7's arrival times, recomputed each season from rank, or refitted after a change to the Renown rules?
G27.why_it_matters: The server cannot place anyone in a league without boundaries, and the document gives none. §14.7 gives two targets: when an engaged player arrives in each league, and each league's share at season end. F40 shows both cannot hold at once under the current Renown rules. The item also leaves open what Dust, Ember and Tide earn at season end, where about two players in three finish, and whether Renown is kept in whole points.
G27.today: server/src/leagues.json, generated by tools/league_model.py and checked by tools/check_all.sh, starts the leagues at Dust 0, Ember 128, Tide 184, Star 300, Nova 644 and Paradox 1,160, with each league's divisions at thirds of its span. server/src/seasons.mjs rounds each Renown amount to the nearest whole point (lines 29-30, 144). Star, Nova and Paradox earn a cosmetic of their league and the season, and the other three earn nothing (reward(), seasons.mjs:46-53). At season end Renown is pulled halfway back toward the lower boundary of the league the player ended in (pulledBack(), lines 101-107). Seasons run back to back from RULEBORN_SEASON_START (server/README.md).

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: Boundaries are the league model's fit to §14.7's shares (Ember 128, Tide 184, Star 300, Nova 644, Paradox 1,160; divisions at thirds), regenerated whenever the rules move. Renown is kept in whole points. Only Star, Nova and Paradox earn season-end cosmetics. The pull-back floor is the lower boundary of the league the player ended in.
options.consequences: Season-end shares match §14.7. An engaged player arrives much sooner than §14.7 says: Ember on day 2, Tide on day 4, Star on day 8 and Nova on day 57, against the first week, week 3, month 2 and month 3 (F40). The climb is fast for the first week and then stalls for about seven weeks. The lower three leagues, about 64% of players at season end, earn nothing.
options.numbers: Boundaries from server/src/leagues.json. Arrival days from F40 (tools/league_model.py, 1,500 players over 4 seasons). Fitted season-end shares (league_model.py output): Dust 3.5%, Ember 29.7%, Tide 30.8%, Star 25.7%, Nova 9.0%, Paradox 1.3%; Dust, Ember and Tide together 64.0%. Under the model's three alternative assumptions the boundaries move by up to 25% (Star 300 → 375 with more engaged players), the others by 13% or less. §14.7's shares sum to 96%, so Dust's target is the other 4%.
options.doc_edit: §18.1: a generated table of league and division boundaries, marked as the league model's output like §14.2's tables, plus a sentence that Renown is whole points and only Star, Nova and Paradox earn season-end rewards. §14.7: the arrival column stays as the target, with a note that the current rules reach Ember on day 2, Tide 4, Star 8 and Nova 57 (F40).
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Fit to the arrival times
options.means: Boundaries are set so an engaged player arrives when §14.7's first column says: Ember in the first week, Tide by week 3, Star around month 2, Nova from month 3. The shares column becomes an outcome, not a target.
options.consequences: The climb is paced as the document describes, but the leagues bunch at the bottom. At season end about half the population is still in Dust, and Ember holds 2% against §14.7's 30% (F40). Top leagues stay rare.
options.numbers: F40: with Ember placed late enough for the first week, 'half the population is still in Dust and Ember holds 2% against 30%'. The boundary values themselves would come from re-running tools/league_model.py against the arrival targets, and no such run exists yet.
options.doc_edit: §18.1 as in A with the new boundaries. §14.7: the share column becomes the model's measured shares.
options.build_change: tools/league_model.py fits the arrival targets instead of the shares; regenerate server/src/leagues.json. check_all keeps checking it.

options.label: Set each season from rank
options.means: There are no fixed Renown boundaries. At a fixed interval (for example daily) and at season end, the server places players by rank among the season's active players: top 1% Paradox, next 10% Nova, 25% Star, 30% Tide and 30% Ember. Dust and Ember floors still stop a player falling below them.
options.consequences: Shares hold by construction, and arrival follows from ranking. A player can drop a league without losing Renown, because others overtook them, and for Tide and above that can happen mid-season. The Renown a league starts at is different every season, so no table can print it.
options.numbers: Shares from §14.7: 1 / 10 / 25 / 30 / 30, with Dust the remaining 4%.
options.doc_edit: §18.1: 'Leagues are placed by rank among the season's active players, at §14.7's shares', plus the floor rule and the recompute interval.
options.build_change: seasons.mjs: place() reads per-season boundaries computed by a periodic job that ranks active players (a read over every account's Renown). leagues.json and league_model.py fall away.

options.label: Change the Renown rules, then refit
options.means: Keep boundaries fitted by tools/league_model.py, but first make one of F40's changes: either a season-end pull-back smaller than halfway, or a small Renown grant per clean heist so that heists create Renown as well as moving it between players. Then fit the boundaries to both the shares and the arrival times.
options.consequences: Both the pace of the climb and the season-end spread can move toward §14.7. §18.1's 'halfway' or §12.9's formula changes, and every league figure is regenerated. Whether both targets can actually be met is unknown until the model is run.
options.numbers: None yet: no league_model run with either change exists.
options.doc_edit: §18.1 or §12.9 as chosen, plus the generated boundary table.
options.build_change: league_model.py gains the rule and is re-run; seasons.mjs changes pulledBack() or settle(); leagues.json is regenerated.

recommendation.rationale: The boundaries fitted to the shares are the right reading now. They are generated by the model and checked by check_all rather than typed by hand, and they give each league the season-end meaning players see. §14.7's arrival column should not be rewritten to days 2, 4 and 8, because it is a design target and F40 shows that the Renown rules, not the boundaries, stop both targets holding. D belongs to F40's decision, and once that is made the same model refits the boundaries. Separately, §18.1's 'rewards are given by league' reads as every league earning something, so give Dust to Tide a small season cosmetic, since about two players in three end there.

F37.question: Where does a player who never raids get the experience and pages that let them progress?
F37.why_it_matters: §14.4 promises that a non-raider restores the launch 24 laws in about 80 days and the full Codex in about 195, from the Library alone. Under the document's own gates, that player earns almost nothing. The Library opens at Keeper 4. Experience from spending is capped by the Spire, which Keeper levels gate. Experience from restoring laws needs pages. In the model the non-raider stalls at Keeper 2. That makes two claims false today: §10.4's claim that the Library is 'the whole of a non-raider's progression' (the floor §14.4 says 13.3 rests on), and §7.6's promise that raiding is 'not the only' path. Even without the gates, §10.4's school rule caps the Library at 12 of the launch 24. The model also leaves out §14.4's 3 pages for a Lab experiment that finds nothing. A non-raider can reach that source without a heist, and pages are how a non-raider earns experience.
F37.today: The server grants no Keeper experience; progression exists only in the economy model. tools/economy_model/data.py:286 defines the never_raids archetype (5 sessions, 0 heists, 3 Lab experiments). model.py pages_today() (lines 579-595) gives it the Library alone. Its docstring says Lab experiments that find nothing and first meetings with a law are left out. Run for 400 days, the archetype ends at Keeper 2 (reached on day 3) with the 3 starting laws, because it never reaches the Library's Keeper 4 gate. test_economy_model.py (around line 411) asserts it stays below Keeper 12 and never restores the Codex. docs/design/generated/pacing.md prints 'never (F37)' for both Codex rows.

options.label: Keep the build's reading: Library alone
options.means: A non-raider earns only the Library's pages, as §14.4 says. The Library is gated at Keeper 4 and there is no other experience source, so they stall at Keeper 2 with the three starting laws.
options.consequences: There is no way to progress without raiding. §14.4's 80 and 195 days, §10.4's 'the whole of a non-raider's progression' and §7.6's 'not the only one' all become false and must be withdrawn. Players who prefer building stall on day 3. The soft-launch trigger that compares non-raider retention with raider retention has nothing to measure.
options.numbers: Model run, never_raids, 400 days: Keeper 2 (reached day 3), 3 laws, no milestones.
options.doc_edit: §14.4: replace both never-raids lines with 'a player who never raids does not progress past Keeper 2'. §10.4 and §7.6 drop the non-raider claim.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Library plus daily goals; launch 24 is the ceiling
options.means: The non-raider's floor is the page sources §14.4's table already lists that need no heist: the Library, plus daily goals worth about 2 pages a day. At least one goal each day needs no heist. Goal pages go to the law the player has marked as the one they are working on, whatever its school. This is the same idea as §7.6's bad-luck floor, and it is how a non-raider gets laws outside their three starting schools. Recommended addition: the tutorial's two Drifting ruins (§16: the first heist at 2:00 and a second ruin at 7:00, both on day 1) pay §14.2's successful-heist experience. Later ruins keep §12.10's pages and Essence and pay no experience; paying it on every ruin is option C. Ruins are counted apart from §14.1's heists a day, which are raids on player islands, echoes and 12.22's fallback targets. A ruin charges no entry fee and never uses up one of G20 C's 20 paid raids, even when it fills a thin target list (12.22). Its Essence counts only toward G20 C's currency backstop (33.3 × B a week). Later chapters (Keeper 12 and up) need heists.
options.consequences: Plain B: a non-raider reaches Keeper 8 on day 46 and restores all 24 launch laws by about day 78, against §14.4's 80. Then they plateau for good, with the Keeper bar at 937 of the 1,020 XP to Keeper 9 and the Spire stuck at level 2. §14.8's home screen, which shows the nearest goal, would then show '83 XP to go' forever. With the tutorial-ruin addition, the same player reaches Keeper 11 on day 87 with Spire 3 open, and plateaus on a fresh bar (1 XP toward Keeper 12). If the tutorial ruins paid only the foiled-heist rate, the bar would stop 19 XP short of Keeper 9, which is worse. Without the working-on routing, the Library-style school rule stops the player at 12 launch laws, and pages that land in unwanted schools make the 78 days late. The non-raider never opens chapter 3, so every season's new laws need heists. Because ruins sit outside §14.1's counts, the two tutorial ruins are extra experience for every player, not only the non-raider. That moves the generated tables by about a day: Keeper 40 for the engaged player goes from day 357 to 358 at the low edge and from 349 to 348 at the top, and the regular player's from 440 to 439 at the top (446 at the low edge does not move). A few purchase rows move more, because buying order shifts (the casual player's Vault level 2 goes from day 27 to 39 at the low edge). G20 C's 20-raid week is untouched, because no ruin counts toward it. Empty Lab experiments (§14.4's 3 pages) would only make the plateau come sooner.
options.numbers: Economy model, rerun.run('never_raids', 'low', 600, codex='launch'), with pages_today() raised for the archetype only. At +2 a day: Keeper 3 on day 6, 4 on day 8, 8 on day 46, then no further (keeper_xp 937 of KEEPER_XP_TO_NEXT[7] = 1,020); 12 laws on day 25, 24 laws on day 78. At +1 a day: Keeper 8 on day 58, 24 laws on day 97. At +11 a day (goals plus the Lab's most, 3 empty experiments × 3 pages): Keeper 8 on day 19, 24 laws on day 33, bar at 857 of 1,020. The plateau is Keeper 8 every time, because Spire 3 needs Keeper 9 (data.SPIRE_KEEPER_LEVEL = 1, 5, 9, 13). With +2 a day and two successful ruins on day 1 (§16's timing): Keeper 8 on day 39, 9 on day 77, 10 on day 82, 11 on day 87, 24 laws on day 76, Spire 3, 1 XP toward Keeper 12. One ruin on each of days 1 and 2 gives the same days. Two foiled ruins on day 1: Keeper 8 on day 39, stuck at 1,001 of 1,020. All days are the fastest case, because the model pools pages across schools; routing to the working-on law is what makes that pooling true. The Library's cap of 12 of the 24 comes from §10.4's school rule with the three starting schools (§14.8). Every archetype with two extra successful heists' experience on day 1, full Codex, both edges (engaged 420 days, regular 520, casual 400): Keeper 40 engaged 357 to 358 (low) and 349 to 348 (top); regular 446 unchanged (low) and 440 to 439 (top); engaged full Codex 92 unchanged (low) and 92 to 90 (top); casual full Codex 241 to 239 (low) and 240 to 239 (top). Scratch scripts: brief/f37_px.py, brief/f37_syn2.py, brief/f37_sep.py, brief/f37_sep2.py, brief/f37_sep3.py.

options.label: Ruins pay heist experience every day
options.means: All three Drifting ruins a day (§12.10), which already pay pages, also pay Keeper experience, so a player who never attacks another island progresses through ruins. The rate is either §14.2's successful-heist rate (30 + 6 × level) or its foiled-heist rate (10 + 2 × level).
options.consequences: A non-raider who plays the ruins passes Keeper 8 and reaches the full Codex and season laws. At the successful rate, three ruins a day fill the Codex on day 88, before the engaged raider's day 92, which breaks §7.6's 'Raiding is the efficient path'. At the foiled rate, raiding stays about twice as fast (day 92 against 175). Ruins sit outside §14.1's heist counts, which G20 C's 20-raid week needs, so every player gains experience and every generated pacing table (§14.2, §14.3, §10.2) moves earlier. At the foiled rate with three ruins a day, Keeper 40 moves from day 357 to 332 for the engaged player, and from 446 to 358 for the regular one. A player who never heists at all still stalls, as in A.

At the foiled rate: Keeper 8 on day 12, Keeper 12 and the launch 24 on day 34, Keeper 24 and all 48 laws on day 175 (§14.4 states about 195), Keeper 40 on day 511. At the successful rate: Keeper 12 on day 20, the full Codex on day 88, Keeper 40 on day 343. The engaged raider in the same model gets the full Codex on day 92 and Keeper 40 on day 357. At 1 ruin a day and the foiled rate: the launch 24 on day 54, the full Codex on day 512. All players with 3 foiled-rate ruins a day on top of their raids, low edge, 700 days: Keeper 40 engaged 357 to 332, regular 446 to 358, casual from past day 700 to day 651. Scratch scripts: brief/f37_low.py, brief/f37_syn.py, brief/f37_eng2.py.
options.doc_edit: §12.10: 'ruins pay §14.2's foiled-heist experience' (or the successful rate). §14.1 says its heists a day are raids and ruins are counted apart. §14.4's never-raids lines become 'the Library, daily goals and Drifting ruins: the launch 24 in about 34 days, the full Codex in about 175'. Every table that moves is republished.
options.build_change: economy_model: a ruins activity (experience and pages, no haul) on top of §14.1's raids for every archetype, then a full re-run and republished tables (ties to G22). The server records ruin heists for experience when Keeper experience is built, and leaves them out of G20 C's paid-raid count.

options.label: Defending earns experience
options.means: §14.2's foiled-heist experience (10 + 2 × level) goes to the defender whose island foiled the raid, so a builder levels by being raided and holding.
options.consequences: Building a strong defence becomes a path of its own, which fits §13's 'defence is designed'. But progress depends on how often other players raid you, which the player does not control, and a weak island earns almost nothing. It cannot be priced without a raid rate. It also opens a way to farm experience: friends can fail raids against each other on purpose.
options.numbers: No figure: the document states no rate at which an island is raided.
options.doc_edit: §14.2: 'foiled heists (10 + 2 × level) to the defender'. §14.4: the never-raids lines are recomputed at a stated raid rate.
options.build_change: economy_model: a defender income from an assumed raid rate. The server credits experience to the defender in Service.grant when a raid is foiled, and needs a check against collusion.

recommendation.rationale: B, with the tutorial's two ruins paying successful-heist experience and daily-goal pages going to the law the player is working on. This makes §14.4's launch promise true (the launch 24 in about 76–78 days against the stated 80) using systems §14.6 and §7.6 already have. Ruins are counted apart from §14.1's raids, so they never use up one of G20 C's 20 paid raids; the cost is that the tutorial ruins move the published tables by about a day. It adds one testable assertion, which suits one-developer scope. The player-experience and scope judges both chose B. The player-experience judge added the tutorial-ruin experience so the non-raider plateaus on a fresh bar at Keeper 11 with Spire 3 open, not frozen at 937 of 1,020 XP. That judge also had §14.1's counts include ruins; the brief does not, because G20 C's 20-raid week is built on §14.1's four raids. The scope judge added the page routing and the test. The balance judge dissented for C at the foiled-heist rate, correctly showing that no page source moves B's plateau past Keeper 8. That leaves chapter 3, season laws and §14.4's 195-day Codex out of a non-raider's reach, and §32's Library-output trigger cannot fix it. It stays the upgrade path if the owner wants non-raiders to reach the full Codex (day 175, raiding still about twice as fast). Confidence is medium because the dissent concerns what the floor is for, not a factual error.

Never raids: the Library alone, averaging about 6 a day while it is levelled out of production income — about 195 days

F37.also_needed: Whatever the option: whether an empty Lab pairing can be re-run for §14.4's 3 pages, and at what rate experiments find nothing (the model leaves these out). For B: confirmation that daily goals always include one that needs no heist and that its pages go to the law the player is working on, and whether the tutorial's two ruins pay §14.2's successful-heist experience, which only works at the successful rate. panel.variant: B, with one addition that removes a stuck progress bar. §14.2 states that a ruin heist pays heist experience like any other heist, so the tutorial's ruins count, and §14.1 states that its heists-a-day counts include ruins. The economy model gives the never_raids archetype the experience from the tutorial's ruins; the engaged tables already book experience for every heist from day 1, so they are unchanged. My rerun, with 2 goal pages a day, 1 successful ruin on each of days 1 and 2, and the rest of the model unchanged: Keeper 8 on day 39, 9 on day 77, 10 on day 82, 11 on day 87, then a plateau with a fresh bar (1 XP toward 12). Everything else in B stays the same: at least one daily goal a day needs no heist, and goal pages may be of any school. §14.4 says later chapters need heists, and the 195-day line goes.
panel.reasoning: Through the player lens, the useful question is what a builder who never raids sees on the home screen, week after week. Option A shows it stuck on day 3. That breaks §7.6's own rule, "Raiding is the efficient path, not the only one.", and the reason §7.6 gives for it: "gating a resource behind one activity is where players stop feeling directed and start feeling forced [210]". C serves a player who avoids other players' islands, but it leaves the player who never heists at Keeper 2, so §14.4 and §10.4 still need rewriting. D ties a builder's progress to how often strangers attack them, which the builder cannot control, and nobody can price it. B is the only option that makes the launch promise true using systems the document already has (§14.6 daily goals already include non-heist goals such as "birth a ruleborn"). I reran the model: at +2 pages a day, the launch 24 are done by day 78 against §14.4's 80, and Keeper 8 comes on day 46. The pages must be allowed from any school, or §10.4's school rule stops the player at 12 laws. Plain B has a flaw I found in the rerun (the scratch script is at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ruleborn/4036626a-ccc0-53cd-b585-d7b6007ab17e/scratchpad/brief/f37_px.py). The player stops at 937 of 1,020 XP toward Keeper 9, which is the level that opens Spire 3 (data.SPIRE_KEEPER_LEVEL = 1, 5, 9, 13), and stays there. At +11 pages a day they stop at 857 of 1,020. §14.8's rule "| The home screen surfaces whichever goal is closest to done, whatever kind it is." would then show "83 XP to go" forever, a goal that can never be reached. That is the opposite of what §14.8 wants. If the tutorial's ruins pay experience, which is the plain reading of §14.2's "successful heists" and matches §12.10's "They carry the tutorial and give new players safe practice with unfamiliar laws.", the same player reaches Keeper 11 and Spire 3, and the stop falls on a fresh bar instead. The engaged pacing tables don't move, and nothing new has to be built, which fits one-developer scope. Confidence: medium.

panel.variant: Drifting ruins pay experience at §14.2's existing foiled-heist rate (10 + 2 × Keeper level) rather than the successful-heist rate (30 + 6 × level). Their pages, which §12.10 already grants, are booked as well. For the published tables, §14.1's heist counts are raids, and the never_raids archetype is priced as 3 ruins a day plus daily goals (about 2 pages), with no haul and no Renown. Ruin pages come from laws the player has not met (§12.12: the game "draws from what they haven't"), so they also get around §10.4's owned-school rule without a separate exception. Economy model, never_raids, low edge, 700 days, with pages_today and award_xp patched for the archetype (scratch scripts in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ruleborn/4036626a-ccc0-53cd-b585-d7b6007ab17e/scratchpad/brief/f37_low.py): 3 ruins a day at the foiled rate gives Keeper 8 on day 12, Keeper 12 on day 34, the launch 24 on day 34, Keeper 24 and the full 48-law Codex on day 175 (§14.4 states about 195), and Keeper 40 on day 511. The engaged raider in the same model gets the full Codex on day 92 and Keeper 40 on day 357. At 1 ruin a day it gives the launch 24 on day 54 and the full Codex on day 512. The doc edits are §12.10, "ruins pay §14.2's foiled-heist experience", and §14.4's never-raids lines restated as "daily goals and Drifting ruins, besides the Library: the launch 24 in about 34 days, the full Codex in about 175".
panel.reasoning:
B's plateau is structural, and no page source can fix it. In the model the non-raider's experience comes only from restoring laws, which stops once the 24 laws of the first two chapters are restored, and from spending, which the Spire caps (it is stuck at level 2). I reran the model at +1, +2, +5 and +11 pages a day, and it stopped at Keeper 8 every time. It never opens chapter 3, never gets a season's new laws, and never reaches §14.4's 195-day Codex. The soft-launch trigger in §32 ("the Library’s page output moves up one level-step each season") cannot move a Keeper plateau, so under B the only fix the document plans for non-raider retention would do nothing.

Only an experience source tied to a heist gets past Keeper 8. Ruins already exist (§12.10, three a day, pages and Essence), carry the tutorial, and involve no victim. That makes them the non-PvP play §7.6 means when it says raiding is "not the only" path for "the many players who prefer building", and it adds no system, which suits one-developer scope.

The brief's C at the full successful-heist rate is too generous. With 3 ruins a day the non-raider fills the full Codex on day 88, ahead of the engaged raider's day 92, which breaks §7.6's "Raiding is the efficient path". Paying §14.2's foiled rate uses a figure the document already has. It lands the full Codex on day 175 against the stated 195, and raiding stays about twice as fast (day 92 against 175).

D cannot be priced: the document states no rate at which an island is raided, and the player does not control it. A (keep the build) breaks §7.6, §10.4 and §14.4 outright.

panel.variant: B, tightened so it can be tested. (1) The pages from the non-heist daily goal go to the law the player marks as the one they are working on, the same idea §7.6 already uses for its bad-luck floor ("Every eighth heist guarantees a page of a law you are actually working on", line 2199). The model pools pages across schools, and this rule makes that pooling true, so the model's 78 days become exact and not just the fastest case. It also settles "any school" with one rule, where a picker by school would need its own design. (2) The model's non-raider floor counts only daily goals (+2 a day). Empty Lab experiments stay out of the floor, because the document states no rate at which an experiment finds nothing. They are extra on top, so the published days still err low. (3) Replace the test_economy_model.py assertion "stalls below Keeper 12" (lines ~409-412) with two: never_raids restores the launch 24 by about day 80, and plateaus at Keeper 8 on the full Codex. The document's sentence then has a test that fails if later tuning breaks it.
panel.reasoning:
Seen through scope and build risk, B is the only option that keeps §14.4's promise without a new system and without moving the engaged player's published tables. I re-ran the model (rerun.run('never_raids','low',600) with +2 pages a day for the archetype only). It gives Keeper 3 on day 6, Keeper 4 on day 8, Keeper 8 on day 46 and no higher. It reaches 12 laws on day 25 and the launch 24 on day 78, against the document's 80. At +1 a day it reaches the launch 24 on day 97. At +11 a day it reaches Keeper 8 on day 19 and the launch 24 on day 33. The plateau is Keeper 8 every time, because Spire 3 needs Keeper 10 (design line 5596) and spending experience is capped by the Spire.

The daily-goal system is already in scope: §14.6 lists goals like "birth a ruleborn" that need no heist. So B adds one content rule (always offer one non-heist goal) and one page-routing rule, not a new engine path. The model change is one line in pages_today() (tools/economy_model/model.py:579-595), and the plateau can be asserted in a test.

C looks cheap but is not. The build must decide whether §14.1's heist counts include ruins, and if they don't, every pacing table in §14.2, §14.3 and §10.2 moves and must be regenerated and republished. G22 already says those tables move by months on unstated assumptions, and C adds another. It also does nothing for someone who never heists at all.

D cannot be tested. It rests on a raid rate the document never states and the model cannot derive. It adds a server path to credit experience to the defender in Service.grant. It also opens a collusion exploit (friends failing raids on purpose to farm experience) that one developer would have to police.

A costs no build work but removes the floor that §13.3 and §10.4 rest on. It also makes the soft-launch trigger that compares non-raider and raider retention (design line 15362) meaningless, so it saves code by breaking a pillar.

The honest cost of B is that the document must say plainly that a non-raider plateaus at Keeper 8 and that chapter 3 and every season's new laws need raiding. The 195-day line has to go.

G22.question: Which staffing order, realm-opening order and Guardian Post staffing should §14.1 state as the basis for the published pacing tables?
G22.why_it_matters: §14.2 says the Keeper and milestone tables are the economy model's output, but three choices that move them by months are not stated in §14.1: which producer a new worker staffs, which realm types open first, and whether posts are staffed. Across these choices Keeper 40 moves from day 337 to day 1,113. Until they are written down, the tables describe a player the document never defines.

options.consequences: The tables stay as generated: Keeper 40 on day 357, everything built on day 719, the 38th character on day 249. They describe a player who leaves every Guardian Post empty. A player who staffs every post reaches Keeper 40 on day 1,113 and never builds everything, so a player who guards trades pace for defence.

options.doc_edit: §14.1 'Logic: what the model assumes': three sentences (staffing Heart first, median realm order, posts unstaffed). Pacing sentences quoting Keeper 40 move to day 357 under §14.2's rule.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

Each milestone becomes a range across two dimensions (§9.6's attempt band and realm order), which is harder to read.

options.doc_edit: §14.1: staffing and posts sentences as in A, plus 'realm order is the player's; tables give its spread'. §14.2 and §14.3 tables gain the realm-order range.
options.build_change: rerun.py prints the realm-order spread for every milestone, not only for Keeper 40 and everything built, and the table check compares both edges.

options.label: Even staffing
options.means: A new worker goes to each producer in turn (one each), not Heart first. Posts are unstaffed, and the realm order is the median.
options.consequences: This is what a player who spreads workers does. Pacing is slower: Keeper 40 on day 424 (+67 days), everything built on day 877 (+158), the 38th character on day 276 (+27).
options.doc_edit: §14.1: 'workers are spread one to each producer in turn'. Every pacing table is regenerated, and sentences that quote them move.
options.build_change: config.py staffing_order = 'even'. Re-run the model and republish pacing.md and the document tables.

options.label: Staff every post

options.consequences: The economy does not finish: Keeper 40 on day 1,113, and never everything built or the 38th character. under-staffing is normal, and choosing which producer goes short is the decision

C42.question: What is the chance that a heist finds a stray, and does a bonus-page chance sit beside it or share it?
C42.why_it_matters: §11.5 says one heist in eight finds a stray. §14.6 says one in eight finds a stray or a bonus page, which makes strays rarer, perhaps one in sixteen. The odds are shown to players in the Codex, so the game must display one number, and the economy model needs one rate.
C42.today: The server and simulation grant no heist strays; the only stray the server grants is at the top of the season track (server/src/track.mjs:51). The economy model takes §11.5 and reads it as one in eight successful heists: HEIST_STRAY_CHANCE = 1/8 (tools/economy_model/data.py:503), with no bonus-page roll. In the model, a stray found with no free home waits until one frees up (model.py _strays()). pacing.md shows that halving the rate to one in sixteen moves nothing it publishes (357 / 719 / 249 either way), because homes, not strays, limit the roster (F38).

options.label: Keep the build's reading: §11.5's rate
options.means: One successful heist in eight finds a stray. There is no separate bonus-page surprise; the Lucky trait's 10% bonus page (§11.3) stays the only one.
options.consequences: An engaged player finds about 0.3 to 0.4 strays a day (4 heists × 60–80% success × 1/8). The Codex shows 'one in eight'. The published pacing does not move. Once the roster is full (around day 249, F38), a stray has no home and the document does not say what it becomes, so §14.6's only surprise needs a rule for that case.
options.numbers: 4 × 0.8 × 1/8 = 0.40 and 4 × 0.6 × 1/8 = 0.30 strays a day (§14.1 heists, §14.5 success arc). pacing.md: 357 / 719 / 249; 38th character on day 249.
options.doc_edit: §14.6: 'any successful heist has about a one-in-eight chance of a stray, with the odds shown in the Codex' (drop 'or a bonus page'). §11.5: add 'successful'.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: §14.6's shared one in eight
options.means: One heist in eight gives a surprise, split evenly: one in sixteen a stray, one in sixteen a bonus page.
options.consequences: Strays arrive half as often (about 0.15 to 0.2 a day for an engaged player), and a bonus page adds about 0.15 to 0.2 pages a day, around 1% of the ~16 a day §14.4 gives. Nothing published moves. Late in the game the bonus page keeps a surprise possible once the roster is full.
options.numbers: 4 × (0.6–0.8) × 1/16 ≈ 0.15–0.20 of each a day. pacing.md's 'one in sixteen' row: 357 / 719 / 249.
options.doc_edit: §11.5: 'About one successful heist in sixteen finds a stray'. §14.6 stays, with the split stated.
options.build_change: data.py HEIST_STRAY_CHANCE = 1/16, plus a bonus-page term of 1/16 a success in pages_today(). The server's grant rolls one surprise when heist strays are built.

options.label: Two separate one-in-eight chances
options.means: Every successful heist rolls twice: one in eight for a stray and, independently, one in eight for a bonus page.
options.consequences: Strays arrive as in A, plus about 0.3 to 0.4 extra pages a day for an engaged player, around 2% of the page economy. The Codex shows two odds. The extra pages move the Codex days slightly earlier, so the Codex rows need a re-run.
options.doc_edit: §14.6: 'one in eight a stray and, separately, one in eight a bonus page'. §14.4's page table gains a row.

A bonus page is already the Lucky trait's job, so a second page roll adds a rule without a purpose. The full-roster case is F38's to settle, for example by having strays wait for a free home, as the model does.

quotes.text: Strays found on heists. About one heist in eight finds a stray in the target universe; carrying it out adds it to the roster with three traits, one of them rare.
No reward for logging in. Surprises replace it: any heist has about a one-in-eight chance of a stray or a bonus page, with the odds shown in the Codex.
