G21.question: What is one target list's 'difficulty band', and how often are the lists rebuilt?
G21.why_it_matters: §24.8 makes target selection a cached file 'per difficulty band', 'generated periodically', and defines neither. The band decides how big each file is and what the device must filter itself. The rebuild period decides how long a republished island's old snapshot stays offered, and how many database rows every rebuild reads. In this build that read count grows through each season (see G33).
G21.today: server/src/service.mjs targetLists() (line 214) builds one list per realm level ('realm-level-N', or the snapshot's own band column when set). Each entry carries the island's Glicko rating and deviation, Keeper level and Renown, so the device applies §12.22's filters itself. A new player's islands are left off the lists while their shield holds (matchmaking.mjs shielded(): their first 72 hours or until their first raid). Lists are content-addressed, so an unchanged band keeps its edge cache. A band keeps its current and previous list, and a band with no islands left loses its list. server/src/main.mjs:181-184 rebuilds every 15 minutes (TARGET_LISTS_MS) and once at start. A lease on a snapshot no island holds any more is granted as an echo (§12.3) for 14 days after it was published: the raider is paid a haul, but no Renown moves, and the owner is not paid, rated or notified. After 14 days, and always for a trace or a friendly heist, it is refused as 'superseded' (service.mjs:346-365, 626-653). For each listed island a rebuild calls seasons.league(owner), which re-sums every Renown row the owner has this season (renownIn(), seasons.mjs:109-115).

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: A band is a realm level, the unit of §12.22's success-band guarantee. Each list carries every entry's rating for the device to filter. Lists are rebuilt every 15 minutes, and each entry's Renown is re-summed from the owner's Renown rows at every rebuild.
options.consequences: A republished island's old snapshot stays offered for at most 15 minutes. A raider who leases it in that window plays an echo: they are paid a haul, no Renown moves, and nothing is taken from the owner. Reads grow through the season. At mid-season a rebuild reads about 63 to 231 rows per island, about 6,000 to 22,000 a day, so the free plan's 5 million reads a day run out at about 230 to 830 islands, before any heist. At 1,000,000 islands on the paid plan, rebuilds alone cost about $156 to $640 a month in reads.
options.numbers: 96 rebuilds a day (main.mjs:181-184). Fixed rows per island per rebuild: the islands, snapshots and accounts join (3), shielded() (1), islandRating() (1), the current season (1) and the standing (1) = 7. Renown rows: renownIn() reads every row the owner has this season, so at R rows a day there are 28 × R at mid-season. R = 2 to 8 is an assumption: each raid books one row for the raider and usually one for the defender, at §14.1's 1 heist a day (casual) to 4 (engaged). (7 + 56) × 96 = 6,048 and (7 + 224) × 96 = 22,176 a day; 5,000,000 ÷ 6,048 ≈ 830 and ÷ 22,176 ≈ 225 islands (§28.3 free plan). Paid: 10^6 × 6,048 × 30 = 1.8 × 10^11 and 10^6 × 22,176 × 30 = 6.7 × 10^11 a month, less 2.5 × 10^10 included, at $0.001 per million ≈ $156 and $640 (§28.3). Writes: one target_lists row per band per rebuild (load.json 'target lists (x96)': 96 a day), plus one standings row for each listed owner not yet seen in the current season, written by the first rebuild after a rollover (seasons.mjs standing(), reached from service.mjs:236).
options.doc_edit: §24.8: 'A band is a realm level; each list carries its islands' ratings so the device filters; lists are rebuilt every fifteen minutes.' §24.8's snapshots row: 'difficulty band' becomes 'realm level'.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Realm level, rebuilt hourly
options.means: A band is a realm level, as built, but lists are rebuilt once an hour.
options.consequences: A republished island's old version stays listed for up to an hour. A raider who picks it plays an echo: they are paid a haul, no Renown moves, and nothing is taken from the owner. A new player's island is shielded for their first 72 hours or until their first raid, so a slower rebuild rarely delays it. An established player's newly opened realm can wait up to an hour to become a target. The Renown on each entry, which the device filters to within 150, can be up to an hour old. Rows read by rebuilds fall to a quarter: at mid-season the free plan's reads last to about 900 to 3,300 islands as built, or about 29,800 if each player's Renown is kept as a running total.
options.numbers: 24 rebuilds a day: (7 + 56) × 24 = 1,512 and (7 + 224) × 24 = 5,544 rows per island per day; 5,000,000 ÷ 1,512 ≈ 3,300 and ÷ 5,544 ≈ 900. With a running Renown total, 7 × 24 = 168 a day; 5,000,000 ÷ 168 ≈ 29,800 (at 15 minutes, 7 × 96 = 672 a day and ≈ 7,440). NEW_PLAYER_SHIELD_HOURS = 72 (server/src/facts.json).
options.doc_edit: §24.8 as in A, with 'every hour'.
options.build_change: main.mjs: TARGET_LISTS_MS = 60 × 60 × 1000 for the lists. The season rollover keeps its own 15-minute interval, since today it shares the same constant.

options.label: Realm level × rating band
options.means: A band is a realm level cut again by Glicko-2 rating (§12.22 step 1's 'within one band'), so the device downloads only targets of nearby difficulty. Lists are rebuilt every 15 minutes.
options.consequences: Downloads are smaller. Files multiply (realm levels × rating bands), and a thin cell is more often empty, so the device more often fetches other files for §12.22 step 4's fallbacks and widening. Rows read per rebuild are unchanged, and rows written grow by one per cell per rebuild.
options.numbers: No band width is stated anywhere; the count of files is realm levels × rating bands.
options.doc_edit: §24.8: 'A band is a realm level and a rating band of N points'. §12.22 step 1 names the same width.
options.build_change: service.targetLists() keys lists by realm level and rating bucket. The device fetches the neighbouring buckets when widening.

recommendation.rationale: Realm level is the unit of §12.22's guarantee, and the build already carries ratings so the device can filter, so the band should stay as built. Hourly rebuilds cut the rows that rebuilds read fourfold, and players see little of the cost: a new player is shielded anyway, and a stale entry is played as an echo that pays a haul and takes nothing from its owner. That fits §24.1's goal that the free tier carries the early game. Separately, and needing no decision, the build should keep each player's season Renown as a running total on the standing row. That is the larger saving: about 7 reads per island per rebuild instead of up to about 230 at mid-season.

quotes.text: Target selection is a file, not a query. Candidate lists per difficulty band are generated periodically as static objects, so choosing a target costs a cached download rather than a database search.
the middle of the list is drawn from the raider-success band for the target's realm level — 60 to 75% at realm level 1, 55 to 70% from realm level 2 (13.2)
Bundle hash as the key, realm type, difficulty band, when published. Never edited
Robbing an echo takes nothing from its owner; its loot is created by the game.

G21.also_needed: For C, a rating band width in Glicko-2 points.

G33.question: Should §24.1 budget rows read as well as rows written, and must the load test be re-run on the edge platform before its figures are trusted?
G33.why_it_matters: §24.1 budgets only writes. But the database plan §28.3 cites bills rows read too, and caps the free plan at 5 million a day, and nothing measures them. The load test runs on local Node and SQLite, so its figures are a lower bound: index writes are not counted, fees and hauls are not booked, and its CPU time is not an edge isolate's. §24.1's cost table could be wrong at scale without anyone seeing it. The target-list rebuild (G21) is already a read cost that grows with the number of islands and through the season.
G33.today: server/load.mjs plays §14.1's players through the service for 3 days (60 players per archetype) and counts SQLite's changes as rows written. It says so at line 16: 'Rows read are not measured'. It prices monthly players with §25.1's one-in-three daily share (facts DAILY_SHARE, load.mjs:140). server/load.json: engaged players write 46.01 rows a day against a budget of 5 (9.2×), regular 23.58, casual 10.53. Re-simulation takes p50 15 ms (p95 20.9 ms) against the free plan's 10 ms, so validationFitsFreePlan is false. The paid plan at 1,000,000 monthly players costs $415 a month if all are engaged, $191 if regular, $60 if casual. Its raiders hold no Starlight, so no fee is booked, and its drawn raids are foiled, so no haul is booked.

options.label: Keep the build's reading
options.means: §24.1 budgets writes only. The load test stays local: SQLite's change count as rows written, local Node CPU, no rows read, raiders without Starlight. Its figures are read as a lower bound.
options.consequences: No new work. Reads stay unbudgeted. Per row, a read costs a thousandth of a write on the paid plan, but one read pattern grows with islands × rebuilds rather than with play. The target-list rebuild reads about 6,000 to 22,000 rows per island per day at mid-season (G21). That exhausts the free plan's daily cap at a few hundred islands and costs about $156 to $640 a month at 1,000,000 islands. Writes and CPU are understated by an unknown factor.
options.numbers: server/load.json as above. Reads $0.001 and writes $1.00 per million past the paid allowance (§28.3). Rebuild reads from G21.
options.doc_edit: §24.1: one sentence saying the budget covers writes and that the load test's figures are a local lower bound.
options.build_change: none: this is what the build does

options.label: Budget reads, measure locally
options.means: §24.1 adds a rows-read budget per active player per day, and the load test counts reads locally by wrapping every query and counting the rows it visits. It also gives raiders Starlight and lets some drawn raids succeed, so fees and hauls are booked, and it measures a late-season state as well as the first days.
options.consequences: Reads become a checked design constraint, and check_all fails a change that adds reads, as it already does for writes. The run must include a population with weeks of Renown rows (for example 56 days); otherwise a 3-day run cannot see the rebuild cost that grows through a season. Figures remain SQLite's, not D1's billing, and CPU remains this machine's.
options.numbers: Candidate budgets from the plans: the free plan's 5,000,000 reads a day ÷ 3,333 daily players (10,000 monthly ÷ 3) = 1,500 per player-day. The paid plan's 25 billion a month ÷ (333,333 daily × 30) = 2,500 per player-day at 1,000,000 monthly. §24.1 and §28.3 give the plan figures; §25.1 gives the one-in-three share.
options.doc_edit: §24.1 Budget line: 'and N row reads per active player per day', with the plan arithmetic. The load test is named as what checks it.
options.build_change: load.mjs: a counting wrapper on db.prepare, reads recorded in load.json and checked, and a late-season scenario. Raiders are seeded with Starlight and a share of drawn raids succeed.

options.label: Budget reads, run on the edge
options.means: As B, plus the load test is run on the edge platform itself (Workers with D1) before soft launch. D1 reports the rows read and written it bills, index writes included, and the CPU a real isolate uses. Those figures replace the local ones in §24.1.
options.consequences: The cost table rests on billed numbers, and the 15 ms against 10 ms CPU question (F47) gets a real answer. The paid Workers plan ($5 a month) is needed at launch anyway, because re-simulation already exceeds the free plan's CPU. The added cost is the work of deploying the server as an edge function and writing a load driver that runs against it. The run also shows whether the target-list rebuild, which issues several queries per island, fits in a scheduled edge invocation at all.
options.numbers: Plan figures as in B. Paid plan $5 a month, $0.001 per million reads and $1.00 per million writes past the allowance (§28.3). load.json: p50 15 ms, p95 20.9 ms against 10 ms.
options.doc_edit: §24.1 as in B, plus 'measured on the edge platform before soft launch'. The monthly cost table is recomputed from the edge run.
options.build_change: As B, plus a Workers and D1 deployment of server/src/http.mjs and a load driver that runs against it, with its figures recorded in server/load.json.

options.label: Run on the edge, writes and CPU only
options.means: As C, but §24.1 still budgets writes only. The edge run reports rows read, with no budget and no check.
options.consequences: Billed writes (index writes included) and isolate CPU become known. Reads are visible in each run but unchecked, so a change like G21's per-rebuild Renown sum can add reads unnoticed between runs.
options.numbers: As in C.
options.doc_edit: §24.1: the edge run is named as what checks the write budget; the cost table is recomputed from it.
options.build_change: As C, without the reads check in check_all.

recommendation.rationale: §24.1 calls its budget 'the design constraint, not an estimate made afterwards', yet it is measured on the wrong machine and ignores the free plan's hard cap of 5 million reads a day, which the target-list rebuild alone can exhaust at a few hundred islands (G21). Validation already needs the $5 paid plan (F47), so an edge run before soft launch costs only the deploy work and replaces local guesses with billed writes and real isolate CPU. Reads cost a thousandth of a write per row, so D is defensible, but only a checked reads budget catches periodic jobs whose cost grows with the number of islands rather than with play.

quotes.text: Budget: about 100 to 200 kilobytes and five writes per active player per day. That is the design constraint, not an estimate made afterwards (24.4).
The paid plan is $5 a month and includes 25 billion row reads and 50 million row writes — several times what a million players generate [199]
the free plan allows 5 million row reads and 100,000 row writes a day with 5 GB storage
a third of monthly players play on a given day

G33.also_needed: For B or C, the rows-read budget figure itself (1,500 per player-day fits the free plan at 10,000 monthly players, and 2,500 fits the paid plan's allowance at 1,000,000). For C or D, a Cloudflare account on the $5 Workers plan.

F51.question: What keeps a realm's edge open to land on, so that a Keeper cannot funnel every crew through one tile?
F51.why_it_matters: §5.4 makes open landing a pillar ('Defenders can't choose where raiders come from'), but the only edge rule in §6.1 protects the last route, not the edge. A realm ringed with blocking terrain and one gap publishes today, and its gap is the landing every crew must take, guarded by whatever stands beside it. That is the 'one guarded gate' §5.4 says the game does not have, and it changes what the hold rates in §13.2 measure.
F51.today: sim/src/island.rs check() requires one open edge tile (LandingBlocked) and a walkable route from some open edge tile to the Vault (Sealed). Island::landings() lists the open edge tiles; the simulation drops a landing anywhere else and verify_on refuses a heist that never lands. Nothing counts how many edge tiles are open.

options.label: No blocking terrain on the edge
options.means: No blocking feature and no Crystal Wall may stand on an edge tile, so every edge tile of a realm is a landing.
options.consequences: Landing is fully open, as §5.4 describes. A Keeper defends the edge only with what does not block: tall grass, fog, light, wards on open ground, guards and laws. 'Cliffs … along every edge' in §5.4's own reasoning has to go or become inland.
options.numbers: Every edge tile open: 36 at realm level 1 (10 by 10) up to 52 at level 5 (14 by 14), 4 × side − 4.
options.doc_edit: §5.4 'Landing' row: add 'No blocking terrain or Crystal Wall stands on an edge tile.' §6.1: the same rule beside the route rule.
options.build_change: island.rs check(): a new Problem, EdgeClosed, for any blocking feature or Crystal Wall on an edge tile; the builder shows it.

options.label: At least half of each side open
options.means: Each of a realm's four sides keeps at least half of its tiles open to land on, counting Crystal Walls as closed.
options.consequences: Cliffs and walls along the edge stay a tool, as §5.4's 'cliffs, tall grass, lantern light and laws along every edge' wants, but no side can be sealed and no single tile can become the gate. A Keeper still shapes where landing is easy.
options.numbers: At realm level 1 each side of 10 keeps 5 open, so at least 16 landings (a corner counts on both its sides); at level 5 each side of 14 keeps 7, at least 24.
options.doc_edit: §5.4 'Landing' row: add 'Each side of a realm keeps at least half its edge tiles open to land on.' §6.1: cite it beside the route rule.
options.build_change: island.rs check(): a new Problem, EdgeClosed, when any side has fewer than half its tiles open, with every Crystal Wall standing.

options.label: Keep the build's rule
options.means: One open edge tile and a route from some open edge tile to the Vault, which is all §6.1 asks.
options.consequences: A Keeper may wall the whole edge but one tile and choose where every crew lands. §5.4's 'Why open landing' then describes something the rules do not guarantee.
options.numbers: As few as 1 landing tile at any realm level.
options.doc_edit: §5.4 'Why open landing': say the edge is open unless the Keeper closes it, and that a realm may have one gate.
options.build_change: None.

recommendation.rationale: It is the smallest rule that makes §5.4's promise true: no side sealed and no single gate, while cliffs along the edge, which §5.4 names as defence, stay possible. A removes a tool the document wants; C contradicts the section's own reason for open landing.

quotes.text: Defenders can't choose where raiders come from; they can only make every edge a puzzle.
cliffs, tall grass, lantern light and laws along every edge
not one guarded gate
terrain can lengthen routes but never close the last route from the edges to the Heart

F51.also_needed: Whether a climbable cliff counts as open for landing; the build treats only walkable tiles as landings.

F52.question: Does a Lantern Glare's reach stretch with the alarm's, so Whispers makes it realm-wide again, or is it a fixed 4 m?
F52.why_it_matters: F33's answer made the Glare a local alarm, 4 m, and its build change took the alarm's reach, which Whispers sets to the whole universe. The defensive weave picks Whispers often, so on the harness two Glares still hold realm 3 at 91.5%, the switch F33 set out to remove. The brief's figures for F33's answer (68.2% and 75.2%) were measured with a fixed 4 m.
F52.today: sim/src/lib.rs spread_reach() is SPREAD_METRES (4) scaled by the sheet's AlarmRange; the Glare's reveal and the alarm spread both use it. tools/heist_harness/sim.py does the same (SPREAD_METRES * sheet.factor('alarm_range')). test_the_decided_glare_still_outweighs_a_realm_where_whispers_stretches_it pins 91.5% against 37.0%.

options.label: A fixed 4 m
options.means: The Glare shows the crew to the guards within 4 m of it, whatever the realm's alarm range. Whispers still carries a raised alarm to every guard in the universe, as its sheet says, but does not stretch the Glare.
options.consequences: F33's answer does what its figures said: one Glare is one strong pick among the kinds, not a switch. Whispers stays exactly what its Tier I cell says it is, an alarm law.
options.numbers: Harness, realm 3, two posts, defensive laws, competent crew, n=200: no wards 39.0%, one Glare 65.5%, two 72.5% (the brief measured 68.2% and 75.2% at n=400); six Snares and Wells 37.0%.
options.doc_edit: §10.3 Glare: 'Shows the crew to every guard within 4 m of it for 5 seconds (8 m from alarm level 4, 12.17) and blinds the crew for 2', adding 'a fixed reach, which laws that widen the alarm do not change'.
options.build_change: sim/src/lib.rs: the Glare's reveal uses SPREAD_METRES unscaled (keep spread_reach() for the alarm). tools/heist_harness/sim.py likewise; re-pin F52's test to the fixed reach.

options.label: Stretch with the alarm (the build)
options.means: The Glare reaches as far as the realm's alarm: 4 m, or the whole universe under Whispers.
options.consequences: A Whispers realm's Glare is realm-wide again, so two Glares and Whispers hold realm 3 near 90%. §5.2's budget has to be re-measured over kits with that case in, and Whispers becomes a much stronger defensive pick than its sheet reads.
options.numbers: Harness as A: two Glares 91.5% against six Snares and Wells' 37.0%.
options.doc_edit: §10.3 Glare: 'within the alarm's reach of it (4 m; the whole universe under Whispers)'.
options.build_change: None: this is what the build does.

recommendation.rationale: F33 was answered to stop one ward kind from deciding a realm; B brings that back through a law whose own sheet only talks about the alarm. A is what the brief's figures described.

quotes.text: Shows the crew to every guard in the realm for 5 seconds and blinds them for 2
Alarm spreads by distance, not everywhere at once: guards within four metres start investigating half a second later
When one guard raises the alarm, every guard in the universe hears it.

F52.also_needed: Whether the 8 m reach from alarm level 4 applies to the Glare, which the simulation does not build for the alarm either.

F53.question: B(V)'s base: 5,000, the every-day check with the fee an attempt keeps counted, or 4,600, the figure F36's answer named, with the fee left out of the check?
F53.why_it_matters: The base is the one dial on the raid faucet. F36's answer chose the rule (every day) and quoted its value before F39's fee was in the attempt; with the fee in, each day priced with that day's fee, the rule gives 5,000. Every haul, fee and cap moves with it: B(3) is 11,250 at 5,000 and 10,350 at 4,600.
F53.today: tools/design_facts.py HAUL_BASE = 5000, listed behind the document under F36; server/src/facts.json carries it. tools/economy_model/raidworth.py levels() prices each day's attempt with that day's fee (attempt_value() takes the fee off when Config.entry_fee is on) and binds each Vault level on its worst day; rerun.settle() ships smallest_passing_base(first_day_only=False).

options.label: 5,000: the rule, with the fee counted (the build)
options.means: The base is the smallest hundred at which an average attempt, less the fee it keeps, pays at least what the crew would have produced at home, on every day at every Vault level.
options.consequences: Hauls are 8.7% larger than at 4,600; the check and the fee agree, so no Vault level has a day on which raiding is the worse choice.
options.numbers: Every day with the fee: 5,000 (4,900 fails). Without the fee: 4,600. On the day each level arrives: 3,100. Birth rule: 1.3455 at both edges either way.
options.doc_edit: §9.6: 'B(V), the base — 5,000 × 1.5^(V−1)', and in 'What a raid must be worth': 'an average attempt, less the entry fee it keeps, pays at least …, on every day at a level'.
options.build_change: None: this is what the build does.

options.label: 4,600: the figure named, fee outside the check
options.means: The base is 4,600, and the check prices an attempt without its fee.
options.consequences: On some days an attempt, after its fee, pays a little less than staying home, the case §9.6's sentence says players skip.
options.numbers: At 4,600 with the fee counted the check fails; without it it passes on every day.
options.build_change: tools/design_facts.py HAUL_BASE = 4600 and facts.json regenerated; raidworth.attempt_value() leaves the fee out; the server tests re-pinned (B(3) 10,350, fee 207).

recommendation.rationale: The owner chose the rule, and the rule is about whether a raid is worth making; a fee the raid costs belongs in that sum.

quotes.text: at every Vault level, an average attempt pays at least what the same characters would have produced working over the heist and its rest
A crew on a heist does not work (5.8), and a raid that pays less than staying home is a raid players skip.

F54.question: A non-raider stops at Keeper 10, 6.5 experience short of 11, for good: show it as a gate, give exactly one more level, or open the ceiling?
F54.why_it_matters: F37's answer made the launch 24 the non-raider's ceiling and Keeper 12 the first level that needs heists. Built, the plateau lands a hair below the next level, which reads as a bug, not a design.
F54.today: tools/economy_model: a never-raids player reaches Keeper 10 on day 82 and holds 2,223.5 of 2,230; test_finding_a_player_who_never_raids_stops_levelling pins it.

options.label: Show it as a gate
options.means: Nothing changes in the rules; the client shows the bar as waiting on the Spire (a gate), not as nearly full.
options.consequences: The ceiling F37 chose holds exactly; the near miss is a display question.
options.numbers: Keeper 10 from day 82; launch 24 by day 76.
options.doc_edit: §14.4: 'a player who never raids reaches Keeper 10 and the launch 24; its bar then waits on the Spire, which needs heists'.
options.build_change: Client: the Keeper bar shows a gate when the only experience left is spending the Spire holds back.

options.label: Exactly one more level
options.means: The tutorial's ruins pay enough more experience to cross into Keeper 11, and nothing else changes.
options.consequences: The plateau becomes Keeper 11, still below 12; the next level's bar starts empty rather than full.
options.numbers: 6.5 experience is the whole gap today; any change to spending or the ruins moves it, so the margin should be set with room (say 50).
options.doc_edit: §16: the two tutorial ruins pay a successful heist's experience and 50 more.
options.build_change: economy_model: the ruins' extra experience; re-pin the test at Keeper 11.

options.label: Open the ceiling
options.means: Daily goals pay 10 experience a day, or a ruin a week pays a heist's.
options.consequences: A non-raider goes past Keeper 12 without heists, which F37's answer ruled out.
options.numbers: Goals: Keeper 16 by day 568. A weekly ruin: Keeper 20 by day 499.
options.doc_edit: §14.2: daily goals or ruins as an experience source.
options.build_change: economy_model and the server's goals, when built.

recommendation.rationale: It keeps the ceiling the owner chose and fixes what reads badly, which is only how the bar is drawn.

G41.question: How much of the game should a player with no network be steered into: is offline the normal path, as §24.12 says, or the exception?
G41.why_it_matters: §24.12 builds the game for offline play first. That is what makes a heist on a train possible, but every heist played offline is shown as confirming and can come to nothing if its lease expired or its result does not reproduce. Most games of this kind stay online. How strongly the phone steers players online decides what the client asks for, what it shows while offline, and what §24.12 should say.
G41.today: The machinery is built: a lease from the server, play on the phone, the outbox (client/data/outbox.gd) keeping a replay until the server has it, validation and a grant (server/src/service.mjs), and a result shown as confirming until then (client/scripts/result_screen.gd). A heist started offline plays the fixture realm. Nothing keeps leases in stock, nothing recommends going online, and the outbox sends only when the next heist is submitted.

options.label: Online only
options.means: A heist needs a connection to start and to submit. With no network the Heist button says so and waits.
options.consequences: The simplest to build and to explain, and nothing is ever shown as confirming. A player underground cannot play.
options.numbers: None.
options.doc_edit: §24.12: replace its opening with online only, and drop the Play and Queue stages' offline cases.
options.build_change: The heist screen refuses to start offline; the outbox stays for a dropped submission.

options.label: Offline as the normal path (§24.12 as written)
options.means: The phone keeps leases and plays as if offline were ordinary; results confirm whenever the network returns.
options.consequences: The widest play, and the most results that wait or come to nothing, shown to players as a normal state.
options.numbers: A lease lasts a day (LEASE_MS, service.mjs:44), with one grace submission.
options.doc_edit: None.
options.build_change: A lease stock, the outbox sending on reconnect.

options.label: Online first, offline the exception
options.means: Online is the rule and is recommended heavily. While online the phone keeps a small stock of leases. Starting a heist offline shows a prompt recommending going online first, and the player may carry on. Hauls stay confirming until the server confirms them, and the outbox sends by itself on reconnecting, with a banner saying so.
options.consequences: Players are steered to the path where nothing waits, and a heist on a train still works. A little more to build than A.
options.numbers: A stock of three leases, refreshed while online; each lasts a day.
options.doc_edit: §24.12: its opening says online is the normal path and offline the exception, and names the stock, the prompt and the confirming states.
options.build_change: A lease stock in the heist repository, the offline prompt on the heist screen, the outbox flushed on reconnect with a banner.

recommendation.rationale: It keeps §24.12's safety for the train and the lift while steering players to the path where nothing is left confirming, as games of this kind do.

quotes.text: Offline is the normal path, not an edge case, and the rules below are architecture rather than polish.

F55.question: Every realm level now holds above §13.2's 30 to 45% at §5.2's budget, and from realm 4 the guards alone do: cut the budget to reach the band, re-tune the raid side against the budget, or move the bands?
F55.why_it_matters: §5.2 sizes each realm's wards by what reaches §13.2's band, and §13.2 says most raids should pay. With every answer built (F35, F33, F52), the competent crew is held 47.6, 60.8, 59.9, 90.6 and 95.5% at realm levels 1 to 5 (n=800), and three guard posts with no wards hold realm 5 at 58.4%, so no ward count reaches the band from realm 4 up. The server's matchmaker and the Workshop hold islands to §13.2's bands, which the budget cannot now reach.

options.label: Cut §5.2's budget to what reaches the band

options.doc_edit: §5.2: the wards 7, 3, 6, 2 and 0 and one post at every realm level; §13.2's table re-set to these measured holds.
options.build_change: tools/heist_harness island.WARDS and POSTS, the server's facts for §5.2's budget, and Island::check's limits in sim/.

options.consequences: Building stays deep at every realm, but no single lever does it: the sweep shows one lever strong enough for realms 4 and 5 pushes realms 1 to 3 below the band. The rules gain realm-level figures, and the answer waits on the owner's sign-off of each.
options.numbers: Harness sweep, §5.2's full budget, n=200, held at realm levels 1 to 5: as built 52.0, 60.0, 61.0, 90.5, 95.0. Guards seeing 0.7 as far: 27.5, 34.0, 37.5, 74.0, 77.5 (2 and 3 inside). Suspicion filling 0.6 as fast: 37.5, 52.0, 38.5, 78.5, 86.5. Both together: 11.0, 23.0, 27.5, 63.5, 66.5. Sight 0.7 with two posts at realms 4 and 5: 27.5, 34.0, 37.5, 47.5, 59.5. Slower guards (0.8) raise holds; a faster crew or a longer clock moves realm 1 only.
options.doc_edit: None until the lever is chosen; then the section that owns it, and §13.2's table re-set.
options.build_change: Realm-level figures for the chosen levers in sim/ and the harness (python3 -m tools.heist_harness levers measures any), then §13.2's table re-run.

options.doc_edit: §13.2: the bands by realm level re-stated at the measured holds.

options.label: B for realms 1 to 3, A for realms 4 and 5
options.means: Realms 1 to 3 keep §5.2's wards and posts and take realm-level raid-side figures (the balance pass); realms 4 and 5 take option A's cut to one post, where no raid-side figure the grid tried reaches the band.

Realms 4 and 5 on one post (A, n=800): 38.0% with two wards, 36.9% with none.
options.doc_edit: §5.2: one post and the wards 2 and 0 at realm levels 4 and 5; the realm-level figures for realms 1 to 3 in the section that owns guard sight and suspicion; §13.2's table re-set to the measured holds.

D keeps building deep where the numbers allow it and cuts only where they do not; A cuts everywhere, B cannot reach the top, C gives up §13.2's reason for the band.

quotes.text: Each realm level now gets the smaller of the wards it needs to reach its hold band (13.2) and eight, the legibility cap 13.2 sets: 8, 8, 6, 7 and 8.
A realm level keeps 30 to 45% if its best setting within eight wards reaches it
Most raids should pay, or raiding dies

The economy model leaves upkeep out of its re-run (tools/economy_model/rerun.py:41). sim/src/combos.rs works out which combinations sound and leaves their cost to the economy. Screens v3's Weaving screen counts a harmony once per partner per shared note (screens_main.js:355-356), refuses a weave into Breaking ('Too much strain', :406), and orders its deck: harmony first, clash last, then cheapest (:361). Its Harmony view counts a harmony once per note, and gives the crown law Kinship a different change in each realm: +25% in Emberreach, ±0% in Skyfield, −10% in Tidehold (screens_meta.js:1066-1086).

options.label: Upkeep on the universe's share, and the drafted rules
options.means: Every realm pays the upkeep share × (woven laws' cost ÷ capacity) of its own hourly Aether, chord draws not charged, so a universe weaving nothing pays nothing. A crown law is priced once, by the Heart's laws, as §8.5's worked example does; the realm laws it harmonises or clashes with elsewhere take their own 15% or 25%. A harmony counts once per shared note, for every law carrying that note. A weave that would take strain to 125% or over is refused. A tier rise happens in place: the law keeps working at its old tier for the new tier's weave time and pays 40 Aether for each point the tier adds. Weaving ranks a law that harmonises first, one that clashes last, then the cheapest, and its comparison shows each candidate's points, the band after weaving, and the harmonies and clashes it would make.
options.consequences: One number, strain, prices upkeep, and §23.5 already says strain belongs to the universe. 'One running none pays nothing' becomes true of the universe, not the realm. The harmony rule matches the simulation's one effect per note (G25) and the Harmony view. The ranking is the design's own deck order.
options.numbers: At §5.5's day-61 row (228 of 276, 83%), upkeep is 20.7% of Aether production at the 25% share. Three laws on one note: each pays ×0.85. Haste and Frictionless (Flow and Spark): each ×0.85² = 0.72.
options.doc_edit: §5.6: 'the realm's stability budget' becomes 'the universe's capacity', and 'a realm running laws worth half its stability' becomes 'a universe whose woven laws cost half its capacity'; §29.1 to match. §5.5 and §8.2: the crown and harmony rules. §5.5's Breaking band: 'no weave may take strain into it'. §5.6: the tier rise. §19.6 and §23.2: the ranking and the comparison. §23.5 adopts weaving one law as a realm law in several realms.
options.build_change: Strain and upkeep on the server, from the woven laws it already reads in each bundle; the builder prices weaves and refuses them past 125%; the economy model adds upkeep so §9.5's sink rule can set the share.

options.label: Upkeep on each realm's own share, and the drafted rules
options.means: A realm pays the upkeep share × (its own woven laws' cost ÷ the universe's capacity) of its own Aether, with crown laws charged to the Heart. The other five rules are as in A.
options.consequences: §5.6's 'one running none pays nothing' holds realm by realm. But a realm's laws are a fraction of the universe's, so upkeep falls to about a sixth of A's, and §9.5's sink rule, capped at one half (F17), may not absorb enough Aether without cutting the Aether Spring ladder.
options.numbers: Day 61 with the cost spread evenly over six realms: each realm about 13.8% of capacity, so upkeep is about 3.5% of Aether production at the 25% share, against A's 20.7%.
options.doc_edit: §5.6 and §29.1: 'its woven laws' cost over the universe's capacity, crown laws charged to the Heart'; the rest as in A.
options.build_change: As A, with upkeep computed realm by realm.

options.label: Screens v3's Weaving screen as the rule
options.means: A harmony counts once per partner per shared note, and a crown law is priced in every realm, so its discounts and penalties compound across realms. Upkeep as in A, since the design shows none. Breaking, tier rises and the ranking as in A.
options.consequences: The Weaving screen is already drawn, but the design's own Harmony view counts differently. A crown law that harmonises widely loses the crown's ×2: what §5.1 calls double stability stops costing double.
options.numbers: A crown law at ×2 that harmonises in k realms: 2 × 0.85^k, which is 1.04 at k = 4, 0.89 at 5 and 0.75 at 6. Three laws on one note: each pays ×0.85² = 0.72.
options.doc_edit: §5.5 and §8.2: harmonies counted by partner and note; a crown law priced in every realm; the rest as in A.
options.build_change: As A, with the design's counting.

recommendation.rationale: A prices upkeep on the one stability figure the document has, which §23.5 already places on the universe and which the server can work out from the bundles it holds. It keeps upkeep near what §5.6's 25% describes, and the harmony rule is the one the simulation and the Harmony view already use. B keeps §5.6's realm wording but cuts the only recurring Aether sink to about a sixth, against F17's criterion. C undoes the crown's double cost once a crown law harmonises in four realms. The other five rules are the same in every option, and each is one sentence.

quotes.text: 25% when the realm's stability budget is fully spent, scaling in proportion to the share actually used
Stability is how much law a universe can hold.
Crown laws count in every realm, so a crown law can harmonise with every realm's laws.
While a slot is being woven it is empty.

options.label: Model the crew, and write the four rules
options.means: The lease and the replay carry one crew manifest (each member's kind, form, level and traits, the Sage, and the casts carried), which G47's commands and G60's actors also use; the server checks it against the roster it holds, and sim/ models them. §11.4 to §11.6 state four rules. The Spire's three places count as a home at the Spire's level, for the ceiling and the rest cut, and a character moves between free places at no cost. options.numbers: Level 10: ×2.00 health and power compounding, against ×1.72 added; carry ×1.55 against ×1.45. A Loyal, Sleepy member after a clean heist, Hearth 5: 45 × 0.75 × 0.75 × 1.5 = 38 min multiplied, 45 min if added.
options.doc_edit: §11.4: 'compounding', and which number grows for each two-number ability (Lantern Wisp, Featherkin, Echoplate, Prism Mite). §11.5 and §11.4: the Spire's places as a home at the Spire's level, and how a character is housed. §11.6: the modifiers multiply. §11.3: Loyal for those who got out. §23.2: reassign follows §14.1's staffing order.

options.label: Write the rules now, model the crew in a later stage
options.means: The four rules are written as in A. Until sim/ models the crew, the client shows level, traits and form as home facts and marks heist numbers as not yet in play; validated heists keep the five fixed roles.
options.consequences: The client can ship the Roster and Character sooner. But for that stage a level and a heist trait change nothing in a validated heist, and players are told so on screen. The rest timers come from the device, not the server.
options.doc_edit: As A.
options.build_change: Client screens first; A's lease, replay, server and sim/ work moves to a later stage.

options.label: Heists by role only

options.build_change: A smaller manifest (kind, form, Sage); no level or trait code in sim/.

A's four rule choices are the ones the repository already reads (compounding) or the smallest that close each gap, and multiplied modifiers make their order irrelevant. B is a fair staging if the client must ship first, but only if the screen says plainly that levels do not yet act in heists. C removes a progression axis the document is built around.

Nearly every empty pair stirs a card, so the shelf can be read off without finding the pairs, and §8.4's 'hidden until discovered' lasts about a week for an engaged player. If the times differ, the timer gives the answer before the result.
options.numbers: While all twelve are undiscovered, 243 of the 264 empty pairs (92%) stir a card. Each stir shows one of 24 law places, so at most 24 empty experiments show every pair: 8 days at §14.1's three experiments a day.
options.doc_edit: §8.6: the stir rule. §15.1: 'Hints appear only after repeated failure' loosened for the Lab. §10.2: a settle time per resonance in place of one per level.

A discovery pays Insight only if G52 keeps it (G52 A), at an amount set with G52's figures; under G52 B or C a discovery's reward is the resonance itself. §7.6: the 3 pages go to the law the player marked as working on (F37) if it is in either school, otherwise to the first law placed. Only restored laws may be placed. While a universe holds a paradox, an unstable pair runs as an ordinary one and the warning says so.
options.consequences: Keeps §15.1's repeated-failure rule, §10.2's one time per level and §8.4's hidden shelf, and gives the Codex one 'hinted' state for both kinds of hint (G49). Every rule is a count or a table the server can check. Chord naming is free and takes no slot, so it never competes with experiments. The design's stir and per-resonance times are refused in §23.5.
options.numbers: A hint needs three empty experiments with one law: a day at §14.1's three a day. Lab level 3 opens at Spire 5, about day 42 (§8.6), and from then names one of the 12 chords a day at most.

B's stir gives the shelf away in about 24 empty experiments and overturns both rules; A leaves a §23.2 must-show and §8.5's promise unbuilt. C's figures (three failures, once a day) can change without changing the choice.

quotes.text: Two law slots, timer, result, hints, paradox warning
Hints appear only after repeated failure, and every hint is tested before release
The Lab names chords — from level 3 it identifies one the player has woven or crossed — and is a teaching surface, not a lock.
Lab experiments that find nothing give 3 pages of a law from those schools

G53.also_needed: Under G52 A only, the Insight a discovery pays, from the economy model alongside G52's other Insight figures; whether the first experiment (§16's 5 minutes) is charged (C49); and whether an empty pair can be run again for its pages, which F37 raised.

G54.question: Is swapping a law on the curation screen a weave at §5.6's price and time, and may generating a defence unweave a law the player wove?
G54.why_it_matters: §5.6 is the only rule for putting a law into a slot: Aether, a wait, and an hour's rest after a removal. Laws also raise production (§9.2), so one realm's laws are both its economy and its defence. If curation swaps for free, every weave can go through curation and §5.6 applies to nobody; if the generator may unweave, a player's production laws change without their choosing.
G54.today: No weaving exists on the server. A realm's laws are whatever its published bundle carries, set in the builder with pylons and sent through PUT /v1/islands/:realm (server/src/http.mjs), which checks only the realm and Vault levels (server/src/universe.mjs problems()). So every law change is free and instant today. There is no generator outside the Python harness (D66). Screens v3's Swap, and the Slow rivers Across/Along choice, apply at once with no price or timer and show only a change in hold (screens_meta.js:540-546, 579-583).

options.label: A swap is a weave; the preview is free
options.means: The curation screen previews any swap at once and for nothing. Applying it removes the old law and weaves the new one at §5.6's price and time, both shown on the button. Re-placing a choice law (Across or Along) changes no law and stays free, like reshaping terrain (§6.1). The generator never unweaves: it weaves only into empty slots and only laws that help the defender, and the first defence's weaves are instant, as C51 proposes for the tutorial's.
options.consequences: One rule puts a law in a slot, so the server prices weaving once (TD.14) and §9.5's Aether sink holds. Curation stays instant to explore and takes time to commit. A player who wove a raider-friendly law for production keeps it in their defence, and the generator works around it.
options.numbers: 40 Aether × 10 to 26 points: 400 to 1,040 Aether a swap. Into the old law's slot: the hour's rest, then 10 min, 40 min or 2 h, so 1 h 10 min to 3 h; into a free slot, the weave time alone.
options.doc_edit: §13.3: 'A swap on the curation screen is a weave (5.6); its preview is free. Re-placing a choice law is not a weave. The generator weaves only into empty slots and never removes a law the player wove.'
options.build_change: Weaving on the server: a weave route charging §5.6, priced by the simulation's one function (TD.14). Curation's Apply calls it. The generator in sim/ (D66) takes the woven laws as fixed.

options.label: Curation is exempt (the design)
options.means: A swap on the curation screen is free and instant, as Screens v3 draws it, and the generator may re-weave any law when it makes a layout.
options.consequences: Curation becomes a free way to weave: players swap there instead of at the Spire, so §5.6's price, its times and the hour's rest apply to nobody, and the Aether sink the economy model counts is lost. The generator can replace a law the player wove for production without asking.
options.numbers: Every weave the economy model prices, 400 to 1,040 Aether a law, can be made for nothing.
options.doc_edit: §5.6: 'Swaps made on the curation screen (13.3) are free and instant.'
options.build_change: The weave route charges nothing when called from curation; the economy model drops weaving spend and is re-run.

options.label: Priced, but instant
options.means: A curation swap pays §5.6's Aether but takes no time and leaves no rest, so the flow §23.2 asks for is never broken. The generator never unweaves, as in A.
options.consequences: Keeps the Aether sink, but one act has two prices in time: a player weaves through curation to skip the Spire's wait, so §5.6's times bind only players who do not know the trick.
options.numbers: 400 to 1,040 Aether a swap; no wait.
options.doc_edit: §13.3: 'A swap on the curation screen costs a weave's Aether (5.6) and takes effect at once.'
options.build_change: As A, with the wait and the rest skipped when the weave comes from curation.

recommendation.rationale: A keeps one rule for putting a law in a slot, so the server, the simulation and the economy model price it once, and it keeps the design's instant preview, which is where the flow matters. B makes §5.6 optional for everyone; C keeps the Aether but turns the Spire's wait into a trick to avoid. Never unweaving keeps production in the player's hands, and §13.3 already has the generator weave only what helps the defender.

quotes.text: Swap a law, move a post, pick a different generated layout, name it.
Weaving costs 40 Aether per point of the law's stability cost.
Removing a law is instant, but the slot then rests for an hour before it can be woven again.
Laws raise production and decide which characters hatch

G54.also_needed: C48's open weaving rules (what a tier rise does to a woven law, whether a weave may take strain into Breaking) and C51's instant tutorial weaves, which the first generated defence would share.

G55.question: Where should the hold figure on curation and the Workshop come from, what origin does a curated defence have, and may a defence outside its band be saved?
G55.why_it_matters: Hold is a rate measured over hundreds of raids (§13.2, §13.4), and players will tune their defence to whatever number the screen shows. Screens v3 shows an instant formula as a hold, so a defence 'holding 38%' on the phone could hold far more in play, and it refuses to save outside 30–45%, a gate no section gives a curated defence. The matchmaker picks a band by the island's origin (§12.22), and nothing says which origin an edited generated defence has.
G55.today: Nothing measures hold outside the Python harness (python3 -m tools.heist_harness; D66), and the Workshop publishes without the band check (D62). The server tags every player island 'authored' (server/src/matchmaking.mjs:196, server/src/service.mjs:271) and rates a new island at the middle of its band (matchmaking.mjs prior()). No stealth-path count exists. Screens v3's curation shows 'HOLDS 38%' from a formula: a layout base, plus 2 for each tile seen on a landing's route up to three, plus a bonus per law (screens_meta.js:105-125), re-scored on every edit and on every tile of the BEST map (js:513-516). The Workshop shows '38% held · fair' (markup 517), and curation's SAVE refuses outside 30–45% (js:558).

options.label: The design: a formula, and save only in band
options.means: The phone computes a hold from the design's formula on every edit, and SAVE is refused outside 30–45% for every defence.
options.consequences: Instant, but the figure is not the hold: the harness measures §5.2's full budget at 90.6% and 95.5% at realm levels 4 and 5 (F55), whatever a formula says. A player could be refused a save for a number nobody measured, or allowed one far outside the band. A gate on saving one's own defence is a new rule (§23.5).
options.numbers: Formula: base + 2 × min(3, tiles seen) per landing + a per-law bonus (js:123).
options.doc_edit: §13.3: the formula and the 30–45% save gate.
options.build_change: The formula in the client; a band check on PUT /v1/islands/:realm.

options.label: Count live, measure on the server, warn
options.means: The screen shows §13.3's stealth-path count at once for every edit. The hold is measured on the server, 800 raids of the reference crew, queued and cached by the island's digest, and shows 'measuring…' until it lands. A curated defence keeps the generated origin while only §13.3's verbs are used, and becomes authored once its terrain is edited. A defence outside its band saves with a warning, and the matchmaker judges it against its origin's band.
options.consequences: The phone never shows an estimate as a hold. One measurement serves curation, the Workshop's publishing check (D62) and the matchmaker's prior, so hold has one home. A new layout waits for its figure, and a player can always save; an out-of-band defence is simply offered more or less often.
options.numbers: At 800 raids and a hold near 37.5%, one standard error is 1.7 points; §13.4 needs about 1,600 raids to see a 5-point shift. One measurement per distinct digest; its CPU cost is not yet measured against F47's plan.
options.doc_edit: §13.3: 'The curation preview shows the island's stealth-path count at once and its hold only once measured (13.4); it never shows an estimate as a hold. A curated defence is generated while only these verbs are used, and authored once its terrain is edited. A defence outside its band can be saved, with a warning.' §23.5: the design's formula and save gate refused.
options.build_change: Stealth paths in sim/ and the extension; the reference crew in sim/ (D66); a measurement queue on the server keyed by digest, read by curation, the Workshop's publish check and prior(); an origin column on islands.

options.label: Count live, measure on the phone
options.means: As B, but the phone runs a small batch of raids in the background and prints the hold with its error; the server still measures for the matchmaker and the Workshop.
options.consequences: A figure arrives without the network, but two measurements of one island disagree by noise, the batch costs battery, and the server's queue is needed anyway.
options.numbers: At a 37.5% hold, one standard error is 3.4 points at 200 raids and 4.8 at 100.
options.doc_edit: As B, with 'measured on the phone, its error shown'.
options.build_change: As B, plus a background batch in the extension.

options.label: Count only
options.means: Curation and the Workshop show only the stealth-path count; a defence's hold is reported later from real raids. Origin and saving as in B.
options.consequences: Cheapest and exact, but a player cannot see whether their defence sits in its band, and the Workshop's publishing check still needs a server measurement (D62).
options.doc_edit: §13.3: 'The curation preview shows the stealth-path count; the hold is reported from raids.' Origin and saving as in B.
options.build_change: Stealth paths in sim/ and the extension; only the Workshop's check uses a server measurement.

recommendation.rationale: B shows the document's own exact measure at once and a real hold when it exists, and one server measurement answers three needs that are open anyway: curation, D62's publishing check and the matchmaker's prior. It refuses nothing a player saves, so it adds no gate. A's figure is not a hold, C measures twice, and D leaves the player's band and the Workshop's check unanswered. B waits on D66's crew in the simulation.

quotes.text: About 1,600 raids per version to detect a five-point shift in hold rate with confidence
A layout is validated by counting its feasible stealth paths: fewer is harder.
Every island is tagged with its origin, so the matchmaker holds it to the right band (12.22).
with the preview re-generating fast enough not to break the flow

G55.also_needed: D66's reference crew ported into the simulation, without which the server cannot measure; and the CPU cost of 800 simulated raids per new digest against F47's plan.

G56.question: Who sets a guard post's facing and a directional feature's direction, does the Workshop sandbox keep §6.1's terrain budget, and is a Workshop island one realm?
G56.why_it_matters: A held guard sees only where it faces, so its facing decides what a defence covers; today every guard on every island faces the same way, which a raider learns once. Ramps, stairs, vines, rapids, waterfalls and tunnels cannot be placed without a direction or two ends, so six of §6.2's 39 features have no rule to build to. And §6.1's moss and terrain points, both written rules, are in no check at all.
G56.today: sim/src/lib.rs:547 posts every guard facing 270°, and an unaware guard keeps that facing (lib.rs:1748-1752); bundles carry no facing. Island::empty lays plain ground (sim/src/island.rs:249-263), moss appears only in fixtures (:750-762), and the extension writes bare ground as plain (client/ext/src/island.rs:141-145). Terrain points are counted nowhere: not in Island::check (island.rs:143-169), the extension's budget() (client/ext/src/island.rs:207-219) or the server (server/src/universe.mjs problems()), though the server knows the Spire level the Heart's budget needs (universe.mjs:129). The Workshop stores one bundle with one realm level (server/src/workshop.mjs:146-149). Screens v3 turns each post with a four-way dial ('Post 1 now faces north', screens_meta.js:552), places every feature with one tap (js:98) and shows a Workshop draft of '2 realms' (js:1163). Every option builds moss as the default ground at 1 point a tile to clear, and a TooMuchTerrain problem with the budget passed in by the server.

options.label: Write nothing new
options.means: Moss and terrain points are built as §6.1 states. The sandbox keeps the budget, since §18.6 lifts only stability. Every held guard keeps the simulation's one facing; the six directional features stay out of the builder until written; a Workshop island is one realm, as the server stores it.
options.consequences: Least to write, but every post on every island faces the same way, so a raider learns once where guards cannot see, and six features, the tunnel among them, cannot be placed.
options.numbers: 33 of 39 features placeable. Budgets: an outer realm 45 to 105 points, the Heart 50 to 140 (Spire 1 to 10).
options.doc_edit: None.
options.build_change: Moss as the default and its clearing, and terrain points in Island::check with the budget from the server; the builder hides the six features.

options.label: The owner sets them; the generator defaults (adopt the dial)
options.means: §13.3 adds 'turn a post': a held post faces one of four directions its owner sets, and the generator faces it toward the nearest shortest route from a landing edge. §6.2: the owner sets the up side of ramps, stairs and vines, a waterfall's ledge side, the rapids' downstream and a tunnel's two ends, and the generator places them by §7.10's rule against the shortest route. The sandbox keeps §6.1's budget at the island's realm level. A Workshop island is one realm.
options.consequences: Uses Screens v3's dial as drawn and gives the generator one rule for every choice it must make. The bundle gains a facing per post and a direction per feature, a rules-version change (§24.11). The editor needs a direction gesture and two taps for a tunnel, which Screens v3 does not draw.
options.numbers: Four facings, 2 bits a post, up to 3 posts (§5.2); six directional features.
options.doc_edit: §13.3: 'Swap a law, move or turn a post, …'. §12.17: a held post faces the way its owner set. §6.2: the owner sets each feature's direction and a tunnel's ends. §18.6: the sandbox keeps 6.1's terrain budget, and a Workshop island is one realm. §23.5: the dial adopted, '2 realms' refused.
options.build_change: Facing and directions in the bundle and sim/, in one rules-version bump with moss and terrain points; the generator's defaults in D66's port; the dial and a direction gesture in the editor.

options.label: Derived from the layout, never set
options.means: No dial: a held post faces the nearest shortest route from a landing edge, recomputed when the layout changes; ramps, stairs, vines and waterfalls take their up side from the heights either side. Rapids and tunnels, which cannot be derived, get an owner's direction and two ends. The sandbox and realms as in B.
options.consequences: §13.3's verbs stay as written and the bundle carries less, but the owner cannot aim a guard, a post turns when the terrain around it moves, and the editor still needs a direction gesture for rapids and tunnels.
options.numbers: Two features need an owner's choice instead of six.
options.doc_edit: §12.17: how a held post's facing is derived. §6.2: which directions follow from height. Sandbox and realms as in B. §23.5: the dial refused.
options.build_change: The derivation in sim/ (a rules-version change); the rapids' direction and a tunnel's ends in the bundle.

recommendation.rationale: Every guard needs a facing and every directional feature a direction; the only question is whose. B gives both to the owner with the generator's §7.10 rule as the default, uses a control the owner already designed, and stores each as a value the simulation and server can check. A leaves a facing raiders can learn and six features out; C hides a rule the owner can neither see nor change, and still needs B's gesture for two features. Keeping the sandbox's budget holds a Workshop island to the same rule as a home realm, and one realm is all the simulation and server carry (D71).

quotes.text: every realm is raised with moss on each tile that carries no feature, and a Keeper clears it for 1 terrain point a tile, from the same budget
Budget: an outer realm has 30 terrain points plus 15 per realm level (45 to 105). The Heart has 40 plus 10 per Spire level.
Patrols or holds its post
It is a free sandbox with every law and terrain feature the player has unlocked and no stability limit

G56.also_needed: Whether a patrol route is also the owner's to set (§12.17's 'patrols'), which this answer leaves to the generator; and the editor's direction gesture, which Screens v3 does not draw.

G57.question: How is each measure in the defender's raid report defined for one raid, what rule does each rehearsal crew follow, and when does the server record the facts the report and the Profile read?
G57.why_it_matters: §13.2 answers a low hold band by showing the defender what the defence did, but defines haul denied only over many raids and the other three measures not at all, and the simulation records none of them. §13's three rehearsal crews have names and no behaviour, so nothing can be built to them. Without definitions and a record, the defence log and the Profile can show only whether a raid held.
G57.today: sim/src/heist.rs:147-167's Outcome keeps grade, banked, capacity, caught, out, pages, cracked and left; the server's verdict adds crew (server/src/sim.mjs:103-107) and is stored in the heist row's outcome (server/src/db.mjs:164-180). No time, sighting or trigger is kept. The server re-simulates every submitted heist today (server/src/service.mjs:588), though §24 samples. The harness's crews are Careless, Competent, Optimal and Clearing (tools/heist_harness/policy.py:460-555); nothing is cautious, greedy or fast. A heist row stays when its replay is deleted (replay_gone, db.mjs:176-179). Screens v3 gives each crew one line (screens_meta.js:590), a report with 'Denied 3,300', 'Held the crew 2:31', places seen and what fired, and a log that says 'Your last 25 raids are kept here' (markup 362).

options.label: Only the verdict's facts
options.means: The report shows what the verdict already holds (outcome, what was banked of the crew's carry, crew caught and out), and §13.2's four measures wait until written. No rehearsal crew is built until §13 gives it a rule.
options.consequences: Nothing new in the simulation, but §13.2's report and §23.2's rehearsal must-shows go unbuilt, and the defender sees whether a raid held and little more, which §13.2 says is not enough at a low band.
options.doc_edit: None.
options.build_change: The defence log reads the heist row; no rehearsal.

options.label: Define each for one raid; write the facts at settlement
options.means: §13.2: denied is the clean haul a full bag would make on this island, priced as G31's answer prices carried loot, less what the raider banked; held is the seconds from the first landing to the last crew member's escape or capture; seen is each place a guard reached Alerted, named by the nearest building or feature; fired is each ward set off, bell rung and guardian Sage power used. §13: cautious waits whenever a guard could see its next tile and never runs; greedy loads until the bag is full whatever the clock; fast takes the shortest route and runs. The simulation keeps an event log, and the server writes the report's and the Profile's facts into the heist row when it settles. Log rows outlive replays, and a row says when its replay is gone.
options.consequences: Every measure has one definition the simulation computes and the server can check. The facts come out of the re-simulation the server already runs, into the row it already writes, so they add no write. If §24's sampling is ever turned on, a heist that was not re-simulated gets its facts when the defender first opens its report, while the replay is kept. The three rehearsal crews are three settings of the one reference crew D66 ports, not three new policies.
options.numbers: One heist row a raid, as now, with the facts added to its outcome. Replays kept 30 to 90 days (§24.3); rows kept after that.
options.doc_edit: §13.2: the four definitions after 'which wards fired'. §13: one sentence per crew. §24.3: 'the battle log keeps every raid's row after its replay is gone'. §23.5: 'the last 25 raids' refused.
options.build_change: TD.13's event log in sim/ (sightings, triggers, landing and end ticks), a report recorder, the crews as settings of D66's reference crew, and settle() writing the facts into the heist's outcome.

options.label: Define each, compute only when opened
options.means: The definitions and crews as in B, but nothing is written at settlement: the report is re-simulated from the replay when the defender opens it, and cached.
options.consequences: Settlement is unchanged, but the Profile's records need the facts of every raid, which C never has, and a report not opened before its replay is deleted (30 to 90 days) can never be made.
options.numbers: One extra re-simulation per report opened.
options.doc_edit: As B, without the §24.3 line.
options.build_change: As B, with a report route that re-simulates on first open instead of settle() writing facts.

recommendation.rationale: B defines each measure once, in terms the simulation already tracks, and records it in the run and the row the server already makes, so the report, the defence log and the Profile read one record. A leaves §13.2's promise unmet; C saves nothing today, because every heist is already re-simulated, and loses the Profile's records. The crew sentences are proposals, and writing them as settings of D66's crew keeps one policy to maintain.

quotes.text: After every raid the defender's report shows how much of the haul the defence denied, how long it held the crew up, where the crew was seen and which wards fired, not only whether it held.
A rehearsal sends one of three simulated crews (cautious, greedy or fast) against the universe as it stands and shows the route it took, where it was seen and what it carried out.
Validation is sampled, not universal
Raw replays and logs are kept 30 to 90 days, long enough for validation and analysis, then aggregated and discarded.

G57.also_needed: Whether 'seen' also counts a guard that only grew Suspicious, which would name more places per raid; and G69's definitions of held and records, which read these facts.

F57.question: Should Screens v3's Shop, Starpass and gifts be drawn in money as F41's answer says, and what monthly gift limit should §22.4 state?
F57.why_it_matters: Every ✦ line in the design breaks §22.1's and §19.12's rule that every price shows in real money, and the build has sold no Starglass since F41 was answered, so the Shop and Season cannot be drawn from the design as they stand. §22.4 promises a monthly gift limit and gives no number, so the build has none: an adult can send any number of gifts and a minor can receive any number. The design's gift sheet also tells every band 'a parent approves first' and sends a gift with no friend chosen and nothing paid. Your fix brief to the designer asks for cosmetics 'priced in Starglass only (9.5)' (screen-review.md:30), and your handoff lists Starglass among the player's resources (README.md:162); both restate v3.5 and record no reversal of F41's answer C. Intent, not an answer.
F57.today: server/src/shop.mjs sells each cosmetic and each season's premium track as its own store product at the store's price (PREMIUM_PRICE 600 cents, §22.1's about €6); there is no balance and no pack (F41 C, built). A gift is the same product bought for a friend and is refused unless the two are friends ('gifts_go_to_friends'). A minor's gift counts against §20.2's €25 or €50 cap, and a gift's intent is kept 30 days so a family approval that arrives late still reaches the friend (GIFT_KEEP_DAYS). Nothing counts gifts sent or received. client/scripts/shop_screen.gd and track_screen.gd show money prices, with Buy, Give and a friend picker. Screens v3 prices everything in ✦: a pill '480 = €4.80 +', tiles '120 ≈€1.20', packs of 100 to 5,000 ✦ at €1 to €50, 'Starglass never expires', a Starpass 'Buy for 600 Starglass' with no money figure, and 'GIFT · 3 left this month', which on a tap says 'Gift sent to Ines · a parent approves first' to every band (screens_meta.js:718, 819). v3.6 still sells Starglass in §9.1, §9.5, §18.2 and §22.1.

options.label: Money, with §20.2's caps as the only limit
options.means: Every ✦ line becomes the store's local price for that item; the packs, the balance pill and 'never expires' go. A gift picks a friend and is paid like a purchase. §22.4's 'monthly limit' is read as §20.2's spending caps: a minor's gifts count in their €25 or €50, and an adult has no gift limit. Approval words show only for a 13-to-15 whose family approval is set up.
options.consequences: Nothing new on the server. An adult can send any number of gifts, and a minor can receive any number from friends, adults included, since invites carry no age check (G35). §22.4's 'monthly limit' then means nothing for adults.
options.numbers: Caps €25 (13 to 15) and €50 (16 and 17), counted in each product's euro list price (§20.2, server/src/facts.json). Premium track 600 cents, about €6 (§22.1).

D86.question: Which of Screens v3's friend features ship at launch: none, preset pings between friends only, or pings with presence, live activity and Beacon posts for players 16 and over?
D86.why_it_matters: Each changes what a player can see or do, which §23.5 says a design cannot add, and none has a rule for 13-to-15s, a cap or a notification. Presence and last seen are new personal facts that §20.5 asks the game not to collect, and 'Raiding Ines' names a target while the raid runs, which §17.8 forbids. Until this is decided, Friends and the Share sheet cannot be drawn from the design. Your handoff lists 'friends' presence and feed' among the server data the prototype fakes (README.md:168), and puts 'Who's online', 'preset pings' and add-by-code on Friends (SCREENS.md:171) and 'post the clip to the Beacon' on Share (SCREENS.md:166). It is your clearest statement for option C. Intent, not an answer: §23.5 builds none of it until the document says what each shows.
D86.today: server/src/friends.mjs has 7-day single-use invites, the friend list, removal, friendly heists, challenge links and the feed: settled heists from the last 7 days, none with a 13-to-15 on either side (G35 B) and none involving a block. Nothing records presence, last seen or activity, there are no pings, and GET /v1/heists/:token/replay serves only the raider and the defender (server/src/http.mjs:11). client/scripts/friends_screen.gd draws the list and the feed. Screens v3's Friends shows '3 online', ONLINE and OFFLINE sections, 'Seen 3 h ago', RAIDING, WORKSHOP and HOME pills, Kofi 'Raiding Ines', and SEND A PING with 'Good heist!', 'Rematch?', 'Raid me!' and 'Nice defence!', the same for 13 to 15 (screens_meta.js:1241-1285). Its Share sheet offers 'Post to the Beacon' to every band and grades moments EPIC, RARE and LEGENDARY (js:1221-1229).

options.label: None at launch (the document as written)
options.means: Friends shows the list, invites, the feed and friendly heists, as built. No presence, last seen, activity pills or pings. The Share sheet shares as §20.7 sets by band, with no 'Post to the Beacon' and no moment grades. No status names a raid's target while it runs.
options.consequences: Friends is quieter than the design. Nothing new is collected, written or moderated, and the server does not change. Pings can come in 1.1 with co-op heists, where §20.7 already puts preset pings, beside constellation chat (§17.1).
options.doc_edit: §23.5 'Where the screens differ', two rows: 'Friends | Online and offline, last seen, a live status naming a raid's target, preset pings | The list, invites and the feed; no presence and no pings | 17.6, 17.8, 20.2' and 'Share sheet | Post to the Beacon; moments graded Epic, Rare and Legendary | Sharing by 20.7's bands; no posts and no grades | 17.6, 24'.
options.build_change: None on the server. TD.23 draws Friends and Share on the design without them.

options.label: Preset pings only
options.means: As A, plus the design's four preset pings from one friend to another, at every band (§20.2 gives 13-to-15s preset phrases), up to a daily cap, seen on the Friends screen and never pushed. A block hides them (§17.8).
options.consequences: Friends can nudge each other with no free text, so nothing needs a filter or review. A message channel opens before 1.1's chat and co-op, with its own cap, retention and deletion. 'Raid me!' and 'Rematch?' point to friendly heists, which take nothing and move no Renown (F48).
options.numbers: 4 phrases (screens_meta.js:1258). The cap is the owner's, for example one ping per friend a day. One row written per ping, against F47's writes budget.
options.doc_edit: §17.6: a row 'Pings | Four preset messages to a friend, at most N a day, seen in the game and never sent as a notification | Active and personal'. §20.7: 'Pings between friends | Preset | Preset | Preset'. §23.5 as A for presence and the Share sheet.
options.build_change: server: a pings table (from, to, phrase, at) kept 7 days like the feed and deleted with an account (server/privacy.json); POST /v1/friends/:id/ping, refused for non-friends, blocks and past the cap; the friends view returns pings received. Client: the ping row on a friend's sheet.

options.label: The design for 16 and over, without targets
options.means: B's pings for everyone. Presence (online, last seen) and activity (Home, Workshop, Raiding, never with a target) shown to friends by adults who choose it and 16-to-17s who turn it on, never by 13-to-15s (§20.2's Private profile). Players 16 and over may post a heist to the Beacon as its replay, which friends watch while the replay is kept; 13-to-15s cannot (G35). Moment grades are dropped, since no rule sets them.

raids are anonymous while they happen
Collect only what's needed to run the game
Friends only, preset pings
